WHEN at Chester, Handel, the great musician, got together a band, whom he had been assured could "sing at sight," to try his manuscript. •On the trial of the c'norous in the "Messiah," "And with his stripes we are healed," the principal singer, named Janson, after. attempting his part several times, failed so egregiously that Handel burst into a rege, and, after vociferating in four or five languages, exclaimed in broken English, "You schauntrel I tit you not tell me dat you could sing at soite 2" "Yes, sir," replied the unfortunate basso, "and so I can; but not at first sight." THE late Duke of York once remarked to Colonel W. at the mess of the 11th Regiment that the colonel was uncqmraonly bald, and, although a younger man than His Royal Highness, he stood more in need of a wig. The colonel, who had been of very long standing in the service, and whose promotion had been by no means rapid, informed His Royal Irghness that his baldness could be very easily accounted for. "In what manner," asked His Royal Highness, rather eagerly. .To which Colonel W. replied, "By junior officers stepping over my head." The Duke was so pleased with the reply that the gallant colonel obtained promotion In a few days afterwards.

After her marriage to Lord Hartington, the Duchess of Manchester will continue to be known by her preserit title. Her intention, in fact, is to retain until her lordly husband's accession to the " dukeage," when, of course, she will take that of the Duchess of Devonshire.

Prominent among the celebrities not at the Royal English Opera on Saturday was Mr. W. S. Gilbert, who turned up at the renovated S. James's. Why is this? People were under the impression that our only composer and our one librettist had fallen upon each other's necks and kissed, and become fast friends again.

Alderman Manfield, who is mentioned asthe prob- able Liberal 'candidate for Mr. Bradlaugh's seat in Northampton, is a large shoe manufacturer. He has a score of shops in London, his shoes are for sale on the boulevards in Paris, and he has shops in every large town. He has been Mayor of Northamp- ton, and is a very popular man, and is well spoken of by the Tories.

In spite of the threatened opposition of the Board of Trade, Sir Edward Watkin proposes to press for- ward his Bill authorising the continuance of experi- mental works with the Channel Tunnel. The Bill is not yet printed, but it will be found that it does not differ in any form from that of last year. It will be backed by Sir Edward Watkin, Mr. Illing- worth, and Mr. Maclure.

After a great deal of -correspondence in the " Times " to which the Clerk of the House of Com- mons lent valuable aid, it has been decided to affix a tablet in Westminster Hall at the spot where King Charles I. stood when on his trial. There was con- siderable disputation about the exact spot, but I think the authorities are now agreed, and this im- portant landmark in English history will be defi- nitely fixed.

Eleven hundred purses or portemonnaies were left behind in public vehicles within the Metropolitan Police District during 1889; and what is stranger little more than half of their careless owners troubled themselves to inquire after their property in Scotland Yard. Perhaps they had no faith in the honesty of cabdrivetis and conductors. If so, the fact that so many cases were duly reported ought to put them to shame.

Last year a new rule respecting presentations at Drawing-rooms was promulgated. Formerly, if a lady went to a Drawing-room she could present any .number of persons, but ncikv she is limited to one in each year, excepting only her own daughters and daughters-in-law. The Queen now contemplates introducing another restriction, and it is proposed that ladies should be allowed to present only per- sons with whom they have personal acquaintance, and whom they are in the habit of visiting.

The Church of England has suffered another serious loss in the death of Bean Plumptre, Dean of Wells, which took place on Sunday. The Dean,who was in his seventieth year was one of the most scholarly men in the Church. He was a man of great versatility, and outside his theological works he won distinction in several branches of literature. He translated Dante and the old Grecian plays, and he won admiration as a poet. One of his best and latest works was his life of Bishop Ben, published in 1882.

The " SpePker " remarks upon Mr. Chamberlain's "reversion to the Toryism of his youth." This will surprise many persons, who will imagine that the writer has fallen into some mistake. The expres- sion, however, is a perfectly accurate one. I am creditably informed that one of the first public acts of Mr. Chamberlain was to canvass against the late Mr. Bright at Birmingham at a time when the lat- ter was denouncing the hereditary branch of the Legislature, and protesting against what he des- cribed as "outdoor relief to the aristocracy."

The O'Shea probate suit, respecting which I con- stantly see allusions in the newspapers, is this : Mrs. Wood, an aunt of Mrs. O'Shea, died leaving about £160,000. She had been long in infirm health. Some years ago she made a will, or rather to speak more correctly, a will was made for her by a sort of conseil de famille, by which she left £130,000 to Mrs. O'Shea, and divided the rest amongst her nephews and nieces. She then went to live near Mrs. O'Shea, who looked after her. Later on, she added a codicil to this will, by which she left all her money to Mrs. O'Shea.

General Booth scores again. After all the critic- ism lavished on the scheme," Mr. Bancroft announces that he is going to send his promised £l,OOO, and this notwithstanding that ninety-nine other doners of the same amount have not been iodnd. Those who come forward in response to Mr, Danoroft's offer do the same. Now, •Mr. Ban- croft is something more than a xetired actor. He is a man of the world, a man of society, and, above all, a man of business who has made the biggest pile ever made in his line.. For these reasons we regard the opinion of one Bancroft as worth more than that of fifty iluxleys.

It is a noteworthy fact, that while the amend- ments moved by Welsh members on the Tithes Bill on Monday were uniformly supported by the votes of between twenty and thirty members for Wales and Monmouthshire, the Government were oxly able to persuade one representative from the Prin- cipality (Alderman Maine) to vote against any of them. The point is significant as showing both the *complete unanimity of the Welsh members and the total failure of the Government to appreciate the real sentiments, as expressed by their representa- tives, of the localities in the interest of which the Bill was avowedly introduced. .

• The progress of total abstinence in dinner-giving circles causes a certain amount of embarrassment now and then. If the person invited does not happen to be aware that his woulkd-be-hosts are total abstiners,and do not give wine to their guests, he is apt to experience, a slight chill of disappoint- ment when the lemonade and iced water are handed round. It may be presumed that emotion the reverse of pleasurable has, on occasion, depicted it- self perfectly distinctly upon the Countenances of diners who are accustomed to drink wine, for it is now proposed that all invitations to wineless dinners are to be accompanied by a small bow of blue ribbon securely fastened to the card.

A-paper of great interest to all Biblical students I was read on Tuesday evening at the Victotia Insti- tute, by Mr. Boscawen, of the British Museum. Ile has translated a Babylonian inscription which proves to be a prayer of King Assurnazirpal, of the nipeteenth century before Christ, or five hundred years before the time of Moses. The imagery and the phraseology are almost identical with many of the most beautiful passages of the Psalms of Israel. The prayer is addressed to Istar, that queen of heaven whose worship the Hebrew prophets so fre- quently denounced. Yet it breathes a high spiritual religion, a devotional spirit of the purest order, such as it has been the habit to consider the exclu- sive characteristic of the Hebrews among the Semi- tic nations.

"Mr. Punch's " cartoon this week, drawn by Mr. Tenniel in his vigorous and characteristic style, represents Mr. Gladstone in the jauntiest of atti- tudes and the sprucest of walking attire, replying to the rumour that he. is about to retire. His hat is slightly on one side, his left hand rests upon his hip, his right grasps his umbrella walking-stick fashion, while he is supposed to be saying "Retire! —What do you think ?" Accompanying the sketch is the new. "Song of the Session" or " What do you think?" as "sung by that-Eminent and Evergreen Lion Comique 'Jolly Glad,' at the St. Stephens Hall of Varieties." It concludes with the lines : I regret, so much, to tease them! My last exit would much ease them. But Retire !—and just to please them ! What do you think ? [Winks and walks round.]

The family contest both wills on the ground of incapacity, and claim that Mrs. Wood ought to be considered to have died intestate, in which case the money would be equally divided between the n ep- hews and nieces. By a clause in Mr. and Mrs. O'Shea's marriage settlement, all moneys inherited by either form plrt of the settlement, which ereates only a life interest to Mr. and Mrs. O'Shea 41 them, with remainder to the children. In the codicil it is 6xo rnetsos stated that Mrs. Wood's money is not to g itYhe settlement,- but in all probability this would not override the Conditions of the settlement. If this be so, the court would have to decide how the life interest is to be divided between Mr. and Mrs. O'Shea, and as the divorce was pronounced against the lady, and the custody of the children is given to the husband, it seems as though Mrs. O'Shea would not personally take much by either will.

"Why working-men do not go to church," is a question that still rages in Newcastle. Reasons, if we may trust the numerous correspondents who have come forward to solve the problem,are "plenty as blackberries." Besides those lately cited, it has been suggested that working-men absent themselves from public worship, because ministers talk of religion in so irrational a way; because there are in church so many hypocritical people; because the clergy betray a lack of sympathy with working-class views; because the pulpits ar6 "the source of un- believable dogma ;" because ministers are cold and formal, and because a great deal of caste feeling reveals itself in church. The "dogs-in-the-manger in pews "are also mentioned. The latest expression of opinion, however, lays the change that has cone over working-men's church-going habits entirely at the door of Mr. Forster's Education Act. It is, ac- cording to his correspondent, the" three R's" that have done it.

Did that stand to their credit? (Laughter.) Did they call that progress? (Laughter.) If that was not an illustration of the Irishman's rise, he did not know what was. (Laughter and applause.) He considered, in view of the circumstances that they were perfectly entitled to count eight hours as a day's work, and be paid for overtime and a half on Sunday and time and a quarter other days. The speaker concluded by the local railway servants present to do their ut- most by making their branches stronger, and in other ways,to remove the reproach of indifference cast against them. The resolution was unanimously carried. , Mr. LEVI JtarEs then proposed :—" That we are also ' of opinion that in order to carry out the former resolu- tion, we should all become members of the Amalgamated I Society of Railway Servants." The speaker excited ' considerable interest by referring to the harsh conduct of certain officials who did not study the interests of the shareholders or of the men. • Mr. BIECHALL seconded, and this motion was also un- animously'agreed to. A vote of thanks passed to the Chairman, and his ac- knowledgment, closed the proceedings. A collecEion, which was made in support of the men on strike, realized £2 17s. Old.

div.head: RAILWAY SERVANTS' MEETING AT THE PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: RAILWAY SERVANTS' MEETING AT THE PUBLIC HALL.

A public meeting in connection with the Amal- gamated Society of Railway servants was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Sunday afternoon. Therawas a large attendance of the class immedi- ately concerned in the object of the meeting. Councillor Dixon presided, and was supported on the platform by Messrs. A. Mear (organising secre- tary of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Ser- vants), John Walker, Thomas Birchall, L. James, W. Bullock, &c.

The CHAIRMAN, in the course of his opening remarks, observed that some of those connected with railways ap- peared to think that men could stand work at all hours and for any number of hours. This sort of thing had gone On to such an alarming extent that a vast number not only of those employed on railways but others, felt that the time had come Rhen some means should be adopted whereby there should be some fair and reason- able limit fixed to the number of hours worked by railway employes. - (Applause.) The limitation of hours had been adopted in a great many works with the ut- niost success, during the period he had indicated. When he adopted it in his . &en case he was told he would never get his work done, and he said what he could not get done would have to remain undone ; but he held that if men were worked qinr fah; and reasonable hours, they would stick to their work and employers would get for them all the services they required. He soon found that he could get more work from men working 54 hours a week than from men working 70 tO 75. He contended that there were men holding situations on the railway system who ought not to be worked above-nine hours on any occasion. A man ought not, for instance on any account, to be compelled to stand upon an engine for 14, 16, or 19 hours. He remembered that when a collision took place on the Great Eastern six months age, that it was stated that a man had been on duty on the engine for 13 hours. Was it right that a man should have to stand the heat and the strain of work on an engine for 13 hours ? Would it not be more reasonable that another man should take his place at the end of nine hours. He concluded by urging all railway servants present who had not joined the Union to do so, and thus advance their own interests while also supporting the cause of their brethren throughout the country. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN WALKER then proposed the following resolu- tion :—" That this meeting sympathises with the Scotch railway men in their efforts to secure a ten hours' day, and will use every effort to give them moral and finan- cial support." He remarked that the very fact of their attendance there on Sunday to give expressions to their sympathy with the workmen who were out on strike in Scotland was in itself suggestive of a grievance amongst railway men. (Hear, hear.) There was not another class in the community that was so situated, in point of having so little opportunity of coming together, and that was the apology, if apology were needed, for holding a public meeting on Sunday. He himself was so much of a Sabbatarian that he should like to see two Sundays in a week. (Laughter.) But railway men were a very long way from that when they had to consider whether the limit of their work should be ten hours a day. He could not but feel a sense of repulsion that they should have to discuss this matter at all. In this country the hours had been nine per day for workmen generally for some years, and yet the class who had the lives of a large propertion of the nation constantly in their hands, met, at this period of the 19th century, on a Sunday afternoon to discuss whether their day should be one of ten hours. In the face of the steady profits that railway companies were making and the services rendered by this large body of men so. steadily and so diligently, and in the main with such successful results, it was to the 'discredit of these- companies that the matter should still have to be dis cussed. (Applause.) It was doubtful sometimes whether' it VMS wise to interfere between labour and capital, but railway- companies were: ordinary business men or tradesmen! They were' specially privileged by the legislature to do a special. thing; they were monopolists established by the- legislature. It was therefore the duty of the legislature to see not only that the public were protected so far as the operations of this monopoly was concerned, but also that the servants of these companies were protected. (Applause.) In Scotland, so far as he could see and hear, the case was very bad. Theservice was in some instances undermanned; that meant of course that the men were . underpaid, and the grievances had been so great that Professor Blackie,and other men who would take no part in other workmen's disputes had stepped out of their ordinary way in order to declare that, after looking at the facts, they believed the Scotch strikers had cause of complaint. It was the duty of those present to came forward under the circumstances and give these men their moral and financial help. (Applause.) He thought, the very least the railway companies could do was to pay the extra hours of their servants as over- time. The profits of the railway companies throughout the United Kingdom during the past six years had been. an average of 33 millions a year. In 1889 their toter receipts were £73,000,000 and their working expenses. £40,000,000, leaving a margin to divide amongst share- holders of £33,000,000. Under such circumstances the expense of payment for overtime was as related to the £33,000,000 so infinitesimally small that it was disgrace- ful to the railway companies to refuse it. (Applause.) There was another point. Just in proportion as Parlia- ment had interfered for the protection of the public had loss of life and injuries to person on, railways been reduced. Every precaution taken had, despite the cry that it would involve more cost to the companies, had a satisfactory result. The dividends had not gone down, and the companies' business had expanded. The speaker concluded by putting it to railway servants whether in view of the facts he had adduced of the proceedings in Scotland it would not be better to consider as to having a concerted strike throughout the United Kingdom, a strike which he was convinced would not last a week. (Loud applause.) Mr. MALKIN seconded the resolution. He expressed the opinion that the 15 to 19i hours a day worked by railway servants were enough to tax the strongest con- stitutions. Trades unionism, he remarked, was taking such large and wide steps that the capitalists were be- coming awake to the fact that mutiny existed among the British workmen ; and was it not time that there should be a mutiny P The speaker commented on the long hours of railway servants, and urged the meeting to extend all the assistance it could to those who were fighting such a noble battle in Scotland. He resumed-, his seat amidst considerable applause. Mr. MEAR supported the resolution. He said he felt with the mover that it was not creditable that they in the 19th century should be talking about the hours ques- tion in the way they were. (Applause.) However, British workmen had begun to move, and Englishmen in particular whenever they began to move they did not stop until they had accomplished something. (Applause.) Mr. Meer mentioning his experiences amongst the Scotch strikers, said no one could possibly conceive what was going on amongst them unless he heard and saw for himself what they had to contend with. It was certainly a standing discredit that they should have been obliged to work 144 hours before they would allow anything for overtime. 18 hours work in a day was a very common thing then, and the Board of Trade returns showed that in Scotland on the Caledonian,North British,Gla,sgow and South Western lines 84,290 instances had occurred in which railway men had worked from 12 to 18 hours' and , upwards, taking two months only. -("Shame.") If the railway servants had furnished these reports they would have been cried down as exaggerated, but the companies had supplied the figures, and what was against them- selves they did not overdraw. (Loud applause.) The speaker read the points of the National Hours programme adopted at Hull, in 1889,which fixed the general hours of duty for railway men at ten per day and rates of pay for overtime, the meeting showing its 'approval of the conditions by hearty applause. Throughout his twelve months' travels, over 11,000 miles, as a speaker on behalf of the Amalgamated Society ' Mr Mear said, he had only known one hand to be held up against this programme. (Applanse.) Mr.Schwa.nn, M.P., a very large railway shareholder, had in his hear- ing, said he should not have been surprised had the rail- way servants in addition to going in for a reduction of their hours of labour also gone in for an increase of wage considering the large dividends the raflway com- panies were making. (Renewed applause.) A report showing the financial position of our railways in 1889 showed that whila more went to increase wages and ex- penses with regard to materials there were still l mil- lions over and above what had been created the previous year. That showed that-Mr. Schwann knew what he was talking about, that he knew there was a surplus from which the men could be paid more if they were to ask for it, and seeing that they only asked for a reduction in hours this was certainly the time for them to go in for the other—(applause)—because it is quite clear that it could be done,and if they were of the same mind as he was they would never rest till it was done. (Applause.) The majority of the railway companies had disapproved or rejected all proposals made to them; and since they had done, and refused to agree to a ten hours day, let the next programme be nothing short of an eight hours day all round. Some might think that asking too

div.head: JOHN WARRINGTON WOOD.
div.p: JOHN WARRINGTON WOOD.

The following is the substance of an article which appears inCasselfs "Magazine of Art" for February. It is from the pen of Mr. T. Wilmot, and it is beau- tifully illustrated. It may be metioned that " St. Michael overcoming Satan," and the "Sisters of Bethany "which are referred to in the article are to be seen in the Warrington Art gallery, besides several busts, and copies of other works ; John Warrington Wood cannot be said to belong to the English school of sculpture. Though he re- ceived his early training at the School of Art at Warrington, his native place, he developed his style in Rome, where he came under the influence of John Gibson, and, in spite of his qualified admiration of Bernini, his artistic sympathies were with the fol- lowers of Canova, the inheritprs of the decaying tradition of classical Greece. A marked revival of the art of sculpture took place in England during his lifetime. But lie played n.o part in the move- ment, and kept aloof in his Roman studio from the storm and stress of his own generation. Living as he did in Italy, he was, perforce. impressed by the consummate style of Denatello, the dignity and grandeur of Michel Angelo; but he looked beyond these masters, further into the past, and got his inspiration from the Greeks and their imitators. His art, no less than the art of Canova and Thor- waldsen, lacks vigour and individuality. He was born, of humble parentage, at Warrington in 1839, and received his early training at the local School of Art. His career as a student was distin- guished, and before he was twenty-two he had won more medals than usually tall to the lot of the youthful sculptor. He exhibited his first original work, a study entitled "Spring," in 18V2; and from this time his success was assured. A few years later he established himself in Rome, and though he paid frequent visits to his birthplace, Italy was his home until his death. His energy was indefatigable, and the list of his waks is along one. His fame rests upon his ideal statues, but he received many com- missions for portraits, and is said to have executed no less than sixty busts. Few have met with more uniform succe3B and good fortune. Once, after an: attack of Roman fever, he was threatened with. blindness, but happily the disastervfas averted, and his sureness of vision was preserved until his death. His first substantial triumph was in 1871. In that year he exhibited a statue of " Eve 'at South Ken- sington, which failed to attract a purchaser. Some citizens of Warrington, however, proud of the'x fellow-townsman's achievement, resolved to give him his opportunity, and having collected a thou-- sand pounds, commissioned him to work his will for his own and his town's glory. At the" same time Mr. A. B. Walker bought the "Eve," who was al- ready packed for her return journey to Rome. The next few years were devoted to unremiOng toil. In 1874 Wood completed a statue of " Elisha the Tishbite In 1877:his colossal " St. Michael over- coming Satan "was set up at Warringten. The block of marble from- which this was chiselled was selected from the quarries-by the sculptor himself. It was known as the "Pearl of Carrara, and .was of, so stupendouA a size that fiyarteen buffaloes- with two cream-coloured Chttpagna omen at their head were necessary to drag.it to the- studio. The works by winch 'Warrington Wood has gained the greater share of hie. public recognition are the statues of Ra.phael: and: Michelangelo which stand at the entranced' the Walker Art Gallery at Liverpool. The site is-appropriate, for Sir Andrew Walker was one of his earliest patrons. Among other examples of hisart, which are doubtless fami- liar to our readers, are "The Sisters of Bethany," "Proserpina" (scared by Plut4 while gathering flowers in the Elysian: fields), "-Samson Killing the Lion," and "Oberon and Titania.° In 1876 Wood carved a medallion of the poet Keats, to whose- honour in the Protestant cemetery at Rome there. was no other memorial than the-atone graven with the words, "here lies one whosename was writ in water." With great generosity the sculptor pre- sented his relief as a free gift, and it was unveiled with much circumstance by Sir Vincent Eyre. Mr. Joseph Severn, who had watched over the poet dur- ing his last illness, paid the following tribute to the accuracy of the likeness: "I went this morning," he wrote to Wood, "to see your medallion, and I was enchanted not only to find such an admirable like- ness, but also such a fine example of your sculpture in the great taste and skill you have bestowed en it. No doubt it will always do you honour, not only as an example of art, but as your fine tribute to the memory of the post. I cannot venture to say how much I was affected by the sight of this monument, and how much it goes beyond my warmest expecta- tions."

-1ii1877 Warrington Wood received the highest 1 honour which can be conferred upon an artist in Rome. He was elected a member of the ancient and famous Guild of St. Luke, an academy which was founded in Rome in 1593, and which was an imita- tion of the still more ancient guild established in Florence in the fourteenth century. The distinction of membership of this guild has not often been con- ferred Upon British sculptors or painters, and in the case of Warrington. Wood it was a recognition that he was worthily banding on the Roman tradition. It was anticipated at the time that the English Royal Academy would follow the lead of the Guild of St. Luke. Butt he was not a frequent exhibitor at Burlington House, and though some discussion took place as to who should propose and second him at the Academy, other counsels prevailed, and he never received official recognition in London. Nor does the slightest blame attach to the Academicians. Warrington Wood sympathised warmly with the aims of the Italian sculptors of his time, buirhe can scarcely be said to have been in touch with his Eng- lish contemporaries. As has already been stated, Warrington Wood's studio in 1871 was in the Piazza Trinith dei Monti.. In 1874 things had so prospered with him that he was able to purchase the Villa Campana, near St. John Lanteran. The villa was built in a severely classical style,- and the' great sculpture gallery bad once held the treasures of the ill-fated Marchese Campana. His treasures were dispersed, and his villa Sold to Warrington Wood, under whose aus- pices it soon became the favourite retort of the artists and connoisseurs of Rome. For Wood was not only a sculptor; he was a man of extraordinary personal charm, and his circle of friends was wide and distinguished. Few Englishmen went to Rome without visiting the most genial and kind-hearted of sculptors. Mr;Luke Fildes, Mr. Alma-Tadema, the Howitts, and many whose names are familiar to all were among his intimates. One of his oldest friends, Rev. Dr. Macduff of Chislehurst, at the request of Mrs. Wood has briefly set down his reniiniscences,:of .the sculptor. The account will give the reader a far' clearer view of the man than either the contemplation of his works or the expression of critical opinion could hope to do, ' and no excuse is needed for printing it in full. "It was in the early spring of 1871," writes Dr. Macduff, " in one of the old Palazzos on the Corso, at one of those delightful and social art reunions, which many Roman visitors know so well, that I had the pleasure of my first introduction to War- rington Wood. This deepened into a sacred.friend- ship of fifteen years, only terminated with his death. "I took in that evening at a glance all he subse- quently proved to be. He was in the prime of early manhood, a remarkable.presvce, a genial counten- ance, a round hazel eye, soft and kindly, but which in hisstudio, when watching the progress ot one of his clay models Or after putting some crucial touch, lighted up in flashes of fire I never saw equalled. Many a time have I been the privileged spectator of these working hours with their enthusiasm of genius.' Like all great craftsmen, he was always happiest at his work. I remember his first visiting me on the shores of a Scdttish lake where rest had

been enjoined on him as imperative, and both clay and tools were left behind. But the genial cur- rent' was irrepressible. The clay procurable in the district was of the most unsatisfactory kind—it mattered not. The best that could be had was sifted, and with extemporised tools and the deft fingers, which were over his best auxiliaries, Elijah the Tishbite ' took its first visible form; the great statute which became the toil and triumph of many subsequent months in the Villa Campana. Though not his happiest effort, The Little Maid that waited on Naaman's Wife' struggled into life on the same spot and occasion.

" One thing it;ick me more than once. He was not so much the born artist as the born sculptor. He was great in form. I would not by any means say he was defective in colour. But the beauty of a Highland landscape or the glory of a setting sun were to him little compared to the contour of a human countenance, or the grace of a female hand and arm.

"As to the charm of his friendship I dare not trust myself to speak. He seeined to carry sun- shine all th 3 day long. His conversation was full of sparl-le, with a sort of chronic determination to enjoy every one and everything. The man was, as is often the case with the truly great, greater than his works.

"To one sister art h 6 was devotedly, nay pas- sionately .attached. His organ was an ever favourite resort in the villa : nor can I forget the day when that organ, before being transplanted to its Roman home, was temporarily erected in a drawing-room in London. He was proud of its amply-tested .power, for Gounod was himself on the occasion the player of his own masterpieces. "I cannot attempt in so limited a space to trace his future career. Broken health (possibly the penalty of too indefatigable labour) came at last, farther chequered by those disappointments inevitable to true workers, who think more of their art than of themselves. The last time we met I spent some hours with him in London when en- gaged on his Wallace statue. His hand had by no means lost its cunning, but his physical powers were sorely impaired. He was no longer the agile friend who in the glory of manhood had been wont to make little of long summer rambles on Ben Lo- mond and Ben Venue. I saw too evidently our dreams of visiting together Horace's Villa, near Tivoli, were never to be realized. " I received with profound emotion the tidings of his death, Rome and Warrington were that day , rarely sympathetic in their sorrow. Mis Roman workmen, who adored him, wept like children. We all felt that one the world could ill spare had pre- maturely left us. His widow, who survives, abun- dantly shared the testhetic tastes of him she mourns. In more senses than one she and her de- ceased mother were true fellow-helpers. • "One of Lord Tennyson's last lines is inscribed on his tombstone in Warrington Cemetery :
His faith and work were bells of one-accord.'"

Warrington Wood died suddenly as.the year 1880 was hastening to its close. His last commission was a statue of the Queen, and of uhis lie had just cora- pleted the clay model. His career was- fortunate and unforeseen. lie began life as a skilled artisan, and his talent for sculpture was revealed by an ac- cident. A bank was being built at Warrington, and a workman defaulting, Wood took his place and executed a design in stone which at once attracted notice. But nature had endowed him with the rare gift of winning and keeping friends, and,Beth in his own country and at Rome he enjoyed an extra- ordinary popularity. He will be remembersd no less for his personal charm and his ready intelli- gence than for his skill and taste as a sculptt-r..
.....-e_.__ RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The racaithly meeting was held at the Town :Ail, onTaesday. Rev. Canon Maitland Wood presided,. and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, .Dr. McDougall, Messrs. J. J. Howitt, S. Taylor, and A. SAlkel4, with Mr. G. Moss (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

The School Attendance Committee reported that the visitors returns for the three weeks ending January 23rd showed a falling off in the average attendance of nearly Eve per cent., as compared with the corresponding period last-year. This was attributttd to the severe weather,. which had greatly affected the attendance of infants, and. the prevailing distress caused by frost. The Committee considered these reasons satisfactory.—Dr. MoDougek asked 'how the distress affected the attendance at school. —Dr. eastaldi said the reasons set forth were correct. The terrible weather and the poverty of the parents had brought the attendance very low. Many parents could not abtain proper clothing for their children, and it would have been cruel to allow them to go through the streeta- half-ciad:—The Clerk said many parents had been out of work a-nd'unable to pay the fees, and many applications had been made tc), the Guardians, but the frost had do- parted before their cases could be dealt with.—Dr. McDougall said if there was no better explanation, he had, nothing Farther to say.—The minutes were passed.
THE ETENING CyAssEs AND PRIZES.

The School Management recommended that a sum not exceeding.Ls, be expended in prizes for Greenway-road , Etening School. Dr. McDougall moved the adoption of the minute, and said it was not intended that the prizes should be a- premium on attendance, but were intended for -those students who-passed the examination and dis- played exceptional merit. It was hoped that these prizes would infuse a spirit of emulation amongst the boys, and encouragethem to persevere with their studies.—Mr. j. J. Flowitt seconded the motion.—Dr. Grstaldi moved an amendment that the subject be deferred until the end of• the scholastic year, when they would know the financial positihn of the evening classes. He considered it would be injudicious- to vote the prizes now.—Dr. McDougall, pointed out that the Board need not spend ss. in prizes if they believed they were not deserved. An estimate I was submitted to the Committee which showed that the.; Board would be in pocket at the end of the school year;l —The Clerk said looking at the matter from a purely finan--1 cial point of view the figures presented showed a great. probability that the voting of this £5 would not be lost- to the Board, because there was a tendency as the season• opened, for the attendance to fall off. They desired the boys to attend the examination, and earn the graut for the Board. The offer of prizes would no doubt induce a larger and more regular attendance, cause the boys to work harder, and by -passing the examination earn a larger grant.—De. Gastaldi said it spoke little for their desire to learn if they needed such an inducement.-24r. Howitt said all human nature was subjected to pre-., miums of that description and we all worked in some way from that point, and he did not know that Dr, Gastaldi was exempt from it. He was aiming for some- thing beyond the present, and the children wanted some • aim the same as they did. The children at this'school had raised £5 by means of a bazaar, for the purpose of carry- ing on their evening treats, and in this matter of prizes for exemplary conduct in education, they ought not to be cheeseparing and stingy. He was sure the rate- payers of Runcorn would not thank them for being so in a matter of this kind.—Mr. McDougall remarkedthat in some towns there was a fund for giving prizes in this manner, but they had not reached that stage in Runcorn. The Board did not want to make money out of the even- ing school, and many a bright lad would look back with pleasure upon prizes what he had obtained at the evening school.—The Clerk said the teachers were doing their best to make the classes a success. They were each contri- buting a night's pay in order to form a fund to buy books for the spelling bee that is to be held at the schools on Monday evening next.—The minutes were adopted.— The Clerk observed that there were 60 students at the class on the previous night.—Mr. Hewitt': That is splen- , did. It is worth £6O for the good it will do.—There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SCHOOL TEACHER.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SCHOOL TEACHER.

At Darwell, near Sheffield, on Sunday evening, a young man, named William Hall, attempted to murder an assistant Board Sc'hool teacher, named Isabella Edge, who did not reciprocate his attentions. She wrote him a letter a week ago to that effect. He met her on Sunday, and after accompanying her home, asked if she meant what she said. She confirmed b.er statement, whereupon he fired a revolver, injuring her dangerously in the face. He was arrested and remanded.

div.head: LORD TIARTINGtTON IN LONDON.
div.p: LORD TIARTINGtTON IN LONDON.

Lord Ilartington, speaking on Tuesday night at tha, Liberal Unionist Club in London, said there must be some strange fascination in political success which could' make men in all other relations of life as honourable as Unionists so utterly indifferent as some of their oppen- ents appeared to be to the moral character of the associ- ates with whom they had entered into so close a political alliance. No one could believe that it was possible•with- out the concurrence of an Irish Parliament to make n, final settlement of the Irish land question, For a log time to comethere would remain in Ireland landlords znd tenants' and if Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Morley maant 'that an Irish Parliament was to have power to deal with them, that was a position to which the people of this country would never consent. The attitude they had taken in this dispute might be summed up la th 4 phrase. "When rogues fall out honest men come ta their own again."

THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
_ BY SYLVANITS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER XVI.

THWARTED, BUT NOT SUBDUED. It was long after midnight, and yet the widow Nevel had not sought her bed. She was now pacing to and fro across her kitchen, and the boy Paul sat nodding in his chair. Suddenly the woman stopped, and Paul started up. "Do you think that message was a false one ?" she asked, looking the boy in the face. "I don't know," he returned. "If he came from the black monk, as he said he did, then I think he spoke the truth." " Oh, they would not have deceived me." "No, ray mistress, I am sure they could not." "But it is very late." "Hark ! There are bells." The widow heard them, and with a wildly flut- tering heart she sank into a chair. "They have stopped in front of the house," uttered Paul, whose ears were bent. " Go—go—open—" Paul started. The widow heard the door opened, and she heard voices in the hall. In a moment more the inner door was opened, and she looked up. She saw a manly form—she heard the magic word— Mother—trembling upon the air. With one low cry of joy she started to her feet, and in the next moment she was clasped to the bosom of her son. "Did I not tell you I'd bring him back to you ?" cried Valdimir, rubbing his hands with joy. "Oh, God bless you, sir!" the widow murmured, gazing through her tears into the monk's face. "So, so," returned the strange man. "The blessing of an honest soul is reward enough for one night, so I'll take myself off for the present." "No,. no," cried Runic. " You'll remain here till morning,"
But the monk could not be .prevailed upon so to do. He had business to attend to, and he could not stop;. and he hurried away as quickly as possible to avoid the thanks that were showered upon him.

After -Valdimir was gone, Burk sat down and re- lated to Ms mother all that had occurred since that day on which he left her to go and see the count.. She trembled fearfully as he related the diabolical attempt that had been made upon him ; and when he had concluded, she sat for a few moments like one in a painful trance. " And do you think," she said at length, while a cold shudder ran through her frame, "that the Duke of Tula was' the cause of all this?" "I am sure of it,.my mother.!' • "Then you are not safe yet." "But I shall See • the Emperor." "I have seen hita;.my son." "Ah—and what, sgid he ?" "Why—lie said if 'we could find out who had done you harm he would punish them. Then I asked him—suppose •it- was a dulse: mad he said in that case he should have to look into the matter. Oh, I fear he would'aet dare to punish the power- ful, Olga"

" Pe-rhaps not ; hr."; yet, my mother, I will give him credit for better things. Yet,': the youth con- tinued, in a sad tone, "there is one-for whom I care more than self, and who is now within the wicked duke's power. Oh, sheis his beyond any power of the Emperor !" "Not absolutely beyond his powr.nr, is she ?" the mother asked.

" Why—of course Peter has thepower to set aside any wardship, but 'twould not be policy- for him to interfere in the domestic affairs of his powerful nobles. I feel sure that his heart would bid him interfere ;but his judgment would oppose it. You have seen Rosalind ?" "Yes." `` And was she unhappy when she- knew that I was missing ?". . .

"Au Rule !" returned the mother, with a kindl- ing eye, " you do not know' how that noble girl loves you. Oh, her heartwas almost broken when she knew that evil had befallen you r!' The widow had it in her mind to tell•of the scene which had transpired upon the duke'esconring into the maiden's presence when she was there,but she thought a second time ere she spoke ; and she then concluded not to speak of it at present, forshe knew 'twould only serve to give her son additional pain, without bestowing any benefit: "-By heavens !" uttered Rude, at the end of a troubled reverie and at the same time • clasping his hands vehemently together; ' was ever man so sur- rounded by impenetrable mystery before! This 'monk is surely a good man. He has served me ;well, and I am sure he would serve me more if op- portunity offered. But who is he? .Have- you found out anything concerning him ?" "-I have not, my son," ".But is it not strang3t•?",- "It is."

And so they conversed-until their -drooping lids would no longer remaial apart, and then, having first rendered up their thanks to Cod,. and asked his. help f..)r the future, they retired to their respec- tive places of rest. Ruric had strange dreams, and for the life of him be could not tell whether they were good or bad. One he dreamed that he was a duke himself, and that he had a wife-whose face he had never seen. She would not raise-her veil until the ceremony was perform-ed. Them, she removed the obstruction, and Duric started On beholding the face of Valdimir the monk And then. Valdimir seemed to say: "All this I have donalor thee. Do you like it?" And Rurie dared net obieet because ,Valdimir had done soinuch for him.,

, And now, while Ric awakes from: his dreams ,and wonders what they meant, let us look in and -see what is going on iii the ducal palace. It was early morning, and the Duke of Tula was, once more in his ow 2 private apartment He had. not slept well, for he, too, had la ad dreams, and. they were troublesome ones. They,hungabout hint even now, and they,filled his mind:: with dark andi gloomy foreboding% He paced to-.and fro across the apartment, sometinaes stopping, and bowing hits head, and then starting on again with new clowds upon his brow. Thus be waned • and pondered until he was aroused by a stealthy footfall close by the door. He stopped and listened. He knew the step. 'Twas the .one he had been waiting far. He moved to the dcor and opened it,. and the hu.mp- backed priest, Savotano, entersd the apartment.. "By St. Paul,Savotano, I feared you wouX -never come," the duke-uttered, as his,workman closed the door behind him.
"I would he come sooner it I could, my- lord; but even now it is early morning.. The sun is hardly above the cityfwalls." "Well—it is early I know; but. I have not slag. well."

"I have iicA slept all, iny lord." "No. Savotano, you lock;woen and weary. But; you have been at work." " Aye—lrnave." " Ahd yeu have come tatell mle the result of -that work. Dees it move yoikso to do such work? I. thought you were usectto.it.''' The priest gazed into lismaster's lace, but-he did not spec*. "Bah?!" uttered Olga contemptuously. "What is the killing of ama o,L But tell me—did you:con- ceal the body so that no one will find it ?"-•
It wos sore minutes- before Savatono voke. frame trembled, and his hands worked, nervonaly together. But at length he said, in a, hesitataag tone-z

"lie is not deadi my lord." ',.Not dead yet But you promisame,he agaild bae "' I know—butt we could not do it."' " Bea ! I gavo.ye credit for more. firmnea%. Not kill a znan ? What is there so terzible in that?

; " Y•o---u--misunderstood me, my lord. --life di all we ccoulei towards killing him, but ha escaped ts." "'Hold !." ;tried the duke, starting forward and ' gra aping tha priest by the shoulder. " You do not Ewan that Rum Nevel has escaped you;"' "He has, my lord." "But not entirely! You do not mean that he has fairly gone from out your bands ?" "He has, my lord. But listen—' "Listen, thou bungler? By the saints, what story can ye tell to make that smooth and reason, able i You had him in your power, and you should have kept him." "But, my lord, thG devil himself is working for that man. We went last night to kill the fellow, and I waited all of two hours for Totma and Viska, but the rascals did not come, and I engaged others."

'And did they prove treacherous 2" cried Olga, in sudden passion. "No, my lord—they did their best, but they were interrupted by that accursed black monk,who came backed by some dozen men." " What ! Do you mean that Valdimir came there 7" " Yes." "And with a band of armed men ?" "Yes."

"Then, by the gods, there's treachery some-. where- ?'' "I know not what to think, my lord," returned Savotano, in an uneasy, perplexed tone. "The only men who are absent are Lesko Totma and. Frederic Viska ; and they are surely our best men." "But you see plainly that there must have been treachery !" exclaimed the duke, passionately. "Oh, how I would like to know the man! And did this monk carry off the gun-maker ?" "He did. And he captured four of our men. I escaped without being seen." "'That is fortunate—" "I mean that the monk did not see me—nor did any of his followers. But the gun-maker saw me." "And do you think he mistrusted you had any hand in the matter of his imprisonment ? " "I should judge so," returned the priest, with a- peculiar twinge of vengeance about the lips. " Th villain knocked me down:" "Aye—the moment he saw me." "But do you think he knows. anything about it?" ".No. Ido not think he does. He can only sus- pect." "Then we'll be prepared for him if your own. men are to be depended upon. But leave that to me. I'll fix that matter with the Emperor. I'll see him this very day, and be sure he shall have a story that can destroy all evidence which these fellows can hatch up.' "But I must flee, my lord." Not yet, Savotano. I must have your help with- in a very short time. By the true God I swear, that the Countess Rosalind Valdai shall be my wife within the present week. I'll place the seal of fact upon that matter at once. Pear not, for I know my influence over the Emperor Will shield you from all harm., Why. Peter would sooner lose • his right hand than lose me." "Then most surely I will remain, my-lord, for I much wish to perform that ceremony for you: But who is this black monk—this Valdimir ?" The duke started across the floor, and-for some • moments he continued pacing to and fro. When he stopped he brought his hands together with anend- ergetic movement, and looking the priest -sternly in the face, he said: • "Let that monk be who he may; whether man or , devil, God or saint, I'll destroy him! Lhave the power, and. I'll use it. As Warden of the city.l ha,ve . the power' arrest him upon suspicion of conspir- acy. I'll do-it! Where is he now ? ' " I know not."

" Nevermi-n-a, I'll to the Emperor first. Ell study my plan, and ere the sun sets it shall be carried out, By heavens, I'll be baffled thus no more.. I could have wished that this gun-maker had been quietly out of the way, for then all would have been clear and plain, and I should not have feared the trouble of his clamoring about my ears. But let him go. I would not give much for the life he has left. I'll dispose of him SOOl4. But that monk—by Ileavens he dies at once, and without consultation with.tbe Emperor; for 1 can swear he is a anspira:,er." " Good! " ejaculated the priest. And thus the business was arranged for be pre- sent. Passion- helped the duke wondrously in his conclusions ?-and the wish was made into the power. But even before the priest left, the stout nobleman began to wish that he bad a very little more power. In fact, as he /lame to reason he began to doubt; but he gave up not one idea of the plan he had formed for the vengeance his soul so madly craved. (To be continued.)

The annual meeting of the alto' ye association was held at the Constitutional Club, NVitton-st., North- wich, on Saturday. The chair w as occupied by the President (Colonel France Ilayhu .rst). There was a large attendance, including rep resentatives frqfll Northwich, Barntou, Winsford, M iddlewich, Runcorn, and Halton. The secretary (Mr. C. J. Hughes) sub- mitted the sii.thannual report, is s which it was stated that much greater interest had bees s manifested in regis- tration matters by Conservative v. oters during the pa.. 4, year than had hitherto been the case., The number of, claims and obfections sustained bj their party was 32$t or a net Conservative gain of eig ht. The result, con- sidering all circumstances, migla t be considered verf satisfactory. The Constitutional Club, Northwich, waS flourishing and.. progressing, ant I their position was greatly strens-,tb.ened. Through the exertions of Mr. Lighthurn and several friends, a i sew Conservative Club was opened =the previous Saturday, at Runcorn. It was u rged that the assistance o!i every member of the association was required with respect to registration during 1891, owing to the prox.ivaity of the general elec- tion. It was unanimously decided to request Sir Richd. Brooke, of Norton Priory (Runc.ern), to fill the office of presic lent. Er. T. Ward was re-elected chairman, ard a high. compliment was paid to him for the excellent work he had performed in connection with the association since; its fermation, Mr. Newell was chosen to fill the joint, offices of hon. treasurer and hon.. secretary.
