IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mosmsy. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past four. ARABI FASYLA.—The Marquis of SALISBURY informed Earl Delawarr that Arabi Pasha was condemned to death not for fighting against his country, but for . rebelling against his Sovereign. Upon the representation of her Majesty's Government, however, the sentence was com- muted. A medical board had reported that the climate of Ceylon had no injurious effect upon Arabi's death. 1 THE Ces-roov OF CHILDREN Biets—The Custody of Children Bill was read a second time, and referred to a Committee pf the whole House. The House adjourned at 5.5. HOUSE OF COMMONS. —MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. CHINESE PIRACY.—Sir J. FERGUSSON told Mr. A. . •Gathorne Hardy, that Chinese pirates had looted the ship Lama, killing four persons who were oil board. Vessels having been despatched in pursuit of the pirates, but their whereabouts had not up to the present been ascertained. AGRICULTURAL IHSTRUCTION.—Mr. RITCHIE, in reply to Mr. Gathorne Hardy, said county and borough coun- cils were empowered to dispose of the money granted under the Local Taxation Act for the purposes of techni- cal education, including instruction in agricultural pro- cesses._ BIG Guns IN THE NAVY.—Lord George HAMILTON, in reply to Mr. Gourley, said that there was no truth in the statement that one of the 111. ton guns was disabled while under trial. It was not intended to replace these guns by German weapons. THE TITHE BILL. The House then went into Committee on the Tithe- Rent Charge Recovery Bill, and continued the consider- ation of clause 3, which, after a lengthy debate, was, as amended, passed, as were also clauses 4 and 5. On clause 6, fixing the extent of the Bill, Mr. Osborne Morgan moved that the measure should not apply to the Principality, but Mr. Raikes regarded the proposi- tion as a joke, seeing that it was the disturbances in Wales which first called attention to the tithe question. The amendment was rejected, and the clause was even- tually added to the Bill. Mr. RANDELI. moved an amendment giving power of appeal from decisicns of the County Court Judges to the High Court, and it was accepted. The consideration of the Bill had not been concluded when progress was reported at midnight. The House adjourned at 12-15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Loin) CHANCELLOR took his seat on the wool-sack at a quarter past four o'clock. STANDING COMMITTEES.—EARL CADOGAN gave notice on Thursday week he should move the adoption of the new standing orders which the committee recommended. BENEFICES lint.—The BISHOP of Lichfield moved the second reading of the Presentation to Benefices Bill, which he stated was in the same terms as the measure which received the approval of their lordships last sea- son. The Bill having been read a second time, the BISHOP of Lichfield moved that it should be referred to a com- mittee of the whole Houses as it passed through a stand- ing committee last year. The motion was agreed to. Bret, PASSED.—The Tramways Order in Council (Ire- land) (Athenry and Tuara Railway) Bill was read athifd time and passed. Their lordships rose at twenty-five minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The SPEAKER took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. QuEsTions.—Mr. Marrinws informed Mr. Howard Vincent that he was doubtful whether time could be found for re-introducing the Reformatory and Indust- trial Schools Bill this year. Replying to Mr. J.Lowther, Baron DE \Voltam said the Government were carefully considering the question of fiscal arrangements with the Colonies. Mr. MaTrHEws, in answer to Mr. Pickersgill, said he advised the remission of a sentence of five years' penal servitnde passed at the last Chaster Assizes, not because therehad been a long sitting of the court, but after a careful review of all the facts. Mr. Goscireis re- plied to a technical point arising out of the Irish Land Purchase Bill; and Sir J;FERGUSSON explained to Sir G. Baden-Powell the latest phase of the Behring Sea diffi- culty. Mr. HOWARD VINCENT gave notice of a bill for further checking the use of false trade marks, and a bill by Mr. Arthur O'Connor for more effectually preventing fraudulent trading was read a first time. THE NEW RIFLE.—MY. MAJORIBANKS moved for a Select Committee to inquire into the merits of the new magazine rifle and all the circumstances attending its adoption. He criticised the weapon in detail, his obser- vations being generally condemnatory. Mr. HANBURY moved an amendment pointing to the undesirability of appointing a commission to weaken the full responsibi- lity of the officials who adopted the weapon. Colonel Noises? spoke in favour of the rifle, and Mr. STANHOPE described it as undoubtedly the best rifle at the time it was chosen. Mr. Seton-Karr, Sir W. Barttelot, and others joined in the discussion. Mr. Majoribankes motion was defeated by a majority of 34, and Mr. Han- _sy's amendment was agreed to without a division. _ 6COTCII EDUCATiox.—Mr. C. PARKER moved a resolu- tion in favour of grants in aid of secondary education in -Scotland. The LORD ADVOCATE .said the Government had the subject under consideration, and in due time would be prepared with definite proposals. The motion was withdrawn. • RAILWAY HOURS.—Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH moved the appointment of a Select committee to inquire whether, and if so in what way, the hours worked by railway servants should be restricted by legislation. The motion was agreed to. THE RELIEF OF DISTRESS 1/4 IRELAND.—CoIoneI NOLAN called attention to the inadequate manner In which the Relief of Distress Act is now being administered in Ire- , land, and urged that relief works should be at once started in Galway and Mayo. He concluded by moving thae tht Act should at once be put at once into operation over a large area.—Mr. KNox seconded the motion, and after some remarks from Sir J. Colomb.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL for Ireland said that it was the intention of the Chief Secretary for Ireland to make a further statement with regard to Irish relief works before Easter, and he was now doing his best to obtain accurate information as to the needs of the various districts. The right hon. gentleman was at this,point interrupted by the arrival of ,midnight. THE TITHE BILIS.—The House then went into com- mittee on the Tithe Rent Charge Recovery Bill. . The 'Committee stage was completed, and the report was ,ordered to be considered on Thursday.t The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMCrNS.—WEDNE6DAY. The Speaker took the chair at 12.15, at which time 'there was a very large attendance of members. PETrrioss.--Colonel SANDYs presented two very large Petitions against a Religious Disabilities Removal Bill. They .came from the Protestant Alliance with 23,656 Signatures, and from certain Baptists, to the number of a 0,084. 'NEW WRIT FOR NoiernsurrosT.—On the motion of Mr. A. MORLEY, a newwrit was ordered ;to be issued for the election of a number for Northampton, in the place of the late fdr. Charles Bra,dlaugh. THE RELIGIOUS DISABILITIES BILL. SPEECH OF MR. GLADSTONE. Mr. Gladstone delivered a speech of rather more than an hour's duration in moving the second reading of the Religious Disabilities Removal Bill, the object of which Was to throw open to Roman Catholics the offices of Lord Chancellor and of Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland. Mr. Gladstone described the Bill as one to remove from the statute book an anomaly, an injustice and .a discredit. Re believed it to be seriously doubtful whether Roman Catholics were in law actually disabled from holding the offices, yet the law was not as clear as it ought to be, and it would be unsafe in the formation of a Govern- ment to recommend for those offices any one about the validity of whose acts there could be the smallest doubt. Ills object was simply to remove the anomaly, and he was willing that any duty of an ecclesiastical character devolving upon either of the two offices should be handed over to whomsoever the Queen might choose to select. Referring to recent publications attacking him, )dr. Gladstone said that the result of his own Pamphlets of 1874-5 on the Vatican and the duty of Eng- lish Catholic was an assurance that the loyalty of our itoman Catholic fellow-subjects in the main remained !vidently untainted and secure. He argued, therefore, Ihat unless the loyalty of the Roman Catholic was tainted The House had no right to inflict disability upon him, be- 'cause the principle of the British Constitution allowed no Siva disabifity on account of religious opinion. Mr. W. H. 4•MITH expressed his wonder that Mr. Gladstone had not Proposed a measure of this kind when lie was respon- *Able for the government of the country, lf it were so gent and necessary to remedy a great wrong. In 1881 Gladstone, when questioned if he would abolish the squalificatioa appertaining to the office of Lord Chan- eelloz, and to the Crown, said that the Government had no intention of doing anything of the kind. The Proposed Bill, Mr. Smith argued, itself laid down 7,sleligious test, for it was admitted that a large portion the I,Qed Chancellor's duties were to be taken away him if he were a Roman Catholic. He regretted at the question had been raised at the present .tu_ornent. There was no demand for the change on the rrt of the Roman Catholics, and no public opinion in 'l)Port of it. He did not know why the Bill was pro- sst'ase___ d unless in connection with Mr. Gladstone's policy ii7ards Ireland. He moved the rejection of the Bill. 0„ Gedge, 'Colonel Sandys, and Colonel Saunderson wstosed the Bill, and Mr. A. Elliot and Mr. Asquith fop eoh its behalf, Announcing his intention to vote the second reading of the Bill, Sir Henry James ;rol_oared that if he thought the Bill would injure '4idtftstantism in the slightest degree, or would Chu,, one portion of strength to the Roman Catholic Oppr as a political power, he-and many others would it. But he held that full and free toleration was °° %tale great reasons why Protestantism had been a citlo gto the country. H.did not think that the day roust-11 me Rule had come, but, even if it did come. they 'were_adissyt the Bill to the new Constitution. If they irit7eTig:,sut out justice because Home Rule might come fn9e it might be argued that they should pass Rue_in9order that justice might be done. The tents _UB2sitnas, disclaimed the idea that the oppo- catholiu_i " Bill were attacking the loyalty of Roman os Ile thought that no case had been made out

jfor the necessity of such a Bill; nor could it be honestly said that the measure had no connection with the Home Rule scheme. Mr. Ds LISLE and Mr.CAUPBELL-BANNER- MAN having also spoken, the House divided, when there voted For the second reading 223 „Against 256 The Bill was, therefore, thrown out by a majority of 33, and the House adjourned shortly before six o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuunsnAT. The SPEAKER took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. PROTESTANT CLERGYMEN IN BAPTIST CHAPELS.—The HOME SECRETARY, answering to Mr. Furniss, said he had been supplied with a copy of the correspondence that had passed between. the Bishop of Exeter and the Rev. Her- bert Marriott, from which it appeared that the Bishop reqvsted Mr. Marriott to resign his license as preacher, on the ground that he was constantly attending Baptist chapels and taking part in services. He had no means of knowing whether the action of the Bishop had caused great dissatisfaction. The Bishop had acted within his discretion, and the matter being outside the Homel,9ffice,' he had no authority to interfere. QUESTIONS.—Mr. STANHOPE informed Major Rasch that he was in communication with the Treasury re- girding an increase in the grant to the National Associ- ation for the employment of Discharged and Reserved Soldiers. Mr. Goscumq informed Sir J. Colomb that the decisions arrived at in the inquiry into the Customs Outdoor Department would shortly be made known. HARGAN'S IMPRISONMENT.—MT. JAMES LOWTHER moved the adjournment of the House, in order to call attention to the continued imprisonment of Walter Hargan for shooting two London roughs in self-defence. Mr. MarrnEws, in defending his course of action, said it could not be permitted that two men should be shot with impunity in London streets in broad daylight. Sir W. HARCOURT defended the Home Secretary's action, and the motion was by leave withdrawn. THE Trrsgs Bu.L.—The House considered the Tithe Rent Charge Recovery Bill as amended, and on the motion of Mr. SEALE-HAYNE a clause was added provid- ing that any rate to which the tithe rent charge is sub- ject should be assessed upon and may be from the owner of the tithe rent charge in the like manner and by the like process as on and from any other occupying ratepayer. Mr. Lloyd George moved a new clause pro- viding for trial by jury and appeal in any proceedings of a criminal or penal character arising under the Act. After considerable discussion, the House divided, when there voted—For the clause, 135 ; . against. 164; majority against 27. The clause was therefore negatived, ; the narrow majority being loudly cheered on the Op- position benches. The discussion was suspended at mid- night, Sir M. Hicks-Beach intimating that he should put the order down after Supply on the following day, when , he hoped it might be proceeded with. New BILL. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for Ireland I obtained leave to introduce bills for the establishment of , local registries of titles to land in Ireland, to consolidate and amend the laws relating to the registration of deeds . and judgments, &c., and for further shortening the lan- guage used in Acts relating to Ireland. They were brought in, and read a first time. The House adjourned at five minutes past twelve.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Sutton, Holmes, Burgess, , Davies, Harrison, Wright and Platt; Councillors Pierpoint. Greening, R. Fairclough, Taylor, Shaw- Green, Monks, Beaman, Muir, Browne, Flood, Garner, Jenkins, Hepherd, Heaton, H. Roberts, Blackhurst, Greenall, Dixon, Hill, Bolton, Cannell, and Hutchinson; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk) ; Dr. Gornall (medical officer) ; Longdin (borough surveyor) ; and Chorley (borough lreasurer).

M LATE MR. S. RIGBY. The MAYou said that on the previous morning Mr. Ziba Armitage called to see him, and said that Mrs. Rigby would be pleased to present to the Council the bust in marble by Mr. Warrington Wood of her late husband, if they would aeceptit. (Applause.) He moved that they accept the gift. Alderman DAVIES seconded this proposition,which was agreed to unanimously. The MAYOR then moved that the best thanks of the Council be given to Mrs. Rigby for her valuable gift. Alderman DAVIES again seconded the motion, which was passed. The MAYOR added that he proposed to hand the bust over to the Museum, Library and Arts Committee with a request that they find a suitable place for it in the Museum. (Hear, hear.)

WATCH COMMITTEE. The Watch Committee having considered the applica- tions of the several proprietors of hackney carriages for the renewal of their licenses for the ensuing year, re- solved that, in order to prevent loitering in the streets, the carriages be licensed to ply for hire on stated stands, and that the following licenses be granted accordingly: —Mr. Edward Connor, 4 carriages in Cairo-st. and 2at the Central Station; Mr. Samuel Wilson, 2 carriages at the Central Station; Mr. John Connor, 1 carriage at the Central Station and onein Horsemarket-st. ; Mrs. Kiernan 1 carriage at the Central Station; The Warrington Carriage Company, Limited, 1 carriage at the Central; Maginn Bros., 1 carriage at the Central Station and 3 in Arpley-st.—lt was also resolved that the standin Crown- St. be appointed for 6 carriages, and that a now Stand in Arpley-st.—Sankey-st. end—be appointed for 3 carriages. Confirmed on the motion of thd MAYOR, seconded by Alderman HARRISON. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIMITING COMMIL rEk.. The above-named Committee recommended that the plans of the following buildings, &c., be approved :-20 houses and shops in Marshhouse-lane, for Mr. Joseph Matthews I corrugated iron roof and shed in Hopwood- st. for the Mersey Shoemaking Company;' 10 houses in We'llfield-st.' for Mr. John Lloyd; and 12 houses in Well- field-st., for Mr. Josephwrildesley. The Committee also recommended that the sum of £4,500 be paid to the trustee of the will of the late Joseph Chrimes, deceased, for property at Bridge Foot, occupied by Mrs. Chrimes and Mr. R. W. Marsh, according to a contract produced. The, Committee further recommended that certain pre- perty, numbered 25 id° 33, Lythgoes-lane, and 4, Pump- yard, Lythgoes-lane, should be closed and demolished. , This property is declared unfit for habitation, and belongs to the Corporation. Alderman PLATT moved the confirmation of the minutes. With regard to the purchase of property at Bridge Foot he said that after the contract was duty signed by the solicitor to the vendor and the deposit money of £4OO paid by the Corporation, the solicit& for the vendor raised some objection to a line of boundary which had already been fully. decided upon inasmuch as they would not have sufficient means of access to the adjoining brewery. The Committee after meeting on the spot decided to give way slightly and make an allowance of about four square yards of land without asking the sellers to reduce the price. No reply had been received to that offer, but if it were not accepted they should have to stand up for the bargain as originally signed. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then passed... THE SANITARY COMMIITEM.7-LNCREASE OF SALARY.—THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS.

The Sanitary Committee recommended that Mr. Owen P. Warner be appointed manager and mechanic of the works at Longford, at a salary of £175 per annum. It also instructs the Town Clerk to take steps to close the dwelling-houses enumerated by us last week, as beht unfit for human habitation. Alderman BURGESS moved the confirmation of these minutes. With regard to the proposed increase of Mr. Owen P. Warner's salary, be said that the salary as in- creased v, ould only be a fair remunerati on for the work and responsibility of the manager of Longford depot. As to the closing of the houses, what the Committee were. proposing to do was simply to carry out instructions re- ceived from the Medical Officer that the houses sche- duled are unfit for habitation. Alderman Burgess next referred to the invitation alse contained in the Com- mittee's minutes to members of the Council to inspect the Intercepting Depots- Councillor MUIR : Are they safe? Alderman BURGESS: That all depends upon whether you are insured. (Laughter.) Alderman Surrozi seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman PLArr asked what steps had been taken by the Sanitary Committee to bring about the very desir- able state of affairs that was said to exist at the inter- cepting depots? Alderman HARRISON also wished to know how many members of the Sanitary Committee were present when the minute in reference to the intercepting depots was passed. Counciller SHAW GREEN inquired if any members of the Sanitary Committee had themselves been round to visit those supposed insanitary properties set out in the schedule before them. His own name appeared as owner of two of the houses, but he held them merely in trust and had nothing to do with them personally. He was of opinion that some practical members of the Commit- tee, in addition to the Medical Officer, should go rcund to see, and should be of the same opinion as the dcctor before proceedings were taken. Councillor FLOOD said another member of the Commit- tee besides-himself had already paid personal visits to the properties irk question. They were thoroughly satis- fied that the property is of such a character, that it vas a great pity it was not pulled down many years ago. (Hear, hear.) Councillor GREENALL said that he was told that in Wash-lane there was a place where there was only one closet for four cottages. He wanted to know if that was in accordance with sanitary law. Alderman BURGESS said he should think it was not. Councillor FIERPOINT moved that the minute in refer- ence to the increase of Owen P. Warner's .salary. and that with regard to the intercepting depets be noc ap- proved. lie quite believed that the Sanitary Committee might be seriously of opinion that there was no misance et the lutereaptiog depute, but he was himself fully alive

div.head: nu EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1891.
div.p: nu EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1891.

to the correspondence that had gone on in the papers and to the motions that had been moved in that cham- ber, all having reference to the question of a nuisance existing at the depot. It seemed to him that it was a little dodge on the part of the Sanitary Committee •to put that resolution on their minutes in order to take some of the wind out of the sails of Councillors Dixon and Jenkins. (Councillor H. Roberts: Hear, hear.) And .he should think his friend Councillor Roberts had had a good deal to do with the engineering of the business. (Laughter.) He thought thatin view of the feeling that was generally expressed in the town with regard to the depots, it would be better to also withdraw the minute with reference to the salary of Mr. Owen Warner. He also expressed a hope that the report of the medical offi- cer would'be printed and placed in the hands of the members of the Council. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JENKINS seconded Councillor Pierpoint's amendment. He was surprised at the Sanitary Com- mittee making such amove as that in passing the minute in reference to the Intercepting Depot. . Councillor Dixotr supported the amendment, and spoke of offensive smells emanating from the Howley Depot. Councillor BOLTON, in supporting the amendment, said it looked as though the Sanitary Committee had so little confidence in themselves that they had to pass a resolu- tion in support of their noble selves. He also thought the time for increasing men's salaries was when works were a success, not when they were a non-success, as he considered Longford was. Alderman Surrox argued that there was now.a great economy in the management of Longford works com- pared with what used to be paid. He was individually of opinion that the nuisance which was said to exist at. the Intercepting Depots was nothing in comparison with the nuisance which would exist under the old midden- stead system. (Laughter.) He arse believed that the Intercepting Depots were saving them £1,500 a year. Councillor 'lmmo asked if Alderman Sutton was in • order.

1 Alderman Strrrow Why? Councillor PIERPOINT : He thinks you are rambling. (Laughter.) Alderman Strrrox, corltinuing, maintained that the Sanitary Committee had always been ready to give all information. (Laughter, and a member "I never knew that before.") Councillor H. ROBERTS held that Councillor Pierpoint had not given a single argument in support of his amendment. With regard to Mr. Owen Warner's he maintained that they should pay him a salary adequate to the responsibility 3f his position. He disclaimed the authorship of the resolution with reference to the inter- cepting depots. Alderman Surrox I was the author of it. (Laugh- ter.) Councillor ROBERTS thought it was time the Council put an end to the pettifogging badgering the Sanitary Committee had had from time to time. The Sanitary- Committee meant to say by their -resolution that, barr- Mg accidents, no nuisance would exist at the intercept- ing depots. They asked them to suspend the motions of which notice had been given until they saw for them- selves whether there was anything to Justify the Com- mittee's resolution or not. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON supported the suggestion that the motions of which notice had been given by Coun- cillors Jenkins and Dixon should be held over till mem- bers of the Council had themselves visited the depots.

Alderman DAVIES suggested as a compromise that the Sanitary Committee's minute In reference to the inter- cepting depots be omitted for the present, and that Councillor Jenkins also withdraw his motion for a time:

_ Councillor R. FAIRCLOUGH supported the minutes of the Sanitary Committee. tie really believed there were other works in Warrington making more nuisance than the inteicepting depots. Councillor SHAW-GREEN supported Alderman Davies's suggestion, although he believed there was sound reason for complaint of the intercepting depots, and personally he could not see what better evidence could be required than that theyhad had either by the Sanitary Committee or anybody else. ' Councillor HUTCHINSON supported Alderman Davies's suggestion. Councillor JENKINS said he had gone to very consider- able trouble to collect evidence in support of his motion. He had collected facts from engineers and machinists and from leading agriculturists in this neighbourhood as to •the quality of the manure from Longford, and as to what would be its fair price, and in many other ways be ventured to think that what he was prepared to lay before them would be of practical assistance to thoir deliber- ations. He was not going to take all that trouble and then have his motion quietly shunted. The MAYOR said that during the past five or six days he had been through the Howley depots and it was utterly impossible to smell anything. , Councillor BROWNS said he did not agree entirely with the first part of the Sanitary Committee's minute, but he did think that every member of the Council oueht to visit the intercepting depots to see for himself if there was a nuisance. New devices were being used for doing away with any nuisance. Councillor Hitt supported the amendment ancrspoke to having himself experienced the nuisances caused by the depots. Alderman Surrox objected to the withdrawal of the minute of the Sahitary Committee. Alderman PLATT thought this was the wrong time of the year to discuss the question of nuisances at the depots.As to Councillor Roberts's talk about pettifogging badgering by people who made complaints that was absurd. Councillor H. ROBERTS: That does not alter the fact. Alderman Purr: If you apply that to me I decline to give you my opinion of yourself personally.

; Alderman BURGESS, in replying to the various questions . put, said with reference to Councillor Shaw Green's re- marks that having appointed a medical officer and an , inspector he must decline to himself become either medi- cal officer or inspector of nuisances, or a common informer. He might tell them there was a much more formidable list of insanitary 'property than the one he held in his hand, one, he was told, that it would take £20,000 to carry out. They would, however, not come to a decision on that larger scheme simply on the recom- mendation of the medical officer. With regard to the I four houses to one closet he would ask the Town Clerk as to the legal bearings of the question. The TOWN CLERK said it was not a legal question at all ; it was a sanitary question. Alderman BURGESS, in the course of some further remarks said that from the return of the medical officer it appeared that the death-rate of the borough for the past year had been 22.5 per 1,000, which was somewhat higher that he liked, but as they all knew they had had exceptionally severe weather. The death-rate in the north-west ward was 229; north-east 25'9; south-east 221 • south-west 193; and Latchford 17.3. He eX- pressed his willingness that the resolution in reference to the intercepting depots should be taken from the Com- mittee's minutes. Councillor ROBERTS and Alderman Surros both ex- I pressed unwillingness to the withdrawing of the resolu- tion, and Councillor FLOOD added that all the members of the Sanitary Committee looked upon Councillor Jenkins's motion as one of want of confidence. The amendment was then voted upon when there were for—Aldermen Holmes and Platt; Councillors Pierpoint, Cannel!, Greenall, Blackhurst, Jenkins, Garner, Hutch- inson, Bolton, Hill, Dixon-12. Against: The Mayor; Aldermen Bprgess, Davies,. Harrison, Wright, Sutton; Councillors Greening, Fairclough, Taylor, Green, Monks, Beaman Muir, Browne, Flood, Hepherd, Heaton, and H. ' Roberts-L-18. The amendment was, of course, declared not carried. Alderman DAvins then moved that the minutes be . passed with the exception of the resolution referring to the depots, the understanding also being that the motion , of Councillor Jenkins would be postponed.

Councillor PIERPOINT seconded. - Councillor H. Roberts and Alderman Sutton opposed the amendment which was, however, supported by Councillor JENEIN3/49 and Councillor Dixon. On being put to the meeting it was voted upon as follows : For: The Mayor, Alatmen Holmes and Davies; Councillors Greenall,Blackhurst, Bolton, Jenkins,Garner, Pierpoint, Fairclough, Green, Monks, Cannell, Dixon, Hill and Hutchinson-16. Against: Alderman Sutton; Councillors Greening, Bolton, Beaman, Browne Flood, Hepherd and H. Roberts-8. The amendment was, therefore, carried. Alderman Surron : I shall not vote any more on this subject. (Laughter.) The minutes of the Sanitary Committee were then passed.

THE PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee contained a resolution that the sub-Committee be requested to inspect and report upon the c,ondition of the unpaved streets in the borough. Alderman DAVIES moved the confirmation of the minutes with the exception of a portion as to the apper- tionment for Garibaldi-st., which as to some of the in- dividual items he said he was informed by the Surveyor was not correct. Alderman WRIGHT seconded.
601311Ciilor BLACKHURST asked for information as to a proposed laying of pipes from Brook Place to Mersey View. _ _

_ Councillor PIERPOINT asked how the necessity for this work had arisen and the estimated cost. Alderman DAVIES said he could not inform Councillor rierpoint the cost, and stated that the brook had been a nuisance to adjoining property for years, and was dan- gerous to children in some places. The nuisance came from the tanneries. Councillor PIERPOINT moved an amendment, "That the Paving and Sewerage Committee's minute relating to the piping from Brook Place to Mersey View, be not carried." Every one of the tanneries, he said was con- nected with the Latchford .system of sewerage which cost from £3,000 to £5,000, and the nuisance proved that that system was not working as it ought to do. Councillor DrxoN seconded the amendment, complain- plaining that the motive power at the gas works was de- fective, hence inability to deal with thesewage at Latch- ford. - Alderman Surrori slid perhaps the best thing wouldbe in order that they might all inspect the brook, to post- pone the matter for two months. (Laughter.) After some discussion Councillor PIEEPOINT withdrew his amendment with the consent of Councillor Dixon. Alderman Sirrros : All this time lost for nothing again. The minutes were then passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICERS' SALARIES. •

The School Attendance Committee rEcommended that the salaries of the school attendance inspectors be in- creased as follows :—Geo. Riley, from 455. to 525. 6d. ; Wm. Jones, from 30s. to 355. ; and Wm. Ba.mber, from 255. to 30s. _

Councillor SHAW GREEN moved the adoption. He re- ferred to the recent examination for labour certificates in that room, at which he said about 70 children were present, the Inspector assuring the committee that theirs was the only case in which an application for such an examination had been acceded to, which only showed the necessity for the trouble the committee had been at in bringing it about. The result had not been so satis- factory as could have been expected, but that was be- cause three months had elapsed since the last examination and a great number of children had not been attending

school. Advocating the increase of the officers' salaries Mr. Green pointed out that the number of the school chil- dren had increased about 3,000 in the past ten years; end the work of the School Department, been almost doubled while the cost had:been infinitesimal, not d. in the 2. _ _

Councillor TAYLOR seconded. Councillor Dizort moved an amendment that the salary be not increased, but found no seconder; and the min- utes were adopted as they stood. THE MUSEUM AND TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION. The return for Decenaber showed that there had been 2,181 visitors to the Museum a decrease ef 24 per cent. compared with the previous December ; 1,327 books had beenissued in the reading-room a decrease of 4 per cent.; and 2,008 in the lending department, a decrease of 3 per cent. The gifts to the Museum included.a nest of house- sparrows, and bank vole, from Mr. J. A: Jackson ; Java Sparrow, from the Town Hall Committee ; bust of Mr. Beamone, from the Old Workmen's Club; "Transactions of the Historic Society," vol. 41, from Mr. W. Owen,J.P. The Museum Committee have resolved that the Technical Instruction Sub-Cotrimittee be directed to open communi- cations with the School of Art Committee with a view to the taking over of the school onbehalf of the Corporation. Councillor ROBERTS moved the confirmation. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded, and the minutes were confirmed. THE CEMETERY. From the report of the Registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee it appeared that the interments during the past four weeks were :—Adults, 66 ; minors' 46; stillborn,and premature, 11; corresponding period last year, adults 55 • minors 57 ; stillborn and premature, 8. The receipts for the pasefour weeks were £B9 Os. Bd., corresponding period last year, £B7 18s. 3d. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Alder- man HARRISON seconded by Councillor TAYLOR. THE TOWN HALL PIRK AND BATHS COMMITTEE. From the report of the bath-keeper to the above- named Committee it appeared that the income from the baths during the fortnight ended Bth January was 13s. ; corresponding period last year Bs.6d. The Committee also notified the approval of the Local Government Board to the sale of a plot of land to the trustees of the Warring- ton Infirmary. The minutes were approved on the motion of Coun- cillor BOLTON.

MARKETS COMMITTEE. The Markets Committee submitted the following reso- lutions :—That the patent sand blast machine be sent to the works of Messrs. E. Bolton and Sons for use in stamping glass upon payment of 5 per cent.. per annum upon the cost • that notice be given to the tenants of all the enclosed stalls in the Market Shed, and after three months the rent of such stalls will be increased by the sum of is. per week; and that Mr. Charles Newall, of School Brow, be appointed assistant inspector of weights and measures at 345. per week. The total income of the Committee from all sources was reported to be £232 Us. Bd. The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Coun- cillor GREENALL, seconded by Councillor DIXON. THE GAS COMMITTEE. The Gas Committee reported that the illuminating ' power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 18.3 candles at both works. The Committee had ordered the payment of a sum of £6,718 19s. 11d, required for the payment of annuities and interest to the 31st Dec- ember, 1890. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Alder- man HOLMES seconded by Councillor FAIRCLOUGH. THE RIVERS COMMITTEE. The Rivers Committee report that the plan of the new bridge over the river at Walton and the new road from Chester-road to Arpley Meadows has been submitted to it by the Ship Canal Company, and, as the plan is in accordance with the recommendations of the several authorities interested, it has been approved. The com- mittee were pleased to record that by timely raising of the cleughs at Warrington Weir on Friday the 23rd January preventible floods in Howley were relieved. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Councillor FAIRCLOUGH, seconded by Alderman DAVIES. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The General Purposes Committee submitted a proposal to request the Local Government Board to make a re- division of the borough into three divisions, for the purpose of County Council elections. It is proposed that No. 1 division should include Town Hall, Whitecross,and Bewsey Wards, with 2,736 electors: No. 2, to include Orford, St. John's and Fairfield Wards' with 2,749 electors • and No. 3, to include Howley, St. Austin's,and Latchford Wards, with- 2,597 electors. The term of the appointment of Mr. Alderman Davies and Mr. J. P. Pickmere as representative governors of the Warrington Grammer School having expired, the Committee have resolved that Alderman Davies and Alderman Burgess be appointed representative governors for the term of five years. The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes. Alderman SurroN seconded. Alderman DAVIES moved that the minutes be passed with the exception of the resolution as to the appointment of GOVEITIOTS of the Gram- mar School. The Town Clerk had very properly, on Major Pickmere's appointment being about to expire written to him asking him whether if he were re-ap- pointed he would be ready to accept the office again, whereupon he replied that not only would he be willing to do so, but that it was his great desire to remain a trustee of the charity. It might be objected that Major Pickmere had ceased to be a member of the Connell, but the Corporation might allow this matter to stand over for a month, and either he himself or Alderman Burgess would be pleased to retire in favour of Major Pickmere. Alderman BURGESS seconded the amendment. He did not think there was a gentleman in that neighbourhood

; more entitled to consideration in the election of Gover- nors by that Council than Major Pickmere. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he had the highest regard personally for Major Pickmere. When he became a mem- ber of that Council elected by a political body entirely in opposition to that which the Major belonged he received from him personal courtesy and kindness which had made him always think or him with the highest possible esteem. But the Grammar School was for many years a very close Corporation and still remained so to a large extent. The revised scheme of the Charity Commissioners' adopted a few years ago, only provided for the appointment of three representa- tive Governors, and the other eight were self-elected. It was perfectly well-known that Corporations managed by , self-elected bodies were rarely successful, and the, pre- ' sent position of the Grammar School was an evidence of the truth of the statement, for if the scheme "of the Charity Commissioners had been broader in every sense the Grammar School would not have been what it was at present. Major Pickmere was undoubtedly well qualified for the position, but he having ceased to be a member of the Corporation it was for the co-optative Governors to recognise the ability of the Major, and elect him themselves, leaving the Corporation to choose from their own body the full number of Governors they were entitled to elect. If they adopted the principle of going bout of the Couacil to fill up these offices they would place themselves in a difficulty perhaps when less worthy men came up for these positions. A Governorship of the Grammar School was a position of some honour, and the members of the Corporation should participate, as he him- self claimed the right to do, in the honours as well as the labours of the town. The minute in question was withdrawn, and the remainder of the minutes were then passed.

THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. The MAYOR announced that Councillor Dixon had agreed to withdraw for two months, a resolution with re- gard to the intercepting depots which he had on tip agenda. The Council then rose.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
THE AGREEMENT WITH THE CONTRACTORS FURTHER CAPITAL REQUIRED.

The eleventh ordinary general meeting of the share- holders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held in the Gentlemen's Concert Hall, Manchester, on Tues- day, at noon. Lord Egerton of Tatton presided, and there was a full attendance of directors. A large num- ber of shareholders were also present.

The report was taken as real Lord Egerton, on rising to move the adoption of the , report, said he was bound to confess that the report was ; not so favourable as were those he had had the pleasure of giving to them on previous occasions. Yet he did not ( think, looking at it from a large, comprehensive view, that there was any reason for any man to take a gloomy i and despondent view of the situation. (Hear, hear.) ! On the contrary, they had come toa period in the under- taking when they should rather congratulate.themselves that they had done so much within the short period 1 of less than three years, aggravated as it had ( been by a winter of frost and flood, that only came once in a century, and which had undoubtedly re- tarded the work practically for a period of three months. The present condition of the works was on the whole a very satisfactory one. (Hear.) He had fortified him- self with the report of their .eminent consulting engineer Mr. Abernethy, who, at the request of the board of direc- tors, had made a careful survey of the works during the last three months. The damage done by the flood to the permanent works was put down as being very slight,and it expressed the opinion thatthere was no obstacle in the way of the canal being completed by the middle of next summer. He then read the report of Mr. Abernethy. Resuming his speech, the chairman said the number of men and boys employed on the canal works was 15,000 ; horses, 187 ' • waggons, 300; steam navvies, 96 ; steam cranes, 144; portable and other engines, 184; steam . pumps, 212; miles of temporary railway, 228. They , would remember that the last time he had the pleasure of addressing them—in August—he mentioned that they I were pushing the contractor to put more men on the I work, and also to push forward the iron work and the brick work. Other differences arose during the past ' year, especially in the summer, between the company and the contractor, as to the amount of money claimed for the payment of various works, and of, to the suffi- ciency of the rates in the contract. Mr. Walker's execu- tors were neither empowered nor obliged to continue the works in the absence of a settlement, and they declined : to place further plant on the works. Negotiations were entered into and the main terms of the agreement were that the remaining portions of the work were to be com- pleted under the control of and by the eompany as from the 24th of November last, all existing contracts being determined from that date. The executors of the con- tract& and the executors' staff, under the management of Mr. Topham, were to act for this purpose as the agents of the company. The agreement also provided that upon the realisation of the plant, which. had cost £943,640, 40 per cent. of the amount realised over and above 2,450,000 was to be paid to the executors. The directors had so arranged because they thought that the executors of the contractor, being engaged in similar works, would have greater facilities for disposing of the plants on good terms than the directors could possibly haves. The agreement must be judged by what the alter- native would have been. The alternative would have been the contractor refusing to put down any more plant, would have been practically the stoppage of the works, and possibly costly litigation on the claims. The directors had gone very carefully into the cost of - the works necessary to open the canal at the present . prices, which were certainly some 15 or 29 per cent. ' higher than they were when the contract was entered upon. In a comparison of the estimates which had been : severally made by their own engineer and Mr. Aber- nethy, they fGundthat £1,700,000 was required to com- plete the works over and above ite authorised capital of the company. These estimates had 10 per cent. added to them in order to provide for any further contingen- cies which they could not foresee. As it would be_nec- • cessary to call the shareholders thgether again to obtain sanction for any scheme for raising the capital said to be required, he would not go into that subject at the pre- sent time ; but he might say—and he had the permission of the Mayor and the Deputy-Mayor (Sir John Harwood) whom he had seen that morning to say—that they had granted him an interview in order to lay before them the present position of the company. He therefore naturally. turned to the Mayor of the present day for some assistance to carry out the work which his prede- cessor had practically initiated. He was not at liberty to mention to the meeting any more than this, but he had the assurance of the Mayor and the Deputy-Mayor - that they would lay the application which he (Lord Egerton) had made to them before their colleagues of the Council who met that afternoon, and would meet again to-day, and that they would seriously consider what steps they might take in the matter. (Ap- plause.) The company bad made Manchester practically at the present time a seaport town, and therefore they thought the Corporation ought to do what Corporations of other seaport tams had done. (Applause.) He con- fidently appealed to the shareholders to support them in the endeavours they were making to complete success- fully this undertaking. (Applause.) Sir Joseph Lee seconded the motion, which was carried with unanimity. The retiring directors were unanimously re-elected. Mr. George Hicks was also re-etected an auditor of the company. A vote of thanks was unanimously passed to the chairman and directors of the company. The meeting then terminated. THE MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE CANAL. Subsequently to the meeting of the Ship Canal Com- pany a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Manchester City Council was held at the Town Hall, the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Mark) presiding. A communication was read from Lord Egerton of Tatton, and the following resolution wa4 passed :—" That it be recommended to the Couneil that the communication from the chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal Corn- any now read be referred to tt special c9l)lMittee that such committee be alltiltaiseel tO with the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal and others, and.obtain full information on the subject, and to pre- sent a report embodying the results of their inquiries and recommendations for consideration at a special meeting of the Council."

Warrington Corporation are tall", up a false position with regard r the allegad nuisance of the Intercepting DeP°l They affirm that no nuisance is caused, and ies,4 they resist the proposal for an inquiry which co demanded by the public. If they have confidell.,4 in their, statement, why should, they object to being put to the test ? As the Chairman ale time ago said, the Sanitary Committee should , the last persons in the world to creatc a nuisaocep; and, we would add, they should be the first pars° b •t to insist updh an inquiry when a charge is broug 40.4 against them of setting up a nuisance. It -of cunning but it wassnot wise to try to get rid ito the demand for an inquiry by asking the Council, on Tuesday, to approve of a minim° which not only invited members to visit Depots, but affimecl that ''no nuisance exists s;y either of the Depots." As the result proved, ttb'e was not satisfactory to the Council, for when 0 minute was pat to the vote it was rejected hi majority of two to one. It is true that Count' 00 , JENKINS consented to withdraw his notice foto inquiry for two months; and it is well t- 0 he has done so, seeing that by that the nuisaace which is scarcely discernible g, winter will probably have begun to assert i its:ft As Alderman PLATT pertinently remarhedy was idle to invite anybody to go down to 'aro Depots now, because even at the worst theYor never as bad in the winter as they are in the 6,, to, mer." It is not sufficient for the initabitant'or be told that at a particular date in raid-wino to the depots are no nuisance, if they have reesool. ;anticipate from pa§t experience that, when Wn 128 weather comes, their health will suffer from nuisance while their lives will be endangered:ort to Councillor PIERPOINT, who led the oppositi the objectionable minute, expressed the hoPe ja the report of the Medical Officer of Health soon be in the hands of the members. .14 to seem from the remarks of Alderman BITEG/gas
At

Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, that the Medical Officer of Health has already prepared an important report. Indeed he said that gentle- man had "a formidable report to present which would cost £20,000 to carry out." Why, if this -report is in existence, was it not laid before the Council? Is it quite fair to Dr. GORNALL to give what might prove to be a travesty of it by stating —without giving the grounds for the statement— 'that it "would cost £20,000 to carry it out"? We -do know this that the Medical Officer of Health has inade suggestions in the past for lessening the -nuisance at the Depots—suggestions which would not have cost £2OO to carry out, and yet they have not been acted upon. But what we wish to press home is this; he has, as we understand, prepared a Report on the Depots, and we wish to know whether the Town Council and the public •are to be afforded the benefit of his observations. In plain terms, is it to be published, or is it to ,be kept back? When Councillor SHAW GREEN furged that, before any decision was come to with tdgard to the demolition of insanitary property, the opinion of some practical person should be taken, in addition to that of the Medical Officer of Health, Alderman BURGESS replied that " the gen- tleman appointed by the Council must do that work." This is sound doctrine ; and it is equally sound as applied to the Depots. The Medical Officer of HeAlth, as "the gentleman appointed by the Council," has reported upon the Depots, even as he has reported upon insanitary property. Let the Report be made public, so that the Town Council and the ratepayers may have before them all the information that can be obtained to guide them in coming to a decision as to the important inquiry which will yet have to be made.

THE Rev. CANON WOOD, vicar of Canon Wood's Warning. the Parish Church, Runcorn, preached a sermon the other Sun- . day in the nature of a warning against Dissenters; and that the warning may not be lost sight of, or overlooked, the sermon has been printed in the "Runcorn Parish Magazine." We have read the discourse, and have been interested, if not edified. It is "milk for babes" so very much "let down" as to be of little or no value for nourishing pur- poses. It would seem that the Canon is sorely exercised in his mind because the Wesleyans of Runcorn have been bestirring themselves in aid of the London Mission ; so, instead of lending a help- ing hand, he tells his flock that "it will be easier and better to avoid giving support to such religi- ous effort outside your own church as you are now invited to countenance and assist." He adds—ii If Igo and take my place upon a Wes- leyan or any Nonconformist platform, I thereby recognise their organisation as forming a legitimate part of the Catholic Church in this land. Now an instructed churchman cannot do this." This is Understood to be a side blow at the Rev. Dr. PRES- TON, vicar of Holy Trinity, who has shown good • sense and catholicity of feeling by standing on the platform with Wesleyans when they were en- gaged in what he believed to be good work. Instead Of blaming the Rev. Dr. PRESTON, Canon WOOD would do well to open his heart and his mind and follow his example. Faith in the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man is not streng- thened by the preacher who in effect says : " Come to my Church if you would be saved; if you recognise any other you will run a risk of going to destruction." The Vicar's great argument against Dissent is that, as shown by the Registrar General's returns, it increases the number of sects; but he does not see that this argument cuts the ground from under his feet so *far as the Roman Catholio Church is concerned. The contention of that church is that the Church of England is a Dissenting offshoot—a schismatic sect. Oddly enough, Canon WOOD seems to " recog- nise " the Church of Rome while ho rofusos to "re- cognise" the Wesleyans and other nonconformists; for he says if members of the Church of England "give up their trust, i.e., if they speak or act as if the Church with her true ministry and her age- long usefulness were but one amongst many sects, then no centre is left—unless it be the foreign Church of Rome." Can it be that the Vicar of Runcorn is on his way to Rome, or is he merely muddled? We incline to the latter theory, since he goes on to admit, after all, that "these Nonconformists" are Christians; and if they are Christians what more does he want? Is it essential to salvation that man must not only be a Christian, but a member of the Church of England? And if-this is his view, will he go a little further and give his autho- rity for this evtraordinary doctrine? It can hardly be found in the Scriptures, for we no- where read that the Founder of Christianity was a member of the Established Church. Indeed, be had some severe things to say about the Estab- lished Church of his day; and gives no counten- ance to any" Church of the Land" as" the mother of them all." If Canon Wood will think less about the State and more about the Scriptures, he Will find it his highest duty, as it will be his greatest pleasure, to recognise and work with all men whom he can speak of as Christians. Were it otherwise, the conelusion would be inevitable that there was something wrong with his own Chris- tianity.

THINGS have not been going Ship Canal smoothly of late in the making of Prospects. the great waterway between Liver- pool and Manchester; but it would seem from the meeting of shareholders, which was held at Man- chester on Tuesday, that the worst has been seen. Differences with the executers of the late Mr. WALKER, the contractor, have led to the contract being terminated, the Company from the 24th of November last taking over the whole of the plant, and proceeding, with a free hand, to finish the canal as best they can. This means that a considerable sum of money will be locked up in plant until the canal is finished; and, further, that work yet to be done will be undertaken at a somewhat higher rate. More land has had to be purchased than Was thought necessary in the first instaneo ; and the sum of the situation is that further capital is -required to the time of £1,700,000. This is of course to some extent discouraging, and yet it may be Said to be the usual experience in the construction of great works. The unforeseen happens, and the linforeseen always costs money. No statement illas been made as to the estimated damage by the 'ate floods; but there can be no question that great damage was done; and that the work has been delayed several months. The con), •Putation at present is that the canal will even yet be completed by the middle of next Summer. but if we add six months to that We shall probably be nearer the mark. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
A lengthy, but highly interesting contribution from "A Nonconformist" on the Vicar of Run- corn's extraordinary sermon, is unavoidably held over until our next issue.

Lord R. Churchill is a man of surprises. He pre- sented himself at the House of Commons, on Tues- day night, not only with the familiar moustaches but with chin covered with hair. It is, just like him; he always was harum-scarum. Re.hastarrie d until his beard has grown, not at Jericho—but in Egypt.

The Rev. F. P. J. Greenfield, formerly chaplain of the Sussex County Asylum, was sued on Satur- day for £lOO as money owing to a turf agent for various betting transactions. He did not appear, and the case went against him. Let us charitably hope that he" went wrong" through being at the asylum; and that this betting man will become a, better man.

In another column, our readers will find an inte- resting biographical sketch of the late Mr. John Warrington Wood, sculptor. It is taken from the pages of the current issue of "The Magazine of Art." Amongst the magazine illustrations of the sculptor's work is one of "The Sisters of Bethany" which, through the generosity of Mr. Robert Davies, has found a home in the Warrington Art Gallery.

The Technical Education Committee of the Lancashire County Council have decided to recom- mend that the whole of the beer and spirit duty shall be applied to aiding technical education. This is stirring up local authorities—large and small ; they all want to be sure of a share. On Monday afternoon, the Newton Commissioners adopted the Technical Instruction Act. They are like Warring- ton and Widnes; they want to be "in it?'

Out-door workers have been frozen out; wages have.been suspended; there has been need for a soup kitchen-; there is a prospect of a loss on the sale of Longford manure equivalent to a rate of twopence in the pound—therefore increase the salaries of the School Attendance Officers, and of the manager at Longford Works. That is the logic of the wise men of Warrington as revealed by the proceedings of the Town Council.

Next week we shall . commence a series of "Notes from Manxland " from the pen of a most able contributor who has exceptional oppoitu- nities of watching the battle which is commencing there between Church and Dissent. As the Isle of Man is in possession of Home Rule, and is about to have a General Election as following upon a Reform Bill, it is hardlynecessary to say that the "Notes" will be of[more than ordinary interest.

Mr. McCarthy's temperate and reasonable statement of views on the Home Rule' question is in pleasant contrast to the "wild and whirling words" which Mr. Parnell has used since be was deposed as leader of the Irish Party. He has had an unusual quantity of bile to work off, but just now there are signs of less bitterness. It is about time Mr. Parnell recognised that he cannot wreck Home Rule as he has wrecked himself.

So far during the present session, Sir Gilbert Greenall, the member for Warrington, has not been in a position to attend to his duties in the House of Commons. The last time he appeared in public it was seen that he was in a feeble con- dition mentally and bodily. At his great age it can hardly be expected that he will recruit, and it would be well if he would relieve himself by re- signing his position as member for the borough. It is the way of the Liberal Unionists to dine and whine together. They had a banquet on Tuesday, and this is one bentonoo from Lord Har- tington's address :—" Their party must sometimes have felt disappointed that the arguments which . . . . had seemed to them so complete and convincing had appeared to have so little effect upon the minds of the great body of their fellow- counteymen." "Little effect "—it is well put ; they will need another dinner after that.

The British Government have scored in connec- tion with the Beliring Sea dispute by appealing to the Supreme Court of the United States. That court has decided that it has jurisdiction in the Sayward case. This does not settle the dispute in favour of England, for the issue has yet to be tried, but it is something gained to refer the case to the law. The people of the United States will have their mouths closed if their own courts de- cide against them.

It was stated at the Warrington Police Court,on Tuesday, that Thomas Lea, a forgernan, has paid as much as 25 2s. 6d. in fines, at different times, for neglecting to send his children regularly to school. Acid to this the time of the School Attendance officers and magistrates in trying the cases—all because education is only two-thirds free—and it will be seen how delightful is the system which still commends itself to the Tory party. When shall we have Free Education pure and undefiled?

The Scotch Railway Strike is at an end, and the men have returned to work without obtaining any substantial concessions. We shall hear a good deal of the loss of both parties to the dispute, but it is not all loss. The struggle will affect not only the Scotch but other Railway Companies. It will have paved, however roughly, the way to a ten if not a nine-hours day. The men were in the right, and right will be might in this matter before long. The ball has been set rolling, and it must be kept rolling. ,

The Mayor of Warrington very properly called attention at the closing of the soup kitchen on Saturday afternoon, to the fact that the Board of Guardians have reduced the number cf. tramps at the Workhouse, by depriving the tramp ward of artificial heat. It seems some of the tramps actually decline what his Worship called "a good chance of being frozen to death! What a sublime stroke of policy! How would it be to extend it by refus- ing food as well as warmth P Starving the inmates to death would certainly reduce the number.

A Chicago correspondent thus summarises the resnits of inquiries into the effect of the M`Kinley Tariff on the position of the American workmen: --" In no case that can be discovered have wages advanced; but in very many instances wages have been lowered, the employers giving as the reason the increase in the price of materials which has been brought about by the now tariff. In cases where wages have not been reduced the workmen suffer all the same in consequence of the in- creased cost of living." How is this for Protec- tion?

Mr. Gladstone has not succeeded in carrying the second reading of his. Disabilities Bill—more shame to the bigots of the House of Commons. As the musty law now stands an Atheist may be- come Lord Chancellor, or Lord Lieutenant of Ire- land, but not a Roman Catholic? The exclusion is a remnant of barbarism, and it ought to have been sufficient to mention it to have it removed from the Statute Book. . What do Tory Catholics think of this Tory insult to their loyalty in the year 1891?

GENERAL Satisfaction commands the vast army of people who use "SUNLIGHT SOAP."—Adrt. S, M. Meissonier, the famous painter, died on Saturday morning in his 79th year. It is believed that most of this great artist's works are at present to be feud in France and America-.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. Yesterday, before Dr. Steele and Major Hazlehurst, Edward Faulkner, a labourer, was charged with stealing; a silver watch worth 10s., the property of John Suther- land, on Wednesday. The police offered no evidence and the prisoner was discharged.—Mr. E. W. Humphreys remarked that it was not fair to charge a man in this way without a shred of evidence.—lnspector Bowyer said the Bench would not have remanded the prisoner on the previous day had there been no evidence. The prisoner was discharged.—William Hunter, a stranger, was charged with frequenting Wilson's Hotel with intent to commit a felony. On the previous day the prisoner was caught in the act of attempting to abstract money from the till. He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. HOT WATER HEATING.—Garland sends estimates free , Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. The half-yearly meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. R. Royle. Thg committee in their 57th half yearly report, state the total sales for the half-year amount to £38,181 is. 51d., being an increase of £lO6 14s. 91d. on the previous half year. The amount disposable, after chargirbe, all expenses including depreciation and interest on capital, deducting the checks purchased and excess dividend, left the net amount £4,864 18s. ()id. The com- mittee recommended a dividend of 2s. 6d. in the £ on £37,763 of check account book brought, which amounted to £4,720 7s. 6d. leaving a balance of £144 10s. 61d.,0ut of which it was proposed to add £7O 193. 6d. to the Reserve Fund and carry forward £73 us. Old. to the next half year. The accounts had been audited by the laccountant of the wholesale Co-operative Society, and were certified as correct. This report and the balance sheet were adopted. It was unanimously resolved that a branch be established at Appleton. It was also decided that at the annual meeting the voting be by capital books linstead of by a show of hands. UMRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. 84W W. UTTON'S, Sankey-it, Warrington.—Advt. SHOCKING FATALITY AT BURTONWOOD. On Tuesday morning an acccident having a fatal result, happened to a girl 17 years old at Burton- wood. The girl in question was employed as a domestic by Mrs. Carter, Alder Farm, Burtonwood, and on the morning named the two sons of Mrs. Carter were engaged in loading a cart with turnips and straw. When binding it, the domestic and Miss Carter, assisted in tightening the ropes. The cart was resting on the two front legs under the shafts, and the leg at the back of the cart, and they were just about finishing binding the straw, when the back leg of the cart gave way, and the cart tilted up, knocking down Mr. Carter, Miss Carter, and the domestic, and covering them with straw. The two Carters managed to extricate themselves, but when the unfortunate servant was got out she was found to be dead. She was lying with her face down- wards, and was much bruised about the shoulders and chest. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1891.

SFIIP CA.IsTA.I. STRIKE. The Ship Canal strike is not likely to be either very long or very serious. The men on the Barton section turned out, it seems, not for an advance of wages, but as a protest against "insulting language" said to have been used towards some of them by a walking ganger. On Thursday some hundreds of the men returned to work ; the rest determined to re- , main out till they got an apology.

ALLEGED THEFT AT NORLEY. On Monday, at the office of Messrs. Trafford and Cook, Northwich, before Mr. S. Woodhouse and Mr. R. W. Wilbraham, two young men, named James Edwards and James Kippax, of Norley, were charged with stealing four ducks and two hens, at Eddis- bury, on January 29th, the property of Dr. Payne, rector of Delamere. When formally charged, both prisoners admitted the offence.—They were re- manded until the 23rd inst., bail being accepted. FANCY Dar.ss BALL AT NEWTON. On Wednesday evening a fancy dress ball took place in the Town Hall, Newton, when all the elite of Newton and the district were present. The Town Hall was beautifully, and even lavishly decorated for the occasion. The room was altogether so metarmophosed, as to have the appearance of a spacious drawing room. Temporary retiring rooms were erected at one end of the hall, and were com- fortably furnished. The windows of the hall were heavily draped with cretonne curtains, and the walls were decorated with bannerettes and mirrors. Several choice plants and flowers were placed up and down the hall, and the band platform was also nicely draped. Cosy nooks were arranged by means of screens, and instead of the ordinary forms, com- fortable couches and easy chairs were in use. The decorations were carried out under the supervision of Mrs. J. Jones, Mr. Handyside, Mr. W. Birley and Mr. 11. H. L. Evans. A special band was engaged from Liverpool. Mr. Chantry of Warrington,catered satisfactorily. Dancing was very spiritedly carried on until about half past two on Friday morning.
ACTION BY A ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCILLOR AGAINST THE RAILWAY COMPANY.

His Honour, Judge Goldthorpe, and a jury were occupied for several hours at the County Court, on Wednesday afternoon, in hearing an action against the London and North-Western Railway Company, brought by Councillor James Hatton, who claimed £lO as damages, alleged to be due in consequence of injuries sustained by plaintiff's horse owing to the negligence of the company's servants. Mr. 11. L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pres- ton represented the railway company. It appeared that in August last the plaintiff sold a horse for .E5O to a Mr. Okell, of Bolton. The animal was taken to St. Helens railway station for consignment to Bol- ton, and placed in a horse-box by the company's servants. About two hours afterwards plaintiff was sent for, and he found the horse injured,in the stables at the railway station, and Mr. Menzies, veterinary surgeon was attending to it. Evidence was called to show that the horse was placed in the box in Mr. Hatton's presence, and that the plaintiff appeared to be satisfied with the arrangements made. The judge, in summing up, said the railway company were bound to find means of secur- ing the horse safely, and jt was for the jury to say whether they considered the horse properly fas- tened. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff for the amount claimed, with costs. "Oil. iF.s Cough Mixture, Chiretta Balsam. Relief in three minutes. Cures Bronchitis.
