THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT." • That business at Widnes Police Court during the past week has been very slack indeed. It is months since the magistrates had to deal with so few offences against the law. That it is sincerely hoped this state of Affairs will continue. That the Irish National League are preparing to run candidates at the approaching Local Board election. That the Vicar of Runcorn by the publication of his sermon dealing with Nonconformity has raised quite a torrent of feeling amongst the Wesleyans to whom he particularly referred,and also amongst the other Dissenting bodies and he is evidently in for a period of very strong adverse criticism. That "live and let live" is a very good motto in religious affairs as in secular matters, and no good comes of arousing sectarian jealousies. That the ratepayers will thank Mr. Imison for his lucid and instructive statement respecting the salaries of the officials of the Board of Improvement Commissioners. That it is generally accepted that figures can be made to prove anything, but when a little " dry light " is put into them in the manner of Mr: Imison the truth is arrived at. That several members felt humiliated at the ans- wering of an anonymous writer with a newspaper, but many beneficial reforms have been initiated by means of anonybous contributions to newspapers, and so long as a correspondent deals in facts and fair and temperate argument, one is at a loss to dis- dover where the humiliation arises. That surely a Commissioner is not above correct- ing error, and putting the ratepayers in possession of the truth, and this was all Mr. Humphreys sought and Mr. Imison courteously vouchsafed, and the ratepayers will be the gainers. That a correspondent in this journal last Saturday went somewhat beyond ordinary lines in a letter dealing with the election of Commissioners. It was suggested that the members of the Board used means to obtain election which no right-thinking man would condescend to employ. That the system of election is had, and in these days of the ballot cannot be defended, but the ratepayers will acquit our local rulers of having obtained election by illegal or unfair means. That Mr. J. W ilde, of the Widnes Alkali Works, has been appointed manager of the St. Helens dis- trict of the United Alkali Company.
EtUNCORN BOARD OF COMIIISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thurs lay. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there were present Messrs. Fisher, H. White, Pritchard, Lightburn, Wiswall, Abel, Mellor, Meadowcroft, lmison, llankinson, Humphreys, Dobson, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), J. W. Barker (surveyor).—The number of deaths registered dur- ing January amounted to 40. Of these two were in- quest cases, and of the remaining 38, nine were due to bronchitis, three to inflammation of the lungs. five to imperfect respiration, three to convulsions, four to whooping cough ; typhoid fever and scarla- tina caused one death each. The 40 deaths showed an average death rate of 26.0 and, exclusive of the inquest casas, of 25.3 per 1,000 of the estimated population.

div.head: tUNCORN AND TECHNICAL EDUCA-
div.p: tUNCORN AND TECHNICAL EDUCA-
TION.

We understand that the Cheshire County Council have determined upon aiding technieal education in the county by making to those local authorities which adopt the Technical Instruction Act, a grant equal in amount to that realized by the levy of a penny rate in the district seeking aid. This penny rate in Runcorn realises about £lBo,and should the Board of Commissioners adopt the Act, and levy a rate to carry it out, the County Council will grant a like amount to the institution. Rumour has been busy with regard to an offer made by Mr. Brunner, with a view to help in the establishment of a Tech- nical School in Runcorn, and in some quarters his proposal has been misunderstood. It cannot be too widely known that Mr. Brunner's promise is as fol- lows :—For every £lOO subscribed in Runcorn for technical education Mr. Brunner will add another £lOO, up to a total of £5OO. Should Mr. Brunner's offer be fully met, and it is sincerely to be hoped that it will be, there would be a nucleus of £l,OOO towards a school. Such a sum subscribed, together with the levy of a penny rate on th general dis- trict rate, would, there is little doubt, induce a liberal response from the County Council.

div.head: MR. W. 11. jUDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MR. W. 11. jUDE AT RUNCORN.

A numerous audience assembled in the National Schools on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of spending a" descriptive musical evening" with Mr. W. 11. Jude, of Liverpool. As a composer and as a musical entertainer, Mr. Jude enjoys an exten- sive and enviable reputation, and of his abili- ties both as a vocalist and as an instrumenta- list it is unnecessary to speak. In his monologue on Wednesday evening there was not one dull, uninteresting moment, and whether Mr. Jude indulged in the grave or in the gay of musical composition the attention of the audience never wandered. The applause throughout the evening was unanimous and hearty, and Mr. Jude kindly re- sponded to several of the encores. The various ; items on the attractive programme were rendered more interesting by the short descriptive sketch with which each was introduced, and Mr. Judes denunciation of the modern sentimental and comic songs, which he said were usurping the place of higher and nobler class of composition evidently met with the approval of his auditors, and he gave some examples of the "good old songs" in his own inimitable style. In • the harmonium solos Mr. Jude showed his power, and the wonderful command which he had of the instrument, which in popular phrase was almost made to speak. The ,1 piano used in the accompaniment of the songs was kindly lent by Mr. Timperley, of Lowlands-road. The concert was in aid of. the prize fund of the [ Parish Church Sunday schools, and a good sum would be realized.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOL FA CHOIR
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL FA CHOIR
CONCERT.

The second concert of the season, organised by the Tonic Sol-Fa Choir, was held in uncorn Public Hall, on Monday evening, and it is gratifying to re- cord that a large and appreciative audience as- sembled. The programme consisted of miscellaneous items and the principal vocalists were Miss Mouls- dale (soprano), Miss Meredith (contralto), E. Mor- lais (tenor), and Mr. Peploe (bass). The choir numbered about 50 voices, and opentd the concert with Macfarren's part song "Shepherds all and Maidens fair." In the course of the evening they also rendered "Softly roam,"" Pat a cake Baker's man," the Madrigal" Matona," " When Allan-a-dale went a- hunting," and" The Urchins' dance." Mr. J. Holford G.T.S.C.,the conductor of the society, again wielded the baton, and the manner in which the various items were sung was highly creditable to both conductor and ' choir. Possessing a thorough knowledge of the tonic sot fa notation, the members displayed taste and expression in their work, and the effects of light and shade in several of the pieces were shown to the fullest advantage. The audience frequently testified their approval by prolonged ap- plause. Miss Moulsdale is no stranger to Runcorn, and she received a hearty welcome•on her re-appearance. She scored an encore for her first item "Sing, sweet bird," which was admirably sung, and in response she gave " Somebody," in charming style. A similar com- pliment was paid her for an expressive rendering of "Kathleen Mavourneen," and she bowed her acknow- ledgment. Miss Meredith was equally successful in pleasing the tastes of:the audience. "In old Madrid," a 1 sentimental song, her sympathetic voice was heard to 1 great advantage, and she acknowledged the recall by an expressive vocalisation of "Daddy." An encore awaited her for " Alone on the raft," in which she did full jus- tice to her talents. A pleasing number was the duet "0 lovely peace," the voices of Miss Moulsdale and Miss Meredith harmonising beautifully, and a unanimous recall was the result.. Eos Morlais has a reputation as a skilful vocalist over a wide area, and ha maintained it on Monday evening. Although apparently suffering from huskiness through cold, the solo "Love is a dream," was sung by him with all his old charm, and later he gave ".By the fountain," in a manner that highly de- lighted the company. For both efforts he was enthusias- tically recalled, and he sang "Bonnie Mary Lea." Mr. Peploe's contributions were "The wandering minstrel," "Bandit's life" (encored), and "The skipper," and he was loudly applauded for each item. His voice is of robust quality, and he sang with considerable spirit and effect. A most successful concert, musically and finan- cially, was concluded by the National Anthem.

div.head: WORK IN COMMITTEE.
div.p: WORK IN COMMITTEE.

The Highway and Buildings Committee recommended that the sum of £6 17s. be paid to the Cheshire County Council for the erection of a sewer ventilating shaft out- side the police station. The Health Committee recom- mended :—That proceedings be taken to close the cellars in Gilbert-st. as dwellings, but that such proceedings be stayed for a period not exceeding six months to allow the owners of the said cellars to close them. That the appli- cation of Mrs. Sayle to have the fees due from her for the maintenance of her daughter in the Hospital amout- ing to £5 less 13s. contra account remitted be granted. —The Financa Committee reported that during the past month the receipts amounted to £939 14s. 91. and accounts amounting to £995 Os. 6d., were passed for payment. There was a balance of £1,185 15s. 10d. to be collectcd on General District Rate Account.—These minutes were passed.

div.head: WATERLOO BRIDGE.
div.p: WATERLOO BRIDGE.

The Waterloo Bridge Committee recommended that Messrs. H. Heys and Co.'s prices for curbs and channels for Waterloo Bridge be accepted.—ln moving the adop- tion of the minute, Mr. Pritchard said there would be 570 yards of curbs and channelling, and the cost would not exceed £4B. At the next meeting the Committee would have a resolution to submit with regard to the material of the footpath. If granolithic were decided upon, it would not be safe to Start upon it until April, when the frost had departed. Satisfactory progress was being made with the ironwork of the bridge, and it would be out of the hands of the contractor at the end of this month.—Mr. Meadowcroft remarked that there appeared to have been no men worth naming on the bridge, and for some time very little progress appeared to have been made. He Fished the Committee to urge the contractor to push forward the work. As to the new portion of the approach of the bridge, it was very much cut up, and deeply covered with mud; could not the Conirnitteo OfLUCO it to be envered with macadam P—Mr. Pritchard replied that according to thecontract the time was up on the Ist March, and the contractor was confi- dent he would have completed his work before that date. After passing the resolution as to the curbs, the Committee would proceed to make the roadway.—The recommendation was adopted.

div.head: _LAIV CLERK'S SALARY AND DUTIES.
div.p: THE _LAIV CLERK'S SALARY AND DUTIES.

Mr. Imison moved that resolution No. 1,160 be am- ended by substituting £135 for £llO as the rate of salary to be paid to the Law Clerk, and that the following words," But the Law Clerk may charge for work inci- dental to the preparation of contracts where the parties contracting with the Commissioners pay the costs there- off, and may also in case of legal proceedings recover costs from the parties opposed to the Commissioners," be added after the words "Parliamentary business." The increased. salary to date from sth February, The resolution, when anionded, to read as follows s—t, That the salary of the Law Clerk be fixed at the rate of £135 per annum, payable monthly, and that such salary be a maximum salary in respect of the following duties : To discharge all the duties of Law Clerk which may from time to time arise, to attend all meetings of the Board, all meetings of the Highways and Buildings Committee, and of the Health Committee, and any other meetings of Committees when required by the respective Chairmen to attend. The only legal work for which extra remun- eration shall be paid, being proceedings in the High Court of Justice and Parliamentary business, but the Law Clerk may charge for work incidental to the preparation of contracts. where the parties contracting with the Com- missioners pay the costs thereof, and may also in case of legal proceedings recover costs from the parties opposed to the Commissioners. To furnish the Secretary with copies of all correspondence within 24 hours of its receipt or despatch." The resolution Was unanimously carried.
THE SALARIES OF THE OFFICIALS. IMPORTANT DISCUSSION.

In accordance with private notice he had given,Mr. Imi- pn,chairman of the Finance Committee,Mr. Humphreys asked that gentleman what had been the increase in the amount of salaries paid to officials of the Board during the past six years, and if he would also inform the Board what was the increase in the rateable value of the town during the like peried.—Mr. unison replied that during the past six years he found that thesalary of the Medical Officer had been increased £25; Inspector of canal boats £lO ; Nuisance Inspector £25; Secretary £4O; making a total of £lOO. The rateable value had increased £4,495 during the same period. In 1885 the rateable value was £50,989; last year £55,474. There ought to be some explanation about these salaries, because many extra ordinary ideas seemed to be abroad as to what the Com- missioners had dose; in fact some people, who ought to know better,displayed a lamentable amount of ignorance. Taking first the salary of the Medical Officer. At the time this salary was fixed, the duties of the office were merely nominal. He only gave the Board the monthly returns such as the births and deaths, information which cott' I have been got equally well from the registrar, Mr. Coleburn, but since that time the duties of the Medical Officer had been made more useful. Instead of having a nominal officer they had an active one whom the Board required to inspect property and to frequently consult with the Committee. Under these circumstances this could not be looked upon as an increase of salary for pre- cisely the same duties, as the whole scope of the office had been altered. He saw that a writer in a newspaper had tried to make out that the salaries had been increased nearly £3OO, but the Board had made a nominal officer into an active one, and had made two new appointments. Of these two new appointments, take first the rate col- lector, who was paid £7O a year. He almost saved his salary in this way. Prior to his appointment the rate was collected at once. The Board laid a rate for the twelve months and the Board collected it as such. Now they took advantage of their collector. to levy the rate every six months,based upon the difference in the assessments between the March rate and the Sep- tember rate ; and they might be surprised to find that last year the alteration gave the Board an income ?f £4O extra, and this year of £32; in addition to which the total collection was very much greater, because the loss from empties and removals was very much less; so that it would be perfectly fair to rake the amount of the saving fromthe salary. (Hear, hear.) The Board.had also appointed the Inspector of Nuisances withinthe six years half of the salary they received from the County Council, a point that did not seem to have occurred to some of their critics. They had also increased the salary of the Canal Boat Inspector £lO. This was a very small salary to commence with, and was only £2O at the present time. Nobody would suggest that a man could do even mere nominal work for very much less than that. The salary

of the secretary had also been increased during the period they were talkinc, about. He thought it had been done at twice. The Board thought the duties of the office had increased to such a great extent that they were entitled to raise his salary. During this period, if they calculated the income on the ordinary general district rate of 25., the board would have an increase in their income of nearly £5OO a year, so that it was unfair to urge that the duties were precisely the same as they were then. The town had grown,the work had grown, and naturally the number of meetings the officers had to attend had entirely altered since six years ago. In the figures given in the paper, it is made to appear that the Law Clerk's salary had been increased from £5O to £lOO. The writer seemed to be unaware that the late law clerk was paid fees for extra services, which almost amounted to the sum now paid as salary. In an accurate comparison it would be necessary to remember the points he had touched upon. Mr. Humphreys said his simple object had been to let the ratepayers, as far as possible know the exact facts, and not be led away by statements which if not actually untrue suppress such an amount of truth as to draw very near to that designation. Mr. Lightburn was in favour of allowing the rate- payers to know all that was going on, and he was very pleased with Mr. liaison's statement, but he wished to qualify it by stating they; 'did not go before the rate- payers in an apologetic manner. The ratepayers ought to have sufficient confidence in those whom they elected, and not wish at every end and turn to 'Scrutinize not in a very charitable spirit, their actions. Those critics outside did not represent in any sense the general rate- payers, so far as lie knew. While much obliged to Mr. Imison he deprecated the making of a statement to please busybodies: Mr. Humphreys said when in a public print there was a direct statement of figures, if those were not contradicted those ratepayers who were inclined to be favourably dispensed to the Board must come to the conclusion that there was something which wanted ex- planation, and Mr. liaison's statement was given in justice' not to the busybodies, for whom he had no regard whatever, but to those ratepayers who in the presence of uncontradicted statements may come to a very wrong conclusion. Mr. Wisnall thought it humiliating that so much notice should be taken of an anonymous statement. Mr. Pritchard thought Mr. Imison's statement quite sufficient justification for what the Board had done in regard to salaries and ought to be highly satisfactory to all concerned. In addition to Mr. unison's remarks he wished to point out that the compounders used to leave the payment of their rate to the close of the year ; now that the Board had a collector they were waited upon al- most as soon as the rate was levied, and thus a consider- able saving in the form of interest accrued. Mr. Meadowcroft said that he had taken an economi- cal view of the questions before the Board, and he had always given free, full, and independent criticism upon any expenditure he thought required it. He was not one of those veio took a high and mighty position, and said the7ratepayers- had no right to question the Board as to the policy they adopted or the course they had pursued. He thought they had a perfect right. (Hear, hear.) The ratepayers did not come there to lis- ten to the discussion or to enter into any conversation with the Commissioners about it, and, whilst he did not attach much importance to anonymouscommunications, yet he took it that the action of the board was sufficient- ly above Board, as to stand criticism in anonymous or from gentlemen who thought fit to declare their per- sonnel. With regard to the collection of the rate, he did not give so much credit to the collector as Mr. Imison. He attributed the improvement in a considerable degree to the fact that there was a very larger population in the tqwn, in the works, and consequently they had less empty property in the town. At the same timethe thought the explanation given was very favourable, and one which ought to have been given in justice to the Board and he did nct think they ought to complain of the time spent upon the subject. Mr. Dobson said it was the first time in his 18 years' experience that the Board had condescended to discuss anonymous letters, and he hoped in future they would not take up the time of 18 members in doing so. The Chairman said the explanation of Mr. Imison was satisfactory to the Board, and would,he thought, be sati- factory to all reasonable ratepayers. The Board had nothing to hide,but if Mr. Humphreys had asked his question to satisfy people who had written the letters he had seen in the newspapers, he did not think that pos- sible, and he would never think of answering them. He felt sure that all the reasonable ratepayers were satis- fied with the action of the Board, and that if theyhad a charge to make against them, they would make it in a manly, straightforward way. (Hear, hear.) These letters had not concerned him one bit.

Mr. Imison said he thought the ratepayers had a duty to the Commissioners, as the Commissioners had to them. The Commissioners gave time and any ability they pos- sessed to the service of the ratepayers, but however estimable a man might be in his private life, when he joined that Board he was almost classed as a fool or a rogue. (Hear, hear.) He did not consider himself either one or the other. Being on that Board had not been any interest to him—not to the extent of a single copper—and so far as he was concerned he did not care if the rate- payers said they did not want him to-morrow. He should have more time to attend to his business, and perhaps more opportunities of recreation and other pursuits, which would be far more beneficial to him than sitting at that table in a heated atmosphere night after night, solving various questions. If the ratepayers thought fit to put anyone in his place they were quite at liberty to do it. The discussion then ceased. AN _EFFORT FOR INCREASED RAILWAY FACILITIES. .

Mr. Humphreys drew the attention of the Board to a new railway which it was proposed to bring into North- wich, through certain very populous and industrial and agricultural districts from the east coast. One of the objects of the promoters was to connect these districts with the Ship Canal and it was proposed to do that by running a straight line from Knutsford to the docks of the Company at Latchford. Mr. Humphreys asked the Board whether it would not be worth their while, as the representatives of the interests of the town, to make a strenuous effort ti) see whether they could not offer the proposed Company an inducement to come straight from Knutsford to what he ventured to say would better dock accommodation of Runcorn. The benefit of being connected with this projected railway could not be over estimated and if the Board succeeded they would be amply repaid for any expense they might incur.—ln answer to Mr. Wiswall as to whether the scheme was placed in a practical form. Mr. Humphreys said the fact that a sum of £211,000 had been deposited in Parliament showed that the promoters meant busi- ness, The capital was fixed at £5,000,000. After some discussion, the subject was 'referred to the Legal and Parliamentary Committee for consideration.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

IVESLETAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—At the meeting of this class held last evening week, Mr. John Jones gave a paper on the eight hours question in which in his opinion it was desirable that eight working hours should be adopted in order to provide work for the un- employed. An animated discussion ensued, in which amongst others the following took part :---Messrs. Robin- son, Limbert, Rhodes, Dawson, Gould, Brown, and Wright. ALLEGED Sam. ROBBERY.—At the Frodsham Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Thomas, Ellen Ellis, an elderly woman from Newport, was charged with hav- ing stolen a cardigan jacket, value 13s. 6d., the property of John Kay and Son, clothiers, Main-st., on the 2nd inst., and Mary Hollins was charged with receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen.—Ellis admitted having committed the robbery. Hollins said she did not know that Ellis had stolen it.—Prisoners were remanded for a week. UNION CHURCH.—On Monday evening, the first of three lectures was delivered in th.e Union Church, by the Rev. John Yonge, of Warrington; on " Nonconformity : Its testimony and sufferings in the reign of Elizabeth." .A good number of lantern pictures were exhibited by Mr. Robinson, of Overton, illustrating some of the most not- able events which occurred during the years 1558 to 1603. The lecture itself was replete with the history of the wonderful spread oi the gcspel during the times of so great persecution. PRIMROSE LEAGUE MEETING.—A meeting of the llod- sham District Habitation of the Primrose League was held in the Girls' School, Church-st., on Monday even- ing. Mr. James Reynolds, J.P. (Chief Ruling Councillor of the Habitation), presided, and was supported by Mr. Alfred Thomas (hon. treasurer), Colonel Ashton (warden). Mrs. Ashton (hon. secietary), and Mr. James Croston, of Upton Hall,near Macclesfield. There was a good attend- ance. Mr. Croston, in an interesting and lucid speech, lasting nearly an hour and a half, touched en all the lead- ing political topics of the day, including the Primrose League, the eight hours movement, free education, foreign policy, taxation, allotments, artizans' dwellings, agricultural and Irish affairs. THE FARMERS' AUCTION COMPANY.—A intkting of the directors and shareholders of this company was held on Monday at the Bear's Paw, Frodsham, Mr. Heywood (chairman of the directors) presided. There were also present—Messrs. A. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, J. Frith, W. Houghton, R. Bate, W. Yarwood, Hutchinson (secre- tary), H. Lowe, &c. The statement of accounts showed that the turn over during the past seven months had been £5,000, there having been 13 salesof stock hold, compris- ing 235 head of cattle (including calves),l,69o sheep,and 36-pigs,which had been sold. The directors had discharged a large portion of the formation expenses out of the pro- I -fit and loss account. They recommended a dividend at the rate of 10 percent. per annum, leaving a balance ift I hand to be placed to the depreciation account.—The Chairman spoke in flattering terms of the prospects of the company, and proposed the adoption of the report I and financial statement.—Mr. Youd seconded, and the proposition was unanimously carried.—The directors wereelected as follows—Messrs. Heywood, Walter Harri- son, W. Houghton, J. Frith, Ellison, Henry Lowe, R. Bate, Percival and Baxter. Mr. C. E. Linaker was re- elected auditor, the Chairman speaking of his qualifica- tions and kindness in praiseworthy terms.—Mr. C. E. Linaker (hon. auditor), said the success during the past seven months had been most encouraging. Votes of thanks to the Chairman, &c., concluded the proceedings.

div.head: RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.
div.p: RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting of the directors and shareholders of this company was held yesterday morning at the Board Room of the works, and our representative was admitted to report the proceed- ings. Mr. F. Rigby J.P., presided, and there were present Major Hazlehurst J.P., Messrs. James Hand. ley J.P., T. Handley, W. Handley, James Pritchard, and J. R. Frith, (manager). The directors in sub- mitting the audited statement of accounts for the past year, reported that " The Revenue Account shows a balance of £4023 ss. 4d., out of which the directors recommend the payment of a dividend of £lO per cent per annum, leaving the sum of £23 ss. 4d. to be added to the Profit and Loss Account the balance of which after payment of divi- dend will be £599 15s. 9d. the Reserve Fund £3354 2s. Bd." The Chairman moved the adoption of the report and the declaration of a dividend of 10 per cent., per annum, free from income tax, on the subscribed capital. He remarked that it was the policy of the company as well as its duty to supply the consumers with gas of statu- tory quality at as low a rate as possible. The increased consumption of gas had helped the Company a good deal, otherwise it might have been. their unfortunate duty tcr raise the price, but owing to a new main having been laid in High-st. and at Weston, the consumption had increased something like six per cent, which upon the rental was a very satisfactory amount—Mr. James Handley seconded the motion, and Mr. Pritchard remarked that the report • was an evidence of the economical way in which the directors had carried on the concern.—Mr. W. Handley said that the last report showed the £4,009 as the balance of revenue, whereas this year without an increased price, the amount was £4,023 so that there must have beenvery great care in the management to arrive at sach a result.—Mr. J. Handley and Major Hailehurst having :made some observations, i The Chairman said the standard price of gas n Run- corn was 3s. 6d., and that the company were entitled to pay a dividend of one per cent. more if they deemed it advisable, the report was unanimously adopted.—On the proposition of Mr. Pritchard seconded by Mr. W. Handley a vote of thanks was aveorded to the chairman, who, in replying, proposed a similar compliment to the secretary and manager, Mr. Frith, for his admirable management. The motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: LECTURE ON NONCONFORMIST HISTORY.
div.p: LECTURE ON NONCONFORMIST HISTORY.

On Thursday evening the Rev. John Yonge gave another lecture on "Non-conformist History," in Wycliffe Church, Warrington. There was , a large audience present. The lecture was illustrated in a very interesting manner by lime-light views which were under the management of Mr, A. H. Lee. The subject of the lecture on this occasion was " Non- conformity : its Testimony and Sufferings in the reigns of Charles 11. and James 11.-1660 to 1658." In the course of his remarks, Mr. Yonge said the period of 28 years which they were to review had been accurately described as one of "humiliation for the country, corruption in the government, cruel oppression directed upon certain classes of the people ; but, on the other hand, so often marked by instances of such rare fidelity to principle, in the ' face of the suffering and persecution, us to make it in some sort an heroic age in the story of the nation and in the struggle for civil and religious liberty." They had to note, moreover, that it was a period that produced some remarkable men, of whom some were notorious alone for their lack of virtue, while others shone forth by contrast all the more luminously for patriotism, power and worth. The first portrait thrown on the screen was that of Charles 11., one who was called and styled a King, but who in actual fact was a vile and worthless man. Never before or since has England possessed such la ruler, as it was devoutly to be hoped she never would know his like again. Views were next given of the landing of Charles at Dover, of old London and of Charles's entering into it. The second Charles proved to be as masterly an adept at break- ing his engagements and his promises as ever his Ifather had been. He had promised all kinds of good 'things about religion and religious liberties. He had spoken respectfully, and even more warmly than that, of Presbyterianism; so that the Presby- terians had imagined that the Restoration of Charles would introduce for them the ecclesiastical milleniun. It was, therefore, looked upon as of evil omen, that, on the very day after his return, Charles should say to one of his courtiers that "Presbyterianism was no religion for a gentleman." A straw might show how the current runs, and this chance word of the king indicated only too plainly how matters ecclesiastical were bound to go. Very speedily other signs of the set of the tide began to appear. Among these was the dom- ineering attitude assumed by the now uppermost party, that of the Episcopal Church, especially in the country. The persecution suffered by John Bunyan—portraits of whom and a view of Bedford gaol were given,—were next referred to. Mr. Yonge also referred to the passing of the Act of Uniform- ity and the ejection of Nonconformist ministers, and their subsequent further persecution. Views illus- trative of the great fire acd the great plague of London were given and these dreadful events were eloquently described by Mr. Yonge. The sufferings of the Scotch Covenanters and the Quakers were touched upon and illustrated, and in the concluding part et his lecture Mr. Yonge gave a highly interest- account of the events which led up to the expulsion from the throne of the persecuting king, James 11., and the accession thereto of William and Mary. Amongst other lantern views that were given were those of the trial of Lord William Russell, the last interview of Lord Russell with his family, portrait of James 11., the arrest of Richard Baxter, Baxter before Judge Jefferies, the Duke of Monmouth's advance upon Taunton, the burning of Elizabeth Gaunt, and the eleven bishops going to the tower.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

OF UNSOUND MIND.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday afternoon,:Annie Mairs, was brought up before Dr. Brabazon charged with being a person of unsound mind, and was sent to the Macclesfield Asylum. BAND or Hon MEETIMG.—The monthly public meet- ing in connection witn the Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening, Mr. J. R. Taylor presiding. His brother Mr. R. J. Taylor, delivered an address to the members, who gave a number of re- citations. Miv Brown sang, and a dialogue, entitled " A-Happy New Year," was taken part in by Messrs. Richard Beardmore, William Percival, Thos. Chorley, and Ralph Heathcote.

THE POPULAH-60SCERT5.—The weekly concert took place on Saturday evening, when there was a large attendance. The Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston presided and delivered an address. The programme opened with a duet by the Misses Tetlow, which was well rendered. Songs were contributed by Miss Macpherson, Mr. and Mrs. Hauxley, Mr. Moore, Mr. J. Thomason, Dr. and Mrs. Williamson, Mr.lHinde' and Mr. H, Tetlow. Miss Hard- man sang twice with banjo accompaniment and also gave a selection on the violin. Dr. Fox and Mr. Roger- son each contributed a reading. The anthem "Praise the Lord," and the glees "Dawn of Day" and "Who will o'er the Downs," were effectually sung, and the concert, which passed off very successfully, was brought to a conclusion by the singing of the National Anthem. THE Locer, BoAnn.—The monthly meeting of the Board took place on Thursday night. Present: Mr. H. Cameron (chairman), Messrs. Swallow, Brazendale Gib- bon, Thomasson ; Mr. T. J. Ridgway, law clerk; Mr. W. Mallard, clerk; Dr. Fox' medical officer of health; Mr. •Jas. Mort,lsurveyor, and Mr. W. Severs, gas managers. Dr. Fox presented his annual report for the Lymm dis- trict, which stated that the number of births registered during the year was 171, which was equivalent to an annual birth-rate of 30•5, which is slightly above the average of 29.7 per 1,000. The number of illegitimate births is .eleven, or a rate of 643 per cent., which is slightly in excess of England and Wales. The number of deaths from all ages and from all causes is 75, which is seven fewer than in the previous year; and the death rate is thus reduced from the low figure of 149 to the still lower one of 134. This is the lowest general death-rate in the ten districts, urban and rural in the Mid-Cheshire Combination. The zymotic is prac- tically nil, as there has not been a single case during the year 1890. The sanitary arrangements throughout the year have been good, and Heatley was now being supplied with water. Dr. Fox suggested that the streets should be named and houses numbered. It would be of advantage in giving notice of infectious diseases, registration, post office, and for other reasons. Mr. Mort was instructed to state estimates for the next meeting.

BEING ON SCHOOL PREMISES FOR AN UNLAWFUL PURPOSE. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, Joseph Percival, was charged with being on the premises of the Girl's School, People's College, Arpley-st., the previous morning for an unlawful purpose. Chief-constable Hunt said the complainant in the case was Mr. Twiss, schoolmaster at the College. The defendant was styled as a tan yard labourer, but was often to be seen loafing about at the railway stations. Between 1.1 a.m. and 12 p.m., on Wednesday morning two little girls, 9 and 10 years old respectively, were in an out- building and saw a man's hand, and one of them was touched by someone, but did not see who it was. Mr. Twiss was called, and saw the prisoner getting away over a wall in the rear. Mr. Twiss followed, and called to Mr. Dixon,veterinary surgeon, who held him till a police- man came up. The man was brought to the police station and charged. The man had been watched some time Since hanging about the premises in Bold-st.—The pri- soner admitted being on the school premises, butdenied having an unlawful object. —Mr. Twiss and another wit- ness gave evidence in support of the Chief-constable's statement,and the prisoner was sent to gaol for a month's hard labour.
THEFT OF NEWSPAPERS.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, Harry Walrus- ley, news agent, 172, Liverpool-road, Sankey Bridges, was charged with stealing, on the lOtk ult., five copies of the" Liverpool Post," value 5d., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. Mr. Preston, solicitor, appeared for the prosecution, and stated the facts of the case.—Charles Lyon, reporter for the" Post," deposed—On the 10th ult., he went with his brother to Bank Quay Station. He counted the copies of the " Post" in a parcel , addressed to Mr. Thomas Edmunds, news agent, and then concealed himself be- hind some waggons. In five minutes, when the station was deserted, he saw the prisoner come in, take three parcels addressed to himself, and then extract several papers from Mr. Edmunds's par- cel. Witness came out of his place of concealment and taxed him with his offence, and' on counting the papers again, found five short. There had been com- plaints for the last six weeks from Mr. Edmunds, nearly every Saturday, about his papers being short. The prisoner begged witness not to be hard upon him, and he replied he did not seek to press it unduly, but was in duty bound to report the matter to the head office.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said it was the first time he had committed the offence, and he would never do. the like again.—Mr. Preston said the prisoner had admitted having taken the papers before, and evidence would now be called to prove this.—The Bench thought this was un- necessary, the prisoner having pleaded guilty.—He was fined £1 and costs (a 2s. in all) ; in default 14 days.
AUDACIOUS THEFT OF POTATOES BY A BOY.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, William Clarke, a boy, was charged with stealing quan- tities of potatoes the property of his late employer, William Percival, greengrocer.—Chief Constable Hunt said the prosecutor was formerly a farmer at Appleton but latterly had given, up farming and taken up potato dealing. The prisoner prior to Christmas was employed more or less on the prosecutor's farm by his brother, ana also assisted the complainant in conveying potatoes to Warrington. During that time he had some potatoes in a portion of the old premises known as Jones's buildings, and prisoner had on leaving the prosecutor's employ- ment retained thekey of these stores. Mr. Percival missed potatoes value 125., on the 7th ult., also £2 worth on the 14th ult.,and on the 30th ult. 21 loads from the stables of the Seven Stars in Bridge-st. He was reporting the matter to Constable Bell in the 'street, and as he was doing so the prisoner passed, and was given into custody by Mr. Percival as the thief. The boy admitted the thefts, and said he had sold the potatoes to Mrs. Broughton, Mar- ket-st.,for Bs. a load. They were worth 10s. a load. He was charged with stealing three loads value £3 95., and replied "I have nothing to say."—Mr. Percival said what Mr. Hunt stated was quite correct, but he had missed a lot more than had been mentioned. The prisoner brought the potatoes away in a hand cart, and got two boys to assist him. Witness had supplied. Mrs. Broughton once with potatoes before Christmas.—Mrs. Broughton having givenevidence the prisoner was committed to jail for 14 days' hard labour for the first offence, and in the other two cases convictions were recorded against him.
CHARGES OF MEFT.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thursday, William Pliggins, nricksetter's labourer, and William Lennox, bricksetter, both of Warrington, were charged with stealing from inside the shop door of John Gandy, Bridge-st., on Tuesday afternoon, a bucket, containing 281bs. of lard, value 93. 4d. Chief Constable Hunt said the bucket having been missed about two o'clock. and the prisoners being suspected they were watched by Detective-Sergeant Monaghan, who about six o'clock saw them coming along Mersey-st., Higgins carrying the bucket of ;lard on his shoulder. Higgins was about to enter a fish shop by a side door. when Monaghan stopped him. Hs said he had bought the lard of a woman for 2s. on Warrington Bridge. Lennox said he knew nothing about it.—Mr. Gandy said the bucket produced, was very like the one he had lost, and he saw Higgins stand- ing about the door,and Ernest Gandy,son of the previous witness, deposed to missing the bucket from the door. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan gave evidence confirming the Chief Constable's statement.-Higgins now said he had bought the bucket from a man for 3s. 6d. and Lennox said Higgins told him he had bought it, and wanted to sell it, and he merely helped him to dispose of it,in a fried fish shop for as.-The prisoners were fined2os. and costs each,in default a month's imprisonment.—John Jeffries was charged with stealing from a building in course of erection in Marsh House-lane, a bass contain- taming certain tools, value 7i., the property of Amos Hamblett. The Chief Constable said Hamblett on Tues- day night left his tools in the building,and the following morning found they were gone, and the prisoner who was his labourer,did not come as usual. The prosecutor consequently lost his day's work. lrhe tools were dis- covered at Leslie's second-hand dealers, Mersey-st., she having given 2s. fox' them.—Amos Hamblett and Mrs. Leslie corroborated this statement, the latter stating that the prisoner brought the tools and said " they " were all " on'the drink," and he would buy them back on Saturday. She would have charged 2s. 6d. when he came back.—Mr. Hunt: That is pawnbroking. You have no license.—The Chairman: You have no right to do that.—Witness: That is all I would have got if I had sold them.—The prisoner said he did not get the tools • from the building but from another man. He and the prosecutor had been drinking together. .The Chairman said the prisoner had been up four times previously for stealing.—Mr. Hunt: Those cases a.re certain but there is a blacker sheet than that against hiln somewhere.—Hamblett, in reply to the chairman, said the prisoner and he had had a beer together on• Monday, but not on Tuesday.—Mr. Hunt: All this week the bricksetters and their labourers have been on the spree. —The prosecutor seemed very unwilling to press the case, but the prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days.—George Williams was charged with stealing on Wednesday night a coat, a vest, and a muffler, value 10s., the property of Thomas Diddlestone, of Pierpoint- at. The prisoner was a complete stranger to the town and had introduced himself into the Dallam forge works and stolen the articles from a cupboard into which the prosecutor, one of the workmen, had put them. The prisoner was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Alderman_ Burgess (chairman), and

• Councillor Voiseli. Assauurngo A CONSTABLE.—John Hopkins was charged with assaultina P.C. Turner, in Scotland road, on the night of the 27th inst. The prisoner's brother, George Hopkins, had, on the previous Wednesday been com- mitted for two months' hard labour for being concerned with John in the assault, the particulars of which we reported last week. John had been apprehended by Tur- ner at Daley's lodging-house on a charge of theft, but brutally assaulted the constable on the way to the bride- well, George coming up and joining his brother in the attack and releasing him from custody, also escaping himself but being immediately re-captured, while John got clear off. He in his turn was now sentenced to two months' imprisonment, with hard labour.—Mr. Brown, the County Court bailiff, was rewarded by the Court for the assistance he had given the constable in apprehend- ing George Hopkins.

-DESERTION FROM TIIR ARMY.--John Payne, charged with deserting the Royal Sussex Regiment, stationed at Preston, was remanded to Walton to. await an escort. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, and Aldermen Harrison
and-Davies.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—James Stokes was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting his wife in Winwick-st., on Saturday night. A police constable having given evidence, Samuel Gough deposed to seeing the man kick and abuse his wife, and said he pulled the man away from her. The wife was called and made a statement that he did not assault her, but Alderman Harrison said after Mr. Gough's evidence they could not believe her assertion, though he could make allowance for her as no doubt she was afraid of the brute assaulting her again. She denied this, and Alderman Harrison told her he could not believe her and she was making herself liable to be committed for perjury.—Witness : He has never been a brute to me.—Alderman Harrison • He is nothing else to abuse a poor little woman ag you are in c?mparison to him.—The prisoner, who had been four times previously before the Bench, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.—Mary Roberts, drunk and disorderly in Market-st., on Saturday night, was fined ss. and costs or seven days. Thomas Lees was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., the same night, with deserting on the 4th of July last, from a milatia regiment sttioned at Ashton, and with breach of the i peace n Winwick-st., on September 12th, 1888. For the first-named offence he was fined ss. and costs or seven days. The deputy magistrate's clerk: There is. no constable to prove the breach of the peace case, and the other case will be dealt with when we get authority. div.head: STRIKE OF SAILORS, &c.
div.p: STRIKE OF SAILORS, &c.

The struggle between the Shipping Federation and the allied unions of sailors, firemen, Sic. commenced at Car- diffpn Tuesdayafterpoon, when the tippers left off work The Federation officials declare that they have 2,000 hands ready to work the tips. At a meeting of repre- sentatives of the allied unionin London, oniTuesday, it was resolved to support the action of workmen who re- fuse to work with non-unionists.
On Thursday morning the whole of the tippers and cranemen at the Bute Docks, Cardiff, struck work be- cause the company had summoned several tippers who left owrk without notice.

Massey met the drop out, and Stephens failing to reply, Thorniley dribbled on, and passing to Holmes,the latter made an effort, being grassed under the posts.- A corkscrew run by Evans was the next point of interest, and although Stephens staved off the attack, another burst of passing between the Bates, Barnes, and Mas- sey again took play on the Leeds line. div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTONI 2ND v. ROCHDALE RAM:MRS.—The 2nd team journeyed to Rochdale, and made a very creditable draw. Williams started for the visitors, and after several scrimmages on the line, the visitors' forwards rushed over, Hilgary scoring,Heesome kicking the goal. In the second half the Rangers scored. Final score :—Warring- ton, 1-4; Rangers, 1-0.

- WIDNES V. TYLDESLEY (A Teams).—At Widnes, before a small attendance. Widnes kicked off, and from a scrimmage in front of goal Minton got possession and scored. Mullinger failed at goal. Widnes were after- wards unable to break through their opponents' excel- lent defence. Half-time result :—Widnes, 1 try, 1 minor; Tyldesloy, 1 minor. Final result :—Widnes, 1 goal, 2 tries, 1 minor ; Tyrdesley. 2 minors. RUNCORN V. ROCHDALE.—RochdaIe was the rendezvous of the Runcorn fifteen on Saturday, when they found the Hornets ground quite unfit for the purpose the piece 1 of land is used for. Teams will soon be tired of having to mudlark to please Rochdale folk. Rochdale was reached in good time, an early start being made. For a time Rochdale fought hard, but soon the Cheshire fifteen asserted their superiority, and won the game by two goals, one try to nothing. Houghton kicked a goal from a penalty place, Davies scoring the other tries after some clever passing. Whilst the first team Were beating 1 the Hornets at Rochdale, Runcorn," A" was doing the rubbing in process for the Hornets" A "at Runcorn, to 1 the tune of 5 goals, 2 tries to Hornets 1 goal. On this form Runcorn" A "are the champions in this district. WIDNES V. TYLDESLEY.—The return fixture between these two clubs was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday afternoon in beautiful weather. Both clubs were fairly well represented, and as may be expected, a mod game resulted. Smith started the ball for Widnes against t strong wind, and the visitors had to play on the defensive. Two minors were conceded to Tyldesley, and subsequently-Smith crossed the Widnes line, and was awarded a try. The attempt at goat, however, failed. From the'drop-out Whelan had an easy chance, but failed to get through, and Cork getting possession obtained a try after an excellent run, which, like its predecessor, was not converted. On changing ends Wid- nes had the advantage of the wind, and immediately forced a minor. Berry subsequently crossed the Widnes line, but the kick at goal again failed. Widnes kept the home team on the defensive for some time, but were un- able to get through. From a scrimmage in the home 25, Evans made an excellent pass to Barber, who dropped a splendid goal from nearly the centre of the field. Wid- nes kept up the pressure until the end of the game, when the score was—Widnes, 1 goal and 1 minor; Tyldesly, 3 tries and 5 minors.

WARRINOTON,A 37. 18 OF DISTRICT.--ThiS match hav- ing been arranged with the object of assisting the Junior teams of the town, was played on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, but unfortunately, the District was con- stituted of only two juniors. The ball was started to- wards the roadway goal, against a stiffish breeze, by the Districts, .Ashurst soon showing up by a capital run well inside the home quarters, where the danger was averted by, Russell. Cragan, and Teare, and the ball carried to midfield, until stopped by Singleton. Clare then got possession, and mainly through his efforts the venue of hostilities was shifted to the goal, the defence of the homesters being somewhat heavily taxed. Some com- bined work by Webster and Daniels tested Hatton's abilities, but he returned well into touch at midfield; but the same player directly afterwards replied but poorly to a long kick from Daniels. Some give-and-take play then occupied the attention of the onlookers, but Hughes pass- ing out to Clare, a kick by the latter caused play to fluctuate near the goal line. For a time the pressure was maintained, but Isherwood brought about slight relief, which was improved by Role and Russell, until Hatton punted back. A minor was, however, conceded to Warrington immediately after this. Following the drop-out, a punt by Plinston enabled his side to gain a footing on the centre line, Hackett being very prominent at this stage. Then the combined team made a bold bid to score, Sampson replying immensely, and from some ensuing play Daniels almost dodged over, only a minor resulting. ...Knowles, Lloyd and Cragan again tested the defence, and after the threatening danger had been averted, a rattling piece of play by Sampson was cheered as were also some exciting events, the ultimate issue being that Mather, after drawing his opponents, flung across to Daniels, who walked over. Three minors fol- lowed in quick succession. A dash was then made by Monks, Ashurst, and Eden, and although neutralized by Lally the advantage was quickly gained by Ken- wright. Here Ashurst passed to Potts, who ran and kicked cleverly, and a spirited rush was only saved in the nick of time by Webster, half-time score being 0-1-5 to 0-0-1. Resuming at centre, Rowe soon got away and passed to Webster, who was floored by his op- ponent before he could reply. Plinston here intercepted a peas, but hesitating, lost a chttacc vt,chntrigtlls2llng' him- self. Clare followed suite, and by a capital effort trans- ferred warfare to the Warrington 25. Rowe and Mather got the oval back,and Daniels receiving,was only stopped by Hatton when dangerous, and a minor concedPd. Some good kicking by Potts and Singleton found the leather hovering in the vicinity of the Warrington goal, until Mather somewhat relieved,the position being further enhanced by Phillips. A grand piece of work now took place,which aroused thepnthusiasm of the spectators. It was started by Mather, and the ball passed through the hands of Russell, Daniels, and most of the team, but the final touch was lacking, enabling Potts to run to neutral ground. There was plenty of excitement when it was now seen that the Juniors had got to the line and scared but the try was disallowed, being held outside the line and a minor was finally conceded. Twice after this Webster after a couple of passes from Russell, made grand attempts to score, and Daniels by a fine dodgy run almost succeeded, but the District was to numerous to penetrate, and the game ended Warrington 0-1-8 to 0-0-2.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. LEEDS PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. LEEDS PARISH CHURCH.

Leeds people were loud in their praises at the display given by the Warringtanians in the —first of their annual engagements, which took place at Leeds on Saturday. Nor were their praises undegerved, for the Warrington- ians gave a fine exhibition of the Rugby game, the com- bination of the Lancashire men being the finest shown this season. There were absentees from the original team chosen by the Warrington executive, and the ser- vices of their umpire, Speakman, were requisitioned. The day as beautifully fine, and the Leeds club having a match away, the gate was considerably augmented, and when Frank Turner kicked off there would be fully 7,000 present.

The usual eXchanges were slightly in favour of the visitors, but from a long throw out Evans rushed upand ran to near the line,passed to his companion, but unfortu- nately the pass was a poor one, and consequently a chance was lost. However, Warrington had gained a footing in the Tykes' quarters, and try as Leeds would, they could not shake the visitors off. A stubborn defence was set up, Bramfitt staving off the attacks repeatedly. James Bate passed finely across to Evans, who effected another strong run, but Turner (Leeds) got the oval away, only to find Boscow snapping it up and compelling a hasty retreat. A spell of exchange kicking by Barnes, Evans, and Bramfitt ended in Leeds touching down. Following the drop out came capital work by Ashton, Jas. Bate, and Jolley, which was ably seconded by a capital display by the Warrington half-backs. Leeds now tried their hand at the passing game, but they compared but poorly with their opponents, and Boscow with a fine screw kick sent the Tykes to the rightabout. Watson put in some telling kicks, but Evans neutralized any advantage gained by another strong run, which was marred by holding the oval a little too long. James Bate had hard lines for a try, grounding in touch in goal. The visitors were, however, not relaxing in their energies, and although the Leeds men on the drop out reached the half way flag, their stay here was but short, for a (*rand display of passing between John and James Bate, Barnes, and Massey, resulted in the Warrington skipper scoring near the corner flag, Frank Turner making a good but unsuc- cessful kick for goal. The Lancashire men still held the upper hand, their forwards playing an excellent cm- 1 bined game. Thorniley, Frank Turner, and Ashton yvere especially prominent in individual display, although Leeds had the advantage of the penalty kick. The War- ringtonians earned a round of applause by a fine display of passing along the line, but Eastwood got the oval away and Boscow fielding the leather well, got it away, when hard pressed. A sharp piece of work by James Bate from a pass by his companion half was luckily foiled by Stephens, but another passing movement by the Warringtonians, initiated by their half backs, ended in Massey preferring to drop at goal, the ball gOing wide of its mark, a minor accruing. From the restart the Leeds men for the first tune entered the Warrington 25, and although Boscow made his mark, which afforded a temporary relief, Watson and Oddy returned to the attack, only to find Frank Turner, Thorniley, Holmes, and Donohue work the oval out of danger. Heaton almost scored a moment later, Massey pulling him up under the posts, and Evans pitercepting a pass to Ward, the game was taken to the 25 flag. A minor eventually resulted to Leeds from a long kick. Janes Bate was to the fore with a clever piece of work soon after the drop out, and some tall kicking by Stephens sent the oval to Boscow, who was surrounded by the Leeds for- fords, and the visiting custodian failing to hold the ball, ; the homesters rushed over, and a try was recorded. Oddy was entrusted with the easy place, and missing the goal ends were changed with the scores equal. A. Stephens kicked off, and although Barnes met the restart finely, the Leeds men adopted rushing tactics, which forced the game on the Lancashire line. Boscow afforded relief to his side, and James Bate cleared a pack with surprising rapidity, and passing to his companion, J. T. Bate ran and passed to Barnes, who was in too close quarters for the chance to avail him of distinguishing himself. Jolley and Ashton were especially noticeable at this portion of the game,the former tackling strongly. Another. fine display by James Bate was neutralized by

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

Surrox Vic-rontA. v. NEWTON ROVERS.—This match was played at Newton on Saturday last in beautiful weather. Final result :--Sutton Victoria, 4 goals; Newton Rovers, 2 goals. HAYDOCIT V. GOLBORNE. —This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. Tunstall started for the homesters, and they were soon crowding round the visitors' goal, Greenall slpoting wide. It was evi- dent that Haydock were by far the weaker team (if taken by their play in the second half) as they soon began to show signs of distress, and when time was called the visitors had won by three goals to nil. WARRINGTON (ASSOCIATION) V. GARSTON (IST TEAMS). —These teams met for the first time on Saturday on the Arpley ground. The visitors came short of their centre forward, while the home team were short of three of their best players—Captain Parry half-back, Ball and Sankey forwards—playing two rekrve men in their places, each side agreeing to play ten men. Williams kicked off for the visitors, the home team commencing a heavy pres- sure on the visitors goal and ten minutes from the start Phillips scored from a foul. Madlen and Thompson on the visitors right came to the fore with a neat run and after a hard struggle in the goal mouth Garston scored. Madden working the oracle the same player scoring a few minutes later. Play, then became of a tame character, Garston having slightly the best of it. Ends were changed with the score standing Garston two, War- rington one. On the resumption the home team com- menced to press very severely but were very weak in front of goal, T. Mather missing two easy chances of scoring. The visitors left obtained possession and worked the globe to the other end, but the home backs and goalkeeper were equal to the occasion. The visitors were not to be denied, hut the goal keeping of Jones was splendid, repelling 'shots again and again. The home team then had a spell at the other end but their backs cleared easily, Madden and Thompson working the ball up and Williams scoring a beauty as the whistle was sounding for time,leavingGarston the winners of a good game by three goals to one. The home team was lacking in combination among the forwards. Warrington Team: Goal, Jones; full backs, Davies and Phillips ; half backs, Ayling and Simkins; right wing, Clayton and T. Mather; centre, Carnforth ; left wing, Cant and J. Mather; referee, Mr. Isherwood.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

They have odd ideas about some of our English national games in France. To the average Frenchman cricket is a mystery, and football a sanguinary scene of brutal bloodshed mid wholesale slaughter. This is how a French reporter describes a football field : —" The sides precipitated themselves upon each other, arms and legs were dislocated, collar bones broken, children of tender years limped'off the field with fatal injuries, and all around were weeping mothers and distracted fathers tending their bruised and battered offspring."

Then " half-time" was called, and as the ends were changed, the French'journalist waxes still more forcibly and frantically descriptive:—" The game was resumsd amidst howls and execrations from both sides, and frag- ments of clothing, and of hair and skin, torn ruthlessly from the heads and bodies of the rivals, strewed the field." At this the veracious reporter appears to have been utterly overcome, for he concludes It was a spectacle both terrible and affecting, and I turned away with tears in my eyes." I wonder what sort of a war correspondent this sympathetic scribe would make? Truly the Parisians must imagine that we are still a race of barbarians. Our football fellows, in the eyes of our neighbours across channel, must be a set of bloodthirsty savages.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

The rupture in the League has now been healed over, and in ipture we are to have plain sailing. If any of the Lancashire clubs feel that their Midlamd rivalsfiave the pull over them financially they are not to rush into print and say so, but they are to nurse their wrath. The action of Mr. Critchley inventuring to suggest the form- ation of a northern league has been repudiated by the members of the Accrington Football Club in special meet- ing assembled, and- the Rovers have denied that Mr. Lewis, in acting in concert with Mr. Critchlev, had their approval. For the thne being at least harmony has been restoied.

Three n*ore Lancashire clubs were swept from the Football Association Cup competition on Saturday, and the Blackburn Rovers are our last sheet anchor. They made light of their task with Chester, and go into the third round with seven goals to spare. Accrington gave Wolverhampton Wanderers such a good game that an extra half hour was needed, during which period the Wolves gained the deciding point. Burnley also lost by a goal, their victors being Notts. Sunderland shook off Darwon with two goals in hand, both those being secured in the last ten minutes. Darwon have protested against two of the Sunderland players as being ineligible. Sun- derland Albion and Notts Forest will have to meet again as their match ended in a draw. The clubs have opposed each other three times this season,the result being a draw in every case. Brown, the Forest goalkeeper, had his collar bone fractured.

Sheffield Wednesday surprised everybody by over- throwing Derby County, and West Bromwich Albion exceeded expectation by easily vanquishing Birmingham St. George's. The following are the clubs now left in League: Blackburn Rovers, Sunderland, Wolverhamp- ton West Bromwich Albion and Notts Alliance; Stoke, Sheffield Wednesday, Sunderland Albion, and Notts Forest.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.
It may be noted that Mr. Harry Fairclough, of the Warrington Cricket Club, has been elected on the Coni- mittee of the Lancashire County Club, in the place of Mr. A. G. Steel, resigned.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE AT A MAYORAL BANQUET,
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE AT A MAYORAL BANQUET,

On Wednesday night Lord Bute, Mayor of Cardiff, presided at the Cardiff Drill Hall over the Mayoral ban- quet, about five hundred guests being present. Dinner was half-way through when a glass globe in one of the Chinese lanterns, which were hung along the upper part of the building, burst and fell down on the gas jets some feet below. This mischance set all the lanterns on fire, and the whole of the upper part of the building was immediately in a blaze. The utmost excitement pre- vailed as the burning material fell down and set the table linen, Sx., on fire. About a dozen pictures, heirlooms in the Bute family, which had been sent by his lordship for the occasion, narrowly escaped destruction; but as it wa4, two of them were considerably injured. The guests staved as long as it was possible with safety, and assisted to put out the fire. A part of the hall roofing has been destroyed, and the other damage, apart from the paint- ings, is by no means inconsiderable.

div.head: CLOSE OF THE SOUP KITCHEN AT THE
div.p: CLOSE OF THE SOUP KITCHEN AT THE
DRILL lIALL.

On Saturday the last of the soup dinners which have been provided, with the aid of public sub- scription by the Aged People's Treat Committee and Charity Organisation Society, to poor children in the Warrington Drill Hall, was given. About 1,190 juveniles partook of the repast. While the dinner was proceeding the Mayor expressed his thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had since the soup kitchen was opened.attended to the wants of the children, also to the subscribers for having re- sponded so liberally to his appeal in the newspapers. It might be remarked, he said that discretion had not been •sed in dining so many children. It was quite possible many of them had a good dinner there who had previously had one at home, but still there was the satisfaction of knowing that a large number of poor children had been fed. whose parents were partly out of work. The relief had been carried out most conscientiously. A fortnight ago he said at the police court there was no bad trade in Warrington. He believed that Warrington was never in a better position than at the present moment as far as trade was concerned, but no sensible man would dare to say that there had not been much temporary distress among brick- layers' labourers; infect all outdoor men,and it was to relieve these and not those who were at work that the soup kitchen was started. Referring to the recent discussion at the Board of Guardians on the object of the distress, the Mayor remarked that the official life of a member of the Board of Guard- ians made him hard, and dried up in his breast that milk of human kindness which ought to exist in a public man. He found there was no artificial heat provided in the tramp ward the other day, although the thermometer stood at 20. No wonder tramps left Warrington and went to places where they were better cared for. Alderman Wright clx- pressed his concurrence with what the Mayor had said, and, speaking as a former large employer of labour, said that after a 14 days' frost certain men were brought to starvation point.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. BRADLAUGH.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. BRADLAUGH.

Three special trains left Waterloo Station at one o'clock on Tuesday to convey the friends of the late Mr. Brad- laugh to Woking, to attend the funeral of the late mem- ber for Northampton. The body was conveyed by one of the trains. There was a large assemblage of people, and their appearance was very different from that of funeral parties generally. No mourning garments were worn, and in some cases gaily coloured ribbons had been tied round the hats of the wearers. Mr. and Mrs. Bon- ner and four or five other members of Mr. Bradlaugh's family 'were amongst the throng, besides Mrs. Besant, Mr. Labouchere, M.P., Dr. Hunter, M.P., and twelve representatives from Northampton. • The remains of Mr. Bradlaugh were interred at three o'clock,in unconsecrated ground at the Brookwood Ceme- tery at Woking, in presence of about 2,000 sympathisers. These included Mr. John Morley, M.P.,-Mr. Labouchere, M.P., and a number of other members of Parliament, as well as numerous delegates representing Liberal, Radical, and Secular associations in all parts of the United Kiucr dom. On the arrival of the chief mourners—Mr. Brad- laugh's son-in-law and daughter, Mr. and Mrs. Bonner, and his neice, Miss Bradlaugh—a procession was formed to the grave, the bearers being several of the deceased's constituents from Northampton. There was no ceremony at the graveside, the coffin being lowered into the vault .amid perfect silence. The coffin was conspicuously plain, being of papier-mache, covered with black cloth. A little earth was sprinkled upon the lid, and a few flowers were dropped into the grave, after which a long stream of admirers filed past the vault, taking a last look. A great many beautiful wreaths were sent, with inscrip- tions testifying to the various good qualities of the de- ceased. Amongst the wreaths was one from deceased's brother, an evangelist preacher. After the interment the company iMmediately returned to London. The postmen of Liverpool were to the fore in recog- nising the valual3le services of the late Mr. Bradlaugh. They sent to his funeral a beautiful wreath, over seven feet in circumference,consisting of rare orchidsieucharis, camellias, and other choice flowers, interspersed with maidenhair ferns and lilies of the valley. The wreath was supplied by the firm of Fishlock Brothers Elliot-st., Liverpool. It bore the following inscription :—" A tribute of sorrow, in grateful remembrance of services rendered to the postmen of Liverpool in their recent struggle for a diminution of Sunday labour." Mrs. Besant writing of Mr. Bradlaugh in the "Weekly Dispatch," says "As all his personal friends know, Charles Bradlaugh's life was one of rare purity ; but the foulest insinuations that profligates could deviie were heaped upon him. When they had exhaustelli their slanders against him they assailed his daughters and my- self, and he was obliged beyond the bar in the House of Commons to listen to insults levelled against us, wound- ing him more bitterly than had they been directed against himself." Mr. Bradlaugh's daughter in last week's "National Reformer" says that when her father fell ill there were two things which greatly troubled him—one finance, the other the motion he was to make in the House of Com- mons on the 27th January. She adds: "Thanks to Dr. W. A. Hunter, M.P., it was my happiness to be able to ease his mind on this last point." Mr. Bradlaugh was poorer than is generally supposed. "AU these last ten years," says Mrs. Besant, "have been one long harass- ing fight against pecuniary embarrassments, kept at bay only by the untiring generous a3aiotance of his friends.' In confirmation of this I may mention that yes angusta domi alone prevented him from acting on the advice of his doctor to spend the winter in some more genial climate. He kept this from his friends, and they, alas! only heard of it when it was too late to offer their help. . .

"Mr. Bradlaugh," writes the editor of a year-book, "was peculiarly sensitive as to his long Pariiamentary struggle. In correcting the -record of the successive efforts which he made to enter the House of Commons, he was always strictly careful as to accuracy. Before Me lies a revised proof of a biography' which the junior member for Northampton corrected just before his ill- ness. There is interesting evidence of the pride he felt in his appointment on more than one Royal Commission shown in a neat correction he has made by the side of the printed matter. In his handwriting now before me, the sentence occurs, His claim to affirm in lieu of tak- ing the oath of allegiance led to a long aud exciting controversy in and out of Parliament.' Such was his own, and the matter-of-fact way, of describing his triumphant struggle." One of the most dramatic incidents that ever I wit- nessed in real life (writes a correspondent), occurred at Plymouth several years ago, after a morning lecture delivered by Mr. Bradlaugh. A lady engaged in mis- sionary workstood up to open the discussion, but instead of dealing with the matter Of the lecture, the recited to Mr. Bradlaugh this verse from the Psalms: "The fool hath said'in his heart there is no God." After she had given the verse she pointed her finger at Mr. Bradlaugh, and with withering scorn, exclaimed, "Thou art the fool." Mr. Bradlaugh calmly reminded the lady that she had not dealt with his lecture, and with great ooartesy invited her to attend the evening lecture in which he would deal with the question of atheism. In a moment his eyes flashed, and with a gesture peculiar to himself, he exclaimed, "Madam, there is another verse in which it is said : He that calleth his brother a fool is in danger of hellfire."- . _

Mr. LabouChere once played a practical joke on Charles Bradlaugh which one could well imagine a subject failing to appreciate; but Mr. Labouchere tells the story him- self and evidently enjoys it. The two members for Northampton were once addressing their constituents at a joint meeting. Mr. Labouchere much against his will, as he was quite unprepared with a speech, was called on to speak first. After some little hesitating delay he rose, and catching sight of Mr. Bradlaugh's carefully prepared notes, which had been placed by the hon. member on a reading desk, calmly, utilised the subjects for his own speech. There has been some talk since Mr. Bradlaugh's death as to whether during his illness he expressed any change in his religious views. Mrs. Bradlaugh-Bonner declares in the " National Reformer" that her father " died as he had lived, a consistent and conscientious Atheist." In order that there might be no dispute about Mr. Brad- laugh's religious position at his death Mrs. Bradlaugh- Bonner states that she has "taken the precaution to procure signed testimony from the independent and im- partial witnesses who had been in attendance upon him I the last few weeks, that he was never heard to utter one word, either directly or indirectly, bearing upon religion or any religious subject."
__,.._. CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

In the course of a discussion which took place on Thursday on a proposal to increase the County Surveyor's salary from £7OO to £9OO per annum, the Cheshire County Council had brought under its notice the general question of high salaries, it was stated that since the County Council took over the roads the expense of surveying had increased from .C7OO to .C 1,890 and that in other departments salaries had been increased all round. Notwith- standing these criticisms, it was agreed to advance the salary in question, on the ground that the Surveyor's duties had been very much increased since the County Conncil took possession of the roads. Technical education, rail way rates and charges, and the bill providing for compensation to property owners for subsidpelace caused by the pump- ing of brine were amongst the other subjects which engaged the attentton of the Council.
