div.head: LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. •
div.p: LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. •

The Lancashire County Council met at Preston on Thursday. In the report of the Parliamentary Committee was contained a recommendation that the Council oppose the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Bill, by one clause of which the Company seek power to erect one or more hotels at Horwich. The opinion was generally expressed that the Com- pany were practically seeking to obtain powers which were vested in the licensing authority. A letter was read from the Directors of the Com- pany stating that the hotel they proposed to build was meant for the convenience of their four thou- sand workpeople. It was unanimously decided to oppose the clause, and .ClOO was granted for that purpose. An important report. was presented by the Technical Instruction Committee. The amount of the grant at the disposal of the County Council was stated to be .£39,000, and in the distribution of the money the Committee recommended that the chief considerations be rateable value and popula- tion. For the rural districts it is proposed to spend £l,OOO in establishing migratory dairy schools and assisting in providing lecturers and instructors. The report was approved.

div.head: WARRIIiGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRIIiGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse yesterday. The Rev, G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs W. Long, R. Heaton, E. Aukland, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, A. Jolley, Smith, S winton, and Kilshall ; S. Sutton (clerk). W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspec- tor.)

THE LIGHTING OF LATCHFOR.D.—The CLERK reported that the Committee having to deal with the question of lighting at Latchford and Grappenhall had held two meetings, and they had decided that ten lamps would be necessary for the lighting of the district. It had been represented that lamps placed on Grappen- hall-road near the canal might have a confusing effect on horses working on the canal.—Mr. LONG said he formerly placed a lamp at his tan-yard which had such a confusing effect on the horses that they were apt to walk into the canal, one having done so, and a number of canal men came and asked him to do away with the lamp. With regard to the disposal of the lamps he thought it would be more advisable to place two or three on Knutsford-road, instead of on the higher , part of Grappenhall-road.—After some discussion Mr. W. I HOUGHTON moved, and Mr. Joni; Hpuoirrow seconded, , that the matter be deferred for another month. Mr. HEATON moved, and Mr. A. JOLLEY seconded, that the lamps be erected forthwith. Mr. Heaton's amendment was defeated by three votes to five, and Mr. Houghton's motion was passed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Sephton reported that the death-rate for the past month was 15.4 per 1,000, as compared with 12.2 for the last three months, and 17.9 in the corresponding month of last year. NEW HOUSES.—The Surveyor reported that during 1890 there were 55 new houses erected within the district of the authority where building bye-laws were in force. -This was all the business of public interest..
WARRINGTON FRIENDL SOCIETIES'
MEDICAL ASSOCUTION.

The Committee of the above Association held their annual knife and fork tea and social gather- ing on Thursday evening, at the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-st. There were present Mr. Jos. Albinson (president), Mr. G. Roughley (vice-president), Dr. Kisby (medical officer), Mesdames Kisby, Albinson, Roughley, Dunbobbin,Bibby, and Edgar,and Messrs. Dunbobbin, Holmes (trustees), Stirrup (treasurer), Burgess, Beswick, Wadsworth, Langley, Edgar, Mather, Rudd, Pemberton, Shaw, Perdue, Fernley, Drury, Boyle, Bibby, Lake (dispenser), and S. Bibby (secretary). After full justice had been done to the good things provided, and the removal of the cloth, the Chairman gave the usual loyal- toasts. which were most enthusiastically received in true English style. Mr. WAusworrm proposed in suitable terms" The Army, Navy and Reetrve -Forces," coupling with it the name of Mr. Lake, an old army man.—Mr. LAKE, in thanking the company for the warm manner in which the toast had been given and received, stated that he had served under the British flag for over 29 years, ten of which had been spent in India. At preeeni he was happy to think that we were at peace with all nations, and hoped that such a state of things would long continue, but nevertheless he felt sure that if the services of the army, navy or re- serve forces were required, they would be able to give a good account of themselves by maintaining their previous record, and upholding the dignity of the empire. Mr. Gibbert proposed" Success to the Warrington Medi- cal Association,' and Mr. Sibby, in returning thanks,said that numerically and financially spe,akin,g,the institution was in a highly satisfactory condition. olts funds amounted, according to the balance sheet, to over £350, and its membership to over 3,700, being an increase of nearly 100 members upon the previous year. The pre- scriptions had been nearly 18,000, and visits to patients close upon 5,000. He had no fear as to the future pros- perity of the association, and thought that the institu- tion had a bright future, especially if the present unity continued to exist amongst its members. Mr. TIIROSSELL proposed the health of the Medical Officer, which was warmly supported by the chairman and the same was drunk with much enthusiasm. Dr. KISBY briefly thanked them, and said that it was his desire to remain, and continue their medical officer for many years to come. He was glad to hear of the success of the society. Mr. LANGLEY proposed the "Town and Trade, of Warrington," and Mr. W. A. STIRRUP replied thereto in a most humorous speech. "Kindred societies" was pro- posed by Mr. BURGESS, and ably responded to by Mr. S. DUNEOBEIN, first president of the association. The health of the chairman, vice-chairman, and other compliment- ary toasts were heartily proposed and drunk. An enjoy- able evening was terminated by the singing of the National Anthem. The toasts were interspersed with songs by Messrs. Dunbobbin,Langley,Shaw, Beswick,and Stirrup.
ACCIDENTS IN THE HUNTING FIELD.

Two accidents occurred on Thursday with the South Cheshire Hounds. Dr. Bond received a severe shaking through his horse falling. The ani- mal itself, which was a very valuable hunter, broke its neck, and had to be destroyed. A more serious accident befel Mr. Greenfield, of Birkenhead, whose horse stumbled in a drain, which was hidden by the grass, and threw its rider, who was seriously injured. The unfortunate gentleman was removed to Worleston, suffering from concussion of the brain, and was attended by Dr. Morton, one of the hunt party.

div.head: GREAT LICENSING APPEAL.
div.p: THE GREAT LICENSING APPEAL.

On Monday, Mr. Collins, for the appellant, contended that the Licensing Act Amendment Act modified the principal Act by requiring notice of objection to be sent to the licensee.—Lord Flerschell remarked that if the appellant's contention was correct the justices could not refuse the renewal to an undesirable house if the new tenant had a good character. After further arguments from Mr. Candy, also in support of the appellant, the Court adjourned. On Tuesday, Mr. Addison, Q.C., in reply on behalf of the respondents, said these was one thing the Legislature had expressly refused to do, and that was to take away the unlimited judicial discretion of the justices in the case of the renewal of licenses, and that upon two considerations—first the statutes, and next upon the entire policy of the Jaw. The Lord Chancellor said it seemed to him that the whole matter was remitted to the justices to do as seemed right to them Mr. Addision thought the more accurate way of putting it was that the matter was remitted to the justices to refuse or to grant as they thought best in the interests of the public.—Mr. Poland, Q.C., followed on the same side, and Mr. Henn Collins, Q.C., having replied on the whole case on behalf of the appellant, the Lord Chancellor said that, in view of the importance of the case, their Lordship would take time to consider the form in which they would deliver judgment.

The dividend of the Great Western Railway Company for the past half-year will be at the rate of 71 per cent. per annum. The mutilated body of Jonathan Grundy, a cattle dealer and well-known agriculturist, was found on the Great Eastern main line at Spalding on Thursday morn- ing. Grundy had evidently been killed whilst crossing the line.

The Queen's Bench on Thursday decided that a school- master who with his wife earned a joint salary of £l5O, could not be totally exempted flom income tax, on the ground that it cost him £3O a year to keep a servant to do the household duties while his wife was in school.

The steamer Meredith, of London, -landed at Shields on Thursday the crew of the steamer Bessemer, of Stockton, which foundered after the collision off Newarp light on Wednesday morning with the Meredith. The Bessemer sank in two minutes. The crew of twelve were rescued with difficulty, and they lost all their effects.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

A MURDERER HANGED. Bartholomew Sullivan was hanged at Tralee gaol at eight o'clock on Monday morning for the murder of . Patrick Flashire, a farmer, who had taken an evicted farm at Ballyheigne, North Kerry, five years ago. Sulli- van was tried and sentenced at the last Nenagh Assizes. MORE COERCION IN TIPPERARY.

A Tipperary telegram states that the Government CO template prosecuting under the Crimes Act on the charge of conspiracy another batch of the leaders in the Smith- Barry dispute in Tipperary. The defendants will include some members of Parliament and the Rev. David, Humphries, who was charged with Messrs. O'Brien ano Dillon in the recent trials, but who was then dig" charged.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AT ENNIS.
div.p: MR. PARNELL AT ENNIS.

Mr. Parnell-On- 1-lin-;;;;--f-ro—ni Dublin to Ennis, 00 Saturday, received a number of addresses at station.; where the tram stopped, and popular demonstrations were made in his support. He reached Ennis on Sus' day afternoon. Addressing a mass meeting in the towo square, Mr. Parnell said Ireland stood fast to her. elairo to be,sovereign within her own domain. She refused W admit any English veto so far as her own business'w3s concerned. As in. 1880, he told the Irish people ithe.„3/ would win, so in a few days they would know the trig," of his declaration that they had won a settlement of thio question, which would be everlastingly creditable to their patriotism. They would gain a Parliament WI" real. real. power to protect the interests of every class and tO settle the question of land and police. Mr. Parriel,, afterwards received numerous addresses from public al3u political bodies. Ennis closes the series of meetings for which definite dates have been fixed. Mr. Parnell left Kingstown on Monday morning for London, travelling from Ennis by the night train. MR. O'BRIEN AND THE PLAN OF CAMPAIGN. The "Daily News" publishes a letter from Air' O'Brien at Boulongp, in which he challenged Mr. Balfour'S statement as to the origin of the Plan of Campaign. Air' O'Brien writes The Plan of Campaign was put for; ward by a few of us on our own responsibility as th_ best means of protection we could devise in extreinl' cases of hardship for a population driven to desperat.ioo by the ruined harvest and falling prices of the terrible autumn of 1886, and by the late refusal of the Tory Parliament to provide for the emergency, or even 0' admit that there was any emergency to be provided for.

MORE INTERVIEWS AT BOULOGNE. Mr. Parnell arrived in London from Dublin on MondY evening, and preceeded by night mail to Boulogne via Dover and Calais. Yesterday morning another intervieW took place between Mr. Parnell, Mr. Dillon, and gr. O'Brien, at the close of which the member for Cork re- turned to London. On arriving in the metropolis Mr. Parnell drove at once to the House of Commons, where% in the course of the evening, he conferred with severa' of his supporters. Mr. Parnell has determined to a.ird: dress no more meetings in Ireland for the present. have also the best reason to believe that Mr. Parnell 110 no intention to go to America at this juncture. The " Star " says the statements circulated by th,,,e " Times " this morning' implying that terms arc heir* made by the leaders of the Liberal party with Mr. nell are wholly unfounded. div.head: M'CARTHY AT LIVEROOOL.
div.p: M'CARTHY AT LIVEROOOL.

Mr. Justin M'Carthy and Lord Aberdeen were the guests of the Liverpool Reform Club on Monday evening. In responding to a toast Mr. M'Carthy stated that there i was unity amongst English Liberals n forwarding the Home Rule cause, and there was every reason to believe that that cause was now approaching very near to suc- cess. He was satisfied that Mr. Gladstone would not bring in a measure which was not likely to be accepted by both the Irish party and English Liberals. Of course • there was one or two matters—the land and police ques- tions, for instance—on which some slight difference of °Pinion might arise. With regard to the land question, hO would say that the Imperial Parliament must either deal with it before or concurrently with Home Rule, or refer it to the Irish Legislature. As for the other question he had mentioned, it would surely be admitted that if the , Irish were fit to govern themselves thsy might be trusted ' With the manazementOf the police. (Applause.) Lord Aberdeen responding to the toast of "Our Par- I Rementary Institutions," said Kilkenny had shown where the majority of the Irish people intended to put their Rust, and Hartlepool had done the same jivith respect to the majority of the English people. LIVERPOOL IRISHMEN AND MR. M'CARTHY. Prior to the banquet Mr. M'Carthy was presented by a meeting of Liverpool Irishmen, under the presidency of Sir. M. CeMahoney, with an address recognising him as the elected leader of the Irish Parliamentary party, and expressing appreciation of his courage and self-sacrifice. Mr. M'Carthy, in the course of his reply, said the present discord had impaired the action of the National League Executive, and he appealed for funds. He saw hopeful Signs of peace before very long.

div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

The annual meeting was held in the club, High- • it, last night week, and there was a large attend- ance of members, Mr. A. R. Norman presided. The lion. Secretary (Mr. W. Handley) read a financial statement, whhich showed that since the commence- xnent of the club, the receipts had been—subscrip- tions on furnishing accounts £124 18s. 11d.,and there had been spent on furnishing the premises £l2O 7s. 9d., leaving a balance of £4 us. 2d. For the same period the receipts on general account had been subscriptions £4l SS. 6d., billiards £lOO 7s. 6d., sundry receipts including Profit on excursion £22 18s. op., making a total of £164 1.1.5. Old. The expenditure on general account was £l2B 17s. 2-W, leaving a balance of £35 13s. 10d., which added to the balance on furnishing account, gave a total amount to the credit of the club of £4O ss. The out- standing liabilities amounted to £3B 10.. 9d., leaving a balance of £1 us. 3d.—The Secretary said the number of members admitted was about 270.—After discussion the statement was unanimously adopted.—Mr. J. T. Brunner, ALF., was unanimously re-elected president and the following list of vice-presidents was approved :—Messrs. P. Speakman C.C., James Handley J.P., T. Handley, S. Taylor, J. R. Frith, J. J. The Committee were authorised to employ a collector to collect subscriptions at such renumeration as the committee might fix. The Committee was constituted aa follows: Messrs. A. R. Norman, J. Clark, E. Marshall, Iv'. Wright, T. Poole, J. Bate, T. Dean, E. W. Humphries, • EPps, W. Carroll, G. Bellamy, and A. Riley.—On the _Proposition of Mr. E. Marshill,scconded by Mr. P. div.head: COMPENSATION FOR SUBSIDENCE.
div.p: COMPENSATION FOR SUBSIDENCE.

Mr. Brunner's Bill to provide compensation for afters of property suffering in consequence of land snbsidences caused by the pumping of brine has anvf been published. It appears to have been very carefully drawn up, and to fairly meet all the re- IPlrements of the case. It provides for the forma- 40n of compensation districts on the application of landowners or local authorities to the Local Govern- Meat Board, and for the appointment of Compensa- tion Boards, whose position and powers will be analogous to those of public trusts. There are three groups of persons specially interested in the cora- Palmation question—the salt manufacturer or brine Pumpers, the landowners, and the ratepayers; and each of these groups is to be represented by one- third the members of the Compensation Boards, the representatives of the ratepayers being appointed by the local authority or authorities. The compen- sation fund is to be provided, according to the Bill, by a levy on all the brine pumpers of the district per thousand gallons of brine raised. As, however very extensive subsidences may occur in some years and none at all in other years, power is given for the formation of a reserve fund and for spreading the compensation payments over several years. Railway and canal companies, the trustees of the River Weaver Navigation, and brine pumpers them- selves are excluded from any benefit under the Act, apparently on the ground that, being directly con- cerned in the proofs of the industry, they must take the risks.

div.head: Utter to tbe Obitor.
div.p: Utter to tbe Obitor.
THE WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN
ASSOCIATION.

Sir,—In the printed circular published by the above- mentioned Association, I find under the head "Objects," the following definition :—" The social, intellectual, and spiritual welfare of young men " ; and under the head " Classes," I read :--" Shorthand, Bible, and Evangeli- cal services." Thus in the first place the social and in- tellectual have the precedence of the spiritual, and in the second case, shorthand stands before the Bible and evangelical services. lam not disposed to be unduly critical; but it does strike me that the classification is a curious one for a Young Men's Christian Association.— Yours truly,
CONSISTENCY.
SANITARY MATTERS AT THE LAST COUNCIL
MEETING.

Sir,—l think it is only just to Alderman Platt, and fair to myself,to saythat my remarks anent the "petti- fogging badgering " of the Sanitary Committee by cer- tain members of the Council, had not the slightest re- ference to himself. Although I have differed with him in the past and still do so in regard to his policy upon sanitary matters, I haye never either publicly or pri- vately doubted in the slightest degree the integrity or purity of his motives. My object in writing this letter is to prevent any misunderstanding arising from the perusal of the published reports of the proceedings in question.—l am, yours truly, Warrington, February 6th, 1891.
H. ROBERTS.

SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS. Sir,—There seems to be some misapprehension of the the meaning of my letter as published in your list issue. I did not mean to suggest that any representative elected at the last election of Commissioners obtained his seat by improper means; for I consider that the last electim was an improvement in many respects upon many of its predecessors in the "good old times "to which I refer. What I complain of is the system which allows the voting paper to be filled up by a partisan, signed by the voter Ln the presence of the crowd and deposited with the presiding officer under the eye of the partisan before referred to, with none of the protectior. offered by the Ballot Act under which all contested elections of every classought to be fought.—Yours truly, RATEPAYER. Runcorn, February 3rd, 1891.

div.head: POLICE TEMPERANCE SOCIETY FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: A POLICE TEMPERANCE SOCIETY FOR WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Permit me to commend the following extract from the "Alliance News" to the careful consideration of your readers, and to suggest further that an effort should be madeto establish a Police Temperance Society in connection with the Warrington Police Force.

Probably the worthy chief Constable (Mr. Samuel • Hunt) would—if he were sufficiently urged to do so— initiate the movement by signing the pledge himself and becoming the first President of the Society. That would be a good thing, wouldn't it ?—Yours truly, CHRISTOPHER.

[EXTRACT.] "The annual report of the Hull Police Temperance Society, read at the anniversary meeting lately, said that during the year 15 new members had been enrolled, but four had violated their pledges. The society at pre- sent consisted of the Deputy-Chief Constable (Mr. Jones), two superintendents, nine sergeants, and W, constables, being a total of 93, against 82 last year. Several members of the force were abstainers, but not members of the society. The chairman of the meet- ing, Alderman Lavard, urged those abstainers in the f9ro who were not members of the society to join it, as by so doing they would be helping to strengthen their own convlctions, and might also be the means of inducing others to become teetotallers. Quite 95 per cent. of the cases of men brought before -the chief constable and the Watch Committee were the result directly or indirectly of the drink. He, there- fore, urged the importance of the men becoming ab- stainers, for there was no class of men who were so liable to temptation as the police. He hoped that at their next anniversary they would be able to rejoice in a much larger increase than that over which they rejoiced that night."

div.head: VICAR OF RUNCORN AND DISSENTERS.
div.p: THE VICAR OF RUNCORN AND DISSENTERS.

Sir,—The "Runcorn Parish Magazine "for the present month contains the report of a sermon preached by the Vicar, in which an unwarrantable attack is made upon Wesleyans in particular, and Nonconformists in general. Why the Vicar should go out.of his way to attack his Nonconformist neighbours we are at a loss to under- stand, and as we wish to think evil of no man, and es- pecially of a Rev. Canon, we will not venture to con- jecture. Had the sermon been preached by an obscure curate, fresh from college, we should have pitied the man, and passed over the discourse in silence; but as it was preached by a dignitary of the Church, and copies of it were sent into the homes of Churchmen and Dissen- ters, it ought not—we think—to pass without remark. We cannot congratulate the Vicar upon his eloquence, logic, or erudition, but we must confess, tltat he has evinced considerable skill in perverting Scripture and misconstruing facts. The text selected for the basis of the discourse was taken from Gal. 3, chap. 26-27 verse, "Ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptised into Christ have put on Christ." The Apostle here teaches that the people to whom he wrote were children of God—that they had become children of God—not through baptism but by personal faith in Christ, and that in baptism they had put on Christ—put on His livery and declared them- selves His disciples and servants. Some time ago we saw a conjuror bring a plum pudding out of an old hat, but the Vicar performed a more wondrous feat still, for he brought the doctrine of baptismal regeneration out of a passage in which the writer had never placed it. Was it not a waste of time for the Vicar to inform his hearers that there could be no re-union until Dissenters had purged themselves of their Nonconformity and ac- knowledged the truth of " The one Body " ? Many of us ardently long for a closer union among the various branches of Christ's Church ; and earnestly pray for the time to come- when there shall be "One Fold and one Shepherd." But the time for organic union with the Church of England is not yet. When the Church has freed herself from State patronage and control, cast out the ritualistic leaven, revised the Book of Common Prayer, and made its use optional,then, and not till then, shall we be prepared to talk about re-union. It is too late in the day for the Vicar, to talk about "ministers not duly ordained administering sacrament without authority," and organisations which cannot be regarded as true branches of the church. sensible mien have long since ceased to believe in apostolic succession, and only a few people attach any importance to episcopal ordination* A priest cannot make a church, nor can the laying on of hands make a true minister of Jesus Christ. He is the best minister who does the most good, and that is the best church, be it Episcopal, Congregational, or Methodist, which makes the best men. "By their fruits ye shall know them." We entertain no unkindly feelings towards the Church of England, on the contrary we esteem her highly for her work's sake and heartily wish her success in her efforts to recover the lapsed classes of society, but when one of her ministers steps aside to castigate us it is only reasonable that we should resent such treatment.—Yours truly. CHARLES FINCH.

div.head: IS THE SYMBOL FOR INSPIRATION "N ?"
div.p: IS THE SYMBOL FOR INSPIRATION "N ?"

Sir,—Mr. Gandy asks why Tolstoi cannot be a Chris- tian and still deny the Fall? The answer of course depends en our definition of what constitutes a Christian. As Christ has left no written account of His teaching, we depend on certain other men's second-hand report of His sayings. Now Christ's own words, as reported, and the Apostles' narratives, I think, undoubtedly convey the idea that He claimed to be of more than human origin— Divine in fact. Christ drew His credentials for this claim from the Old Testament, as being the Messiah therein predicted. Tolstoi, in denying the Fall, logically des- troys the claim of the rest of the Old Testament to be a ,

Divine Revelation. The whole Book must abide the fate of its first chapter : if that succumbs to the overwhelm- ing array of adverse facts, nothing can save the succeed- ing chapters from sharing in its degradation. But myi friend wants a Gospel to himself. He is kicking against. the pricks. He is in a fair way to be 'excommunicate. There arc still Methodists in whose breasts the gangrene of religious intolerance and persecution rankles as it did in the bosoms of those who denied John Wesley a pulpit. And we see how ill it' becomes a Wesleyan—a dissenter from dissenters—to cavil at dissent from the absurdity of his own dogmas. Have these modern Inquisitors arrived at that pitch of dissentient perfection as to be able to say to others" Thus far shall ye go and no further ? " Is Methodism a modern reproduction of the Garden of Eden in which is the tree of knowledge, with fruit fair to see, but forbidden to the children of the chapel? And is the Aldermanic form of my friend to be re- garded as the serpent tempting the dwellers in this Methodistic Paradise to eat that their eyes be opened? If so, I can only hope that the same penalty will not be inflicted upon him as upon his prototype ; abdominal locomotion would be very inconvenient in his case. By the way, I believe the serpents preceded man geologi- cally by many "periods." It would be interesting to learn how they progressed ere yet they had been con- demned to go upon their belly." Perhaps the gnostics will step in and supply this very desirable bit of pre- Adamite natural history. Allow me, sir, to say how much pleasedl was with the last letter of Master of Arts. I like the flavour of dig- nity, honesty, and earnestness so manifest in that letter. That is how I wish the subject to be treated, and will, as far as is in me, try to follow so excellent an example. But the suavity and gentlemanly tone of your correspon- dent must not purchase my acceptance of his opinions. Our friend is too hasty. " Festina lente " is a good motto in polemics as in other things. I see he has has- tened to furnish me with a complete set of ready-made objections to his own assumptions! Of the three objec- tions which he " knows " I shall make, I propose only touching the first as to "the existence of God." And I notice this merely to say that far from offering any ob- jection, lam more than half inclined to make the same assumption with him. But I shall most decidedly object to his assuming that the God of nature and the anthro- pomorphic God of the Jews are one and the same. I should indeed, be sorry to degrade my conception of the "Supreme" by midi an association. The God of the Bible is said to have created man in His own image. The reverse I believe to be the case. My opinion is that man created this God after his own image, with most of his own attributes, passions, and failings. I cannot bring myself to imagine the Supreme committing an error and repenting Himself" that he had done it! Now whatever we may think about this imaginary vacillating deity as the source of what inspiration there may be in the Bible, I feel great repug- nance in attributing to the originator of the universe any part, either as Author or Editor, in the production of a work so distinctly human in its composition and its errors. Upon no reasonable supposition can this "Power not ourselves" be conceived to have lent itself to the production of this heterogeneous conglomeration of phy- sical misstatements,—more or less moral maxims—gro- tesquely absurd and objectless, miraculous interferences, and disturbances of the laws of nature, futile attempts to prove one thing by demonstrations of something else. In short I think the believers must have formed a very low estimate of the literary and editorial abilities of their deity if they think he permitted the perpetration and per- petuation of such a blundering account of his own work. In the penultimate paragraph cf his first letter, " has done for me what I have never been able to do for myself, i.e., classified, labelled, and pigeon-holed me as an Agnostic, and tells me that, as such, I am disqualified from deciding what is and what is not a Revelation. But being an Agnostic—accepting the title for the nonce—does not destroy such abilities as a man may have far literary criticism or disqualify him for com- paring: the idea of revelation or inspiration with the other incongruous and incompatible ideas and assertions in the same pages. From one not knowing to one knowing it is a fair question :—" Where does the inspiration come in " ? I have asked it before, but as yet have had no answer, except in the Irish way of asking another question. I am quite aware that Euclid's definition of a poinp and ' line are self-destructive. A thing which has neither breadth nor thickness must be a non-existent, and the end of it can be no other than nothing. But it is well understood that the definition as it stands wants quali- fying by the addition of the words "least possible." And this everyone supplies for himself, if he wishes to bring it within a sphere of practical geometry. But if we found Euclid affirming that parallel lines would meet, if continued far enough, we should:not place much confidence in the succeeding propositions. And this not- withstanding any claim that might be made as to his being an inspired writer and his book the book of truth which it is—the book of Demonstrative Truths, between which and the Book of Assertions I draw no further parallel. Finally does not the I. Genesis, supposing it to be original and not a copy of an earlier fable, do not the facts of its containing accounts of the origin of man and of things prior to his appearance on earth neces- sarily involve the claim to Divine inspiration? And if so, is that claim valid ? I would gladly receive an answer to these queries in the spirit in which they are asked— that of an earnest, if mistaken, enquirer.—Yours, &c. JOHN PEERS, The Haws, Feb. Ist, 1891.

MR. JOBS GANDY AND THE FERNLEY LECTURE. Sir,—l had no idea that a second letter upon the above subject would have been necessary. The issue was clear and distinct; Mr. Gandy affirmed that Pro- fessor Beet "makes the deliberate statement" that the gospels "were not written by their reputed authors— Matthew, Mark, Luke and John." I replied that Mr. Beet says no such thing; and now my friend changes his ground and tells us that he gave "what he conceived to be the only construction that can be put upon his words." The reply to this is that his "only construction" is an obvious fallacy. It is not the same thing to say that a book is anonymous and therefore its reputed author is not or could not be known. A popular work was issued in this country over forty years ago called " Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation" with no name attached; but the author who had sore reason to preserve his incognito could net do so, and id! the world knows that it was due to the pen of one of the Chambers Brothers. Thus the reputed author was long well-known, though his work was issued without any name attached. Now my friend had no right to put a construction upon Mr. Beet's words, which neither reason nor fact could warrant. How is it that he never notices my reference to page 99 of the book in which Mr. Beet distinctly affirms, that the Ist Epistle of John and the Gospel now hearing his name "are undoubtedly .from the same pen? The fact is that Mr. Gandy entirely misses the whole drift of Professor Beet's excellent work. It was not the writer's intention to prove directly the authorship of the Evangelical writings, but to prove the truth of the Gospel of Christ—as the good tidings the world specially needed. When he comes to the question of the docu- ments he begins with the acknowledged and indisputable Epistles of St. Paul and shows how perfectly the Gos- pel narratives are in harmony with the writings of the Apostle, and the meaning is simply this—no matter whether the Gospels are anonymous or not, the absolute truth of the narrative is unquestionable since they cor- respond so eviden`ly with the history and teachings of a man whose writings the world is compelled to accept as genuine and authentic. Mr. Gandy may therefore modify the very jubilant spirit with which he quotes Professor Beet's words that the names attached to the Gospel, do but" embody a very ancient tradition." Mr: Beet's purpose and method was not to examine and set forth how absolutely true this" ancient tradition " was. He choose a short and readier way to his end ; and had my friend given a closer attention to his argument he would have experienced an " opening of his eyes" corn- , pared with which his former enlightenment would seem like unto the man's who said he saw men as treesi walking." But I am warned, Mr. Editor not to trespass beyond a certain space, and will be brief. I would like to ask Mr. Gandy to transfer his reading to translations of the Christian literature of the second century, and to compare his own loose statements with actual facts. He will meet with a,fine old figure, Irenneus who about A.D. 177 wrote a work now extant, in which ' he may read the following passage :—" Matthew among the Jews wrote a Gospel in their own language. Mark also the disciple and in- terpreter of Peter delivered to us in writing the things that had been preached by Peter; and Luke the companion of Paul, put down in a book the Gospel preached by him (Paul). Afterwards John, the disciple of the Lord, who also leaned on his breast, likewise pub- lished a Gospel whilst he dwelt in Ephesus in Asia." Now, I must ask my friend to understand that this testi- mony goes back to the earlier part of the 2nd century A.D. 101 to 150, and is substantially the very testimony of Polycarp, a disciple of St. John the Apostle; for Ireumus was a disciple of Polycarp. So that between the Apostle St. John and Irenieus there only stands one man, from whom Tremens would receive all information as to the writers of the four Gospels. A fragment in Eusebius, the ecclesiastical historian—is quoted from a then extant work—(between A.D. 264 and 337) of Papias. Now who was Papias? He was born about A.D. 70, was a com- panion of Polycarp—and became Bishop of Hierapolis. He knew two of the immediate disciples of Christ, whom he named Presbyter John (not the apostle) and Aristion. In this quotation Papias tells us that Presbyter John said "Mark having become the interpreter of Peter wrote down accurately whatever he remembered—that was ,either said or done by Christ." Speaking in his own name, Papias further says "Matthew composed the Oracles in his own language and each one interpreted them as he could." Thus a testimony from the apostolic age from one who lived to about A.D. 165, when he was martyred by Marcus Aurelius—and from Irenceus —who wrote a few pars later A.D. 177, shows how impossible "the ancient tradition" could be other than absolutely true. By the year 177 the wt.ole Cliurch of Christ—from

Jerusalem to Antioch, from Asia Minor to Gaul, from Alexandria to Rome received our Gospels under the names of their reputed authors—and not until long ages after- wards was their authenticity ever questioned. The attempt is too late now, and even such a consummate sceptic as Renan has been compelled to yield to the force of evidence and to admit that all our gospels are the genuine productions of their reputed authors, and has furthermore added his testimony to that of all his- tory—that the Acts of the Apostles—is the undoubted work of St. Luke, the companion of Paul, and the author of the third Gospel. I quotefrom Dr. Wage's little work on the authenticity of the four Gospels p.p. 18 and 31, and recommend my friend to study this small tract in conjunction with Dr. Kennedy's" Gospels, their age and authorship," and he will find a sufficient answer to his unfounded remarks about Pentecost, and that all his ob- jections to the authority of the Apostles and St. Paul's teaching are utterly worthless. Let me close with a word to my old friend Mr. John Peers. He has been "tempting some of us "—so he says —" who annually transport our bodies to the sea-side for change of air and scenery to do something of the sort for the mind, to lift it out of the ruts of every day life,and range untrammelled over the world of extraneous thought." Excellent advice certainty, but rather late in the day since, speaking for myself, it was taken from better masters long years ago. But let me say that life is too short to be fighting the same battles over again, and against old weapons which have been worsted in a thousand fights. I don't object to range " untrammelled " within practical spheres; but I have no inclination for expeditions to the Moon with Jules Verne, and am not emulous of following our adventurous Peers into regions of empty air after the fashion of Mother Shipton, on nothing more substantial than a broomstick.—Yours Sze. • Penketh, 30th January, 1891
JOHN DIGNUM.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1891.
INQUEST AT NORTHWICH ON AN EARLESTOWN MAN.

On Monday afternoon Mr. Henry Churton held an inquest at the Northwich Infirmary, on the body of Michael Wall, aged 30 years, of Earlestown, who died the previous afternoon from the effects of fall- ing into a stoke-hole of a boiler house, on Saturday night. Dr. Reilly in his evidence spoke of the in- juries, and stated that during Saturday night the man's temperature rose to 104. A juror then asked if the nurse should not have been sent for medical assistance, so that he could have seen before one o'clock on Sunday. The Coroner expressed the opinion, seeing the staff was an honorary one, that they should have full confidence in them. Then a heated argument took place between the Coroner and several members of the jury as to their right of asking questions. Later on the nurse was asked a query, and instead of its being ans- wered by her, the Coroner said he saw nothing whatever in the question, and pointed out that the man became comatose three hours before his death,remarking—"Per- haps you do not know what comatose means ?" The juror said perhaps not; but he wanted an answer to his question.—The Coroner then charged the juror with wasting time, and urged that there was nothing to indi- cate but that the man died from the effects of a pure ac- cident. After some further warm discussion, a juror expressed the opinion that it was unnecessary for twelve, men to be caned together it they were not to . satisfy themselves by asking questions relating to the cause of death. The foreman having expressed the opinion that it would be well in future to allow witnesses to answer questions direct, a verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.

div.head: AN ALLEGED SCANDAL AT NEWTON.
div.p: AN ALLEGED SCANDAL AT NEWTON.

This week gossips at Newton have been provided with food sufficently amply to satisfy "Mrs. Grundy." It was currently reported, on Monday moming,that the:wife of a certain clereial gentleman, at Newton, had eloped with some swain who is not atresident at Newton. From the inquiries which have been made it turns out that no elopement has taken place, although it is true that the lady in question has taken her departure from the martial roof, leaving her husband and children behind. It appears the root of the mischief lies in the advent, some months ago, of a gentleman to Newton, who took up his residence with a relative. As the story goes, he fell sick, and, on the invitation of the rela- tive, the wife assisted in the nursing of the sick man. Ultimately the invalid zecovered, but it ap- pears he still required an amount of attention, and so the assistance continued. The husband must have seen how matters were going, and a certain amount of unpleasantness has resulted, until last week, the wife left home, ostensibly to go to Preston, but it turns out she did not go there. The matter has so affected the unfortunate husband, that he has re- signed the post he held at Newton, and will pro- bably leave the parish: - moet-likerly-raore win be heard of the case in the law courts.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST AN EARLESTOWN MAN.
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST AN EARLESTOWN MAN.

At the Birkenhead Police Court, on ,Tuesday, before Mr. Preston, a young man named Charles Wilson, of Newton Common, Earlestown, was charged by warrant with stealing £ll 145., the moneys of Mr. J. B. Delany, cabinetmaker, Conway- st. He was also charged with embezzling .E 2 13s. Bd., £3 125., and .£2 35., the moneys of his employer, Mr. J. B. Dalany. Mr. J. T. Thompson apoeared for the prosecution, and Mr. R. B. Moore on behalf of the prisoner. Mr. Thompson said the pri- soner's defalcations in all amounted to between £5O and £6O. He understood Mr. Moore was going to ask his worship to deal with the case summarily, but, looking at the serious nature of the offence, he (Mr. Thompson) would ask him to send the prisoner for trial at the sessions. where he would no doubt receive a greater punishment than his worship could inflict in such a case. Mr. Delany said the prisoner had been in his employ about fifteen months, first as time- keeper, and afterwards he had charge of the cash. On Monday morning, the 24th December, after prisoner had been absent on the previous Saturday he asked him for the balance of his cash for the previous week, but he replied he was not quiet ready, but would let him have it after dinner. After he (Mr. Delany) returned from his own dinner he, learned that in the meantime prisoner had gone out, and he had not since returned. After his disappearance his defalcations were discovered, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. In reply to Mr. Moore, Mr. Delaney said when prisoner came to his place he offered Ins services for a guinea a week, which he paid him for four or five weeks, when his salary was raised to 255. A short time afterwards it was increased to 30s. He got a good character with the prisoner when he .engaged him. Evidence of the apprehension of the prisoner in London being. given by Inspector Moore, to whom he admitted his guilt. Mr. A. B. Moore said the prisoner would plead guilty, and he asked his worship to deal with him himself. His Worship said the prisoner did not come into court with clean hands, as he hid been in trouble before.—Mr. Moore said that on that occasion he was not sent to gaol, but was fined £5 and costs. It was found that he was really not the person responsible for the meney he was then charged with embezzling, thougly he was paying the amount off at the rate of 10s. whilst he was with Mr. Delany. The fact was that he was at that time travel- ling in Lancashire and Wales for a firm at £1 a week, and deducted his expenses from the money he received from the customers, and it was in connection with these deductions.that he got into trouble.—His Worship did not think it was a case liecould deal with, and as a warn- ing to others in the prisoner's position he would have to send him for trial. The prisoner was then committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions.

LORD NAPIER OF MAGDALA.

at the conclusion of which, having attained the rank of major,he was selected by the late Sir Henry Lawrence for the responsible post of Engineer to the Durbar of Lahore. After further promotion to the rank of colonel, he was appointed Chief Engi- neer under the new Punjab administration, when he was enabled to carry out his long-cherished plans for covering that almost trackless country with ar- teries of military and commercial highways, after constructing magnificent canals destined to fertilise the arid Dooab, and eventually to cause the con- struction of numerous public buildings, barracks, &c., requisite to the efficient administration of the province. During the mutiny of 1857 he served in the capacity of chief engineer with the army of Sir Colin Campbell, and the part he played in the sup- pression ot the rebellion greatly enhanced his pre- viously high reputation. It was he, who at the siege of Lucknow planned that bridging of the Goomtee river, which exercised so great an influence on the operations for the overthrow of the enemy, and he was afterwards appointed to the command of the force employed to destroy the rebels reunited under Tantia Topee ; but on Sir Hugh Rose claim- ing the execution of the task, Colonel Napier acted as his second in command. He served as second in command under Sir Hope Grant in the brief but brilliant Chinese war, and in 1860 he was made Major-General, and received the honour of knight- hood. The most remarkable military undertaking in the career of Lord Napier was the war in Abys- sinia, undertaken in 1870, to liberate certain per- sons held captive by King Theodore. He achieved a brilliant success. Theodore was thoroughly de- feated in an engagement on the heights of Islamjie, April 10th, 1868, and soon after released his pri- soners. The English commander followed up this victory by the storming of Magdala on the 13th, when Theodore, in despair, committed suicide.. On Sir Robert Napier's return to England in July, he received the thanks of Parliament ; the sum cf £2,000 per annum was settled on him and his next heir in consideration of his services ; and he was elevated to the peerage by the title of Baron Napier of Magdea ; and received other marks of honour. In January, 1870, he suceeded Sir Win. Mansfield, as commander-in-chief of the forces in India; he was appointed Governor of Gibraltar in 1876 ; and in 1878 he was selected by the Government to be the commander-in-chief of the English expeditionary force in the event of this country declaring wkr against Russia—a contingency which was avertgd by the Treaty of Berlin. At the time of his death— which took place on the 12th January, last year— Lord Napier was Constable of the Tower. A public funeral was accorded him in St. Paul's.

The Napiers are famous, both as fighters and writers, in the annals of British war, and the sub- ject of this obituary was early destined to follow the ime career as so many others , ! the illustrious family to t)thich he belonged. He was a son of Major C. F. Napier, the Royal Artillery, and as born in Ceylon, in 1810. Le entered the corps of the // • \.\ Bengal Engineers in 1828, an Linction in the Sutlej campaign,

div.head: AN ORPHANAGE ON FIRE.
div.p: AN ORPHANAGE ON FIRE.

PARIS, THURSDAY MORNING.—A private telegram re- ceived here from Moscow states that an asylum for orphans in that city has been destroyed by fire, and that nine children, inmatas of the institution, perished in the flames. Some other parsons had vary narrow escapes.
ANOTHER OUTBREAK OF PLEURO- PNEUMONIA.

We understand that there has been another out- break of pleuro-pneumonia at Padgate, the disease having this time broken out on the farm ot Mr. Cox, butcher. The cattle on the premises have been slaughtered, one—a bull—being shot.
DISASTER IN AMERICA, EIGHTEEN MINERS DROWNED.

A Dalziel telegram from Hazleton, Pa., dated Wednes- day, states that 25 miners in the employ of the J.C. Hayden Company at Jeanville, two miles from this place, were drilling a mine yesterday when one of them struck a vast body of water. In a few moments, the entire slope was flooded and the gang was overwhelmed by a terrific rush of water. Only six men out of the 25 es- caped. The accident is charged to the negligence of -the mine inspectors, who failed to tell the miners of the presence of the body of water and to warn them to ob- serve proper care. .
Another similar accident is reported from Nanticoke, where a mine was flooded owing to a collapse of a por- tion of the workings. Tlaree.persons were drowned.
NEW YORK, TITURSDAY.—The mining accident at Jeane- vine, Pennsylvania is fully confirmed. Eighteen miners were drowned by die flood of water which broke into the workings.
SUDDEN DEATH IN A PUBLIC-HOUSE,
MAJOR EDMUND BARTTELOT.

Major Barttelot, was the son of Sir William Barttelot, ,nd was born on March 28, 1839. lie served in the Afghan and Egyptian campaigns, and afterwards joined the Emin Pasha expedition under Stan- ley. It was while acting as commandment of the rear column of the expedition that ,e was killed at Yambuya, on 'uly 19, 1888, under circum- ances which have since

well-known writer dealing in characteristically vigorous languaga with the revelations which were made towards the end of last year, and which so closely affected the reputa- tions of those who took part in tilt relief expedition, remarks that in "November a mephitic fog from tile Yambuya camp blotted everything else out save its own intolerable malodorous stench. Mr. Stanley left Major Barttelot and Mr. Jameson in charge of his rear column of some 400 natives, and it is the publication of the stories of what went on in this camp which has practically destroyed all the pride we had been taking in the Story of the Emin Relief Expedition. It is a long and terrible tale, full of unredeemed brutality, in which the conduct of our countrymen does not shine by contrast with that of the Africans. Of Major Barttelot it is charitable to assume that he was more or less mad, and perhaps the heaviest censure that Mr. Stanley incurs .is for having put such a madman in charge of human lives. His record was not unknown. The only good resulting from the whole of the sad business is the awe which it may strike into the hearts of other young white ruffians whom we breed, equip, and let loose to slay and flog and violate the unfortun- ate aborigines."
MR. GLADSTONE'S SPEECH ON THE DISABILITIES BILL.

The " Star " says :—Everyone who listened to Mr. Gladstone's speech admitted that it was one of the best and most eloquent he has ever delivered. Wednesdays are dull, droary days in the House, whqn the most notable feature of the Assembly is empty benches, but there has rarely been such a Wednesday. The House was densely crowded, and all the accommodation for visitors was taken up before he was well started with his magnifiCent speech. Few speeches that Mr. Glad- stone has delivered in the House were so full of varied styles of 'oratory-. Now he struck resonant blows upon the brass-bound box before him ; then, with a smile as "child-like and bland," he asked the Tories to put themselves in an awkward position by cheering. Once he clapped his hands in the course of a strenuous sen- tence. But it was in his allusion to the death of Mr. Bradlaugh that Mr. Gladstone thrilled the House.
CONGRATULATIONS.

Mr. Gladstone on Thursday morning received numerous congratulations upon the remarkable speech delivered by him on Wednesday in the House of Com- mons. The right lion, gentleman has not been incon- venienced by the physical strain upon him, and rose on Thursday as early as usual. He goes at the week end on a visit to Dollis Hill until Monday.

div.head: AT \FARRINGTON.
div.p: AT \FARRINGTON.

On Wednesday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, de- puty coroner, held an inquest at the police station, touching the sudden death of James Rohan,aged 35, at the Pelican Vaults, Buttermarket-st.,on Monday. The evidence was of the following substance. The deceased had lodged with Mrs. Lofthouse in Bank- St., for for four or five years, and had been ailing for the past fortnight, going on the Friday to see Dr. Joseph. He left home between six and seven o'clock on Monday morning, and was seen by his landlady about 11 that morning with his brother and another man. The deceased had it appeared insured his life five or six years previously, but when out of em- ployment, he being a bricksetter's labourer by call- ing, had given Mr. Allen landlord of the Pelican,his policy to pay up, but had never mentioned to his brother or his landlady about being insured. The deceased used to do work at the Pelican Vaults, but got no pay, receiving his meals and the like, he having been known to Mr. and Mrs. Allen for some 16 years. She had given him gruel on Saturday and Sunday last, but on Monday, at his request gave him ham' ind eggs for breakfast, meat and potatoes for dinner, and a glass of beer and a small brandy during the day. He became much worse on Monday, and Mrs. Allen sent for the doctor, but he was cut. Dr. Joseph when he saw the deceased on Friday found him to be suffering from premonitory symptoms of delirium tremens, and the deceased himself admitted that he had been drinking, though all the wit- nesses except the medical man, denied that he was ad- dicted to excess in this respect. Dr. Joseph told the deceased he must have sleep and light food, and subse- quently told Mr. Allen, who called about the deceased on Saturday, and whom the witness also saw on Sunday, the same thing, but told the Coroner he was not sure whether he gave Mr. Allen explicit directions as to the food, ex- pressing however a decided opinion that ham and eggs, beer, and brandy ought never to have been given to the deceased, who it seemed had been having gruel only, on Saturday and Sunday.—Dr. Joseph also expressed the opinion that death, which took place about half-past one on Monday afternoon, was due to syncope, following delirium tremens. The Coroner said there appeared to be nothing suspicious in the case, but the facts of the man dying in a public-honse under, such circumstances,. and the publican holding a policy of insurance for £lB 155., on his life were abundant grounds for the inquiry. As to supplying the man with ham and eggs when the doctor had prescribed light food it was not surprising that he should die after this.—A juror said if a man had been having gruel two days it was natural he should want something substantial ; and it was mistaken kind- ness on Mrs. Allen's part to give him it.—At the request of the jury Mr. Allen was called. He said the doctor had merely told him to give the deceased nourishment and he should not think that meant gruel. Witness had held the insurvice policy 5 years, but for no benefit of his own. The man had been practically living with him and the money would pay for his burial, his keep, and one thing and another.—ln reply to the coroner Mr. Allen said he was willing to allow the benefit of the policy to go to the deceased's relatives,and the coroner called in the brother and informed him this. The witness con- tended most strenuously that the deceased had nothing like delirium tremens, but thought he had died from breaking up of the constitution,though admitting that he had never seen a man in delirium tremens.—The coroner said if he had it would have perhaps made him more careful than he had been.—The jury after a quarter of an hour's animated consultation gave in a verdict to the coroner, who on being asked by a pressman what it was read out the following Died from neglect possibly .caused through drink," but expressed his inability to understand it. Subsequently it was amended as follows: —" That the deceased died from general decay, possibly caused through drink."

LATEST NE WS.

THE CREWE MURDER. ---- George Davies, one of the brothers convicted of mur- dering his father near Crewe, has been removed from Stafford to Chatham. THE LATE SCOTCH STRIKE. Yesterday, at Greenock, Alexander Scott was sent to prison for thirty days for threatening a signalman during the recent strike. CHARGED WITH MANSLAUGHTER. A coroner's jury at Jarrow yesterday found George Stock, engraver, guilty of the manslaughter of his eighteen weeks old child, by neglecting it so that it died. A SECOND STEAMER SUNK. The steamer Drumhendrie, of Glasgow, was sunk at the mouth of the Mersey soon after midnight on Thurs- day with the London steamer Knutsford. The crew were saved by a river boat. RESIGNS HIS CANDIDATURE. Sir Charles Tennant, till now candidate for Peebles and Selkirk, has retired from the position, feeling him- self out of sympathy with the section of electorate likely to support him by reason of his position as vice-chairman of the North British Railway. BIG RAILWAY DIVIDENDS. The Press Association is officially informed that the directors of the Midland Railway Company will recom- mend to the proprietors a dividend on ordinary stock for the past half-year at the rate of 7 per cent. per annum, carrying forward £70,000. The dividend of the North Eastern Railway Co. was yesterday at York, declared as 8/ per cent.

div.head: CARDIFF STRIKE.
div.p: THE CARDIFF STRIKE.

The strike at the Cardiff Docks continues. The Car- diff Trades' Council have resolved to break down the federation movement. The ship Bluejacket was taken to Newport Docks, there to discharge. The Bute Dock Company have issued a notice to their workmen requir- ing all persons in their employ to give due notice before leaving their employment, on pain of prosecution.
A SWISS AVALANCHE. SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE.

BERNE, FRIDAY.—An avalanche has fallen near Reuti Glanus, overwhelming twenty-two woodcutters who were at work in a wood below. About ten of the men have been rescued alive, and some dead bodies have been recovered. The search continues, but there is no hope that any of those hitherto undiscoverd will bei found alive.
ANOTHER RAILWAY MYSTERY. MURDER AND MUTILATION OF A GIRL.

On Thursday night a guard, walking along the Mid- land Railway, near Child's Hill, Cricklewood, London, found the mutilated body of a young girl apparently about 15 years of age. The face was cut away, both legs and one arm were cut off, and the brains were scattered about the rails. There was a wound in the back that had apparently been caused by a stab. The line at this part is protected by a very high fence and rtms near some meadows. It is difficult to explain how the body came to be upon the railway.

div.head: DENMARK SAFE.
div.p: THE DENMARK SAFE.
NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—The liner Denmark, reported disabled at sea, arrived here to-day under her own steam.
THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS IN ITALY.

ROME, FRIDAY.—RoyaI decr-e-ei-Ti-a]ve'jji;t-1;e-e.n pub- lished, accepting the resignation of Signor Crispi's Cabinet, and entrusting Marquis Di Rudini with the formation of a new Ministry. The Marquis conferred with the King this morning. • A COUNCILLOR MURDERED BY HIS DAUGHTER.

PARIS, FRIDAY.—A shocking tragedy is reported from Blois Francois, Saul. A municipal councillor of that city was to-day shot dead by his daughter, who fired five shots at him with a revolver. Having committed the crime the murderess surrendered to the police.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at quarter past four.
The House went into Committee on the Custody of Children Bill, after a brief discussion raised by Lord Morris on the principle of the bill it passed as amended through committee.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. SANITARY HElitil.ATlONS.—Upon motion for the appoint- ment of Police and Sanitary Regulations Comrnittee.Mr. H. FOWLER pointed out the desirability of preventing local authorities from bringing forward private bills for purposes now covered by provisional orders. Mr. MT- CHIE concurred, and commented upon recent great im- provement of the sanitary condition of provincial towns consequent upon increased expenditure. After further debate the Committee was appointed, and Mr. Fowler's resolution to carry out the purpose of his speech was adopted.
- HOME RULE A.LL ROUND.-Mr. CLARKE gave notice for this day four weeks of a motion for Home Rule in Eng- land, Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

TITHES BILL, &c.—Mr. SMITH, replying to Mr. Glad- stone, said the Tithes Bill would be considered on Mon- day instead of Mr. Morley's motion on Irish Government. If the Tithes Bill was not finished before Thursday Mr. Morley's motion must stand over. AN ANOMALOUS FRANCHISE.—IipOLI motion to go into Committee of Supply Mr. JAMES ROWLANDS moved that the Government should abolish the Anomalous Franchise of liveryinen of the city of London. The . HOME SECRETARY opposed the resolution. After observations from Mr. Pickersgill and Mr. J. Stuart and others the resolution was rejected by 148 to 120. The House counted out at a quarter-past seven.

The proposed new assessments if adoPted by them would amount to—gross £7,759 158., rate' able £6,594, an increase of gross £477 14s. rateabler £402, but in this increase there are included nes( assessments to the amount of—gross £202 We., rateable £172. The report was adopted.

CMILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT AT LA.TCHFORD• On Monday and Tuesday and Wednesday evetii ings the children of the Christ Church Infant Sch.° gave an enjoyable and highly successful entertain' ment in the Schoolroom, Wash-lane, which yr,/ crowded on each occasion. The children were very prettily attired. To Miss Warburton and .o_7 pupil teachers belong the credit of having traillel them so effectively. The programme, which we.) 1 a miscellaneous character, opened with a musics bell drill. The seasons—spring, summer, autuMll4 and winter—were personified by four little childrt the singing of whom was very good. A represenla tion of "Little Red Riding Hood" formed an attraei tive part of the proceedings. The chief item i °t nterest in the second part of the entertainMells was the crowning of the May Queen, the varlotl- characters being pleasingly impersonated by scholars. The May-pole dance, by a dozen lat boys and girls, was neatly performed. Vv.: Pr it°: gramme concluded with a national song (in Ch acter) and "God save the Queen."—Over £lO 'fel:. realised for the benefit of the schools by the ON' nights' performance. The entertainment was re' peated last evening in the Parish Room.

div.head: NORTHAMPTON ELECTION.
div.p: THE NORTHAMPTON ELECTION.

The writ for the election, of a member for Nerthamp- toe was received on Thursday, and the Mayor fixed the nomination for Monday, and polling for Thursday next. There will be three candidates :—Mr. Germaine (Con- servative). Mr. Manfield (Gladstonian Liberal), and Dr. Aveling (Labour and Socialist candidate). By an un- usual if not unprecedented coincidence, the election will be followed on the Succeeding day by a municipal con- test owing to the bankruptcy of a Liberal councillor. This also will be on strictly party lines.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The third concert of the season of the Musical Society will be held on Tuesday evensng next. As will be seen from the. programme on another column, the concert on this occasion will be of ex- ceptional interest, inasmuch as the whole of it is undertaken by members of the society. There are several items of interest in the programme, one of these being a string quartette composed by Mr. F. ti Crossley, the conductor of the society.

div.head: CHESTER CATHEDRAL.
div.p: CHESTER CATHEDRAL.

At a meeting of the members and friends of Holy Trinity Literary and Debating Society on Monday evening, Mr. William Owen, A.R.1.8.A., read his paper on "Chester Cathedral." The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, 8.A., presided. The paper was well illus- trated with maps,drawings,&c., whigh ,together with the clear explanations of the lecturer, afforded a very easy means of recognising and differentiating the various styles of archrtecture dealt with, com- prising the Norman, Early English, Decorated, and Perpendicular. In conclusion Mr. Owen paid a tribute to the late Dean Howson, to whose efforts the recent restoration of the Cathedral was due. Mr. Owen strongly advocated the teaching of archi- tecture in our schools, and not only in those of higher grade. A cordial vote of thanks was passed to him, on the proposition of Mr. A. J. Jolley, secon- ded by Mr. H. J. Westbrook, and supported by Mr. William Coates.
THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.

At the meeting of the Warrington Union Assess- ment Committee, held yesterday, the Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton), who is a member of the Lancashire County Council,mentioned that the County Council at the meeting the previous day had been consider- ing the question of the disposal of the sum of money handed over to it by the Government, and which is to be used to further technical education in the county. He said that the County Council desired to render aid to agricultural education, but they felt that they could only in the first instance give assistance to those who were doing something to help themselves. Looking round his own divi- 'sion of Winwick, he did not know of any way by which it was to get a proportion. He believed that steps were being taken to induce Lord Sefton or Lord Derby to call a general county meeting to make some arrangements whereby the agricultural districts of the county may participate in the ad- vantages of the fund. He was of opinion that ar- rangements would be made for the appointment of migratory lecturers who would go to different coun- try districts,and by speech and in other ways endea- vour to advance the knowledge of the people as to the latest scientific improvements in connection with agriculture. Carrati.Ey, Hiab Class Tailor, Bold-et. Warrington.—ildrt.
